cards.n: Reciting the six terms earns nothing on Q2: the rubric rewards showing how a specific choice answers this writer's purpose and audience.
x: writer, audience, purpose, context, exigence, message
exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context, message

cards.q: Define message in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The message is the central idea or claim a text communicates: what the writer asserts about the subject. It is one of the six components; the other five (exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context) explain why the message is framed as it is, for whom, and to what end.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + its place among six
cards.n: Stating the message is summary; a Q2 thesis earns the point only when it says how choices convey the message to this audience.

cards.q: Define writer (or speaker) as an element of the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The writer is the person or institution producing the text, together with the identity, experience, expertise, values, and relationship to the audience they bring to it. Those traits shape what the writer can credibly say and how the audience receives it, which is why the exam's headnote identifies the writer.
cards.h: → who + what they bring to the text
cards.n: Biography is not analysis: a detail about the writer earns credit only when tied to a choice it enables, such as an anecdote only this writer could tell.

cards.q: Contrast the author and the speaker of a text.
cards.a: The author is the real person who wrote the text; the speaker is the voice or persona constructed inside it. Usually they align, but an author may adopt a speaker whose views or tone differ from their own, as in satire, so analysis attributes choices to the author and attitudes to the speaker.
cards.n: Reading a satirical narrator's proposal as the author's sincere view inverts the purpose; ask whose voice is speaking and what the author wants us to think of it.

cards.q: Recall what each letter of SOAPSTone stands for.
cards.a: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone. It is a classroom checklist, not CED language: the CED's rhetorical situation is exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context, and message, so add exigence and message when you use it to read a passage.
cards.h: → six words, then what it leaves out
cards.n: SOAPSTone is not in the CED; using its letters as essay paragraphs produces a list, not a line of reasoning.
x: Speaker Occasion Audience Purpose Subject Tone

cards.q: Apply the rhetorical situation to a photograph or political cartoon.
cards.a: Treat the image as an argument: identify its maker (writer), the viewers it targets (audience), what prompted it (exigence), when and where it appeared (context), what it claims (message), and what it wants viewers to think or do (purpose). Then read framing, caption, labels, symbols, exaggeration, and juxtaposition as choices serving that purpose.
cards.h: → six components, then visual choices as rhetoric
cards.n: In the synthesis essay, a chart or cartoon cited as decoration earns nothing; say what it argues and how its design serves that argument.

cards.q: Define the choice-effect-purpose chain in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: It is the unit of commentary: name a specific rhetorical choice, explain its effect on the intended audience, then connect that effect to the writer's purpose in this situation. It turns the enduring understanding (writers make strategic choices based on their situation) into a sentence a reader can score.
cards.n: Commentary that stops at the effect ('this creates emotion') floats; the link to purpose and audience is what Row B rewards.

cards.q: Identify the six components of the rhetorical situation in this headnote: 'In October, after a wildfire destroyed the only public library in a mountain town, a retired schoolteacher who had volunteered there for thirty years wrote a letter to the county newspaper urging residents to approve a bond measure on the November ballot to rebuild it. She argues that the library was the town's only free indoor public space.'
cards.a: Exigence: the fire that destroyed the library, with a bond vote weeks away. Purpose: to persuade residents to vote yes. Audience: county newspaper readers who vote, including people who never used the library. Writer: a retired teacher and thirty-year volunteer. Context: a small town after a fire, before an election. Message: the library was the town's only free indoor public space and must be rebuilt.
cards.n: Naming 'the library' as the exigence confuses subject with trigger: the exigence is the fire plus the coming vote.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical triangle.
cards.a: The model showing the three interlocking elements of any rhetorical act: the speaker (ethos), the audience (pathos), and the subject or message (logos). A change in one reshapes the others.
cards.n: The triangle maps appeals onto positions: ethos lives with the speaker, pathos with the audience, logos with the subject.

cards.q: Explain why a rhetorical analysis should read the passage's headnote before the passage itself.
cards.a: The headnote supplies the writer, audience, occasion, and date, the components that make choices explainable. Knowing that a speaker is a surgeon addressing new nurses lets commentary say why her anecdote about a night shift persuades them, rather than only noting that she tells a story.
cards.h: → headnote names writer, audience, context → choices can be tied to them → commentary instead of summary
cards.n: 'The headnote gives background' is too vague; say which components it supplies and which choice they help explain.
o: The headnote is the exam's shortcut to the rhetorical situation, so skipping it forces the essay to guess at audience and purpose.
Row B commentary must explain how choices work for a specific audience, and the headnote is where that audience is named.

w.a: The headnote is important because it gives background information about the passage.
w.why: vague; never says which components it supplies or how they serve analysis

w.a: You should read the headnote so you can summarize the speaker's life in your introduction.
w.why: biography is summary, not analysis of choices

w.a: The headnote tells you which rhetorical devices the writer is going to use.
w.why: false; it gives the situation, not the devices

cards.q: Explain why the same sentence can be effective in one rhetorical situation and ineffective in another.
cards.a: Effectiveness is measured against a purpose and an audience, not in the abstract. A blunt statistic can persuade a budget committee that needs numbers yet feel cold at a memorial, where the audience needs its loss acknowledged; the sentence is the same, the situation is not.
cards.h: → effect depends on purpose, audience, context → change the situation → change the effect
cards.n: Judging a sentence 'good writing' in the abstract earns nothing; effectiveness is always relative to this audience and purpose.
o: Because writers choose with a particular exigence and audience in mind, a choice is a good one only relative to those conditions.
Audiences bring different beliefs, values, and needs, so the same words meet different expectations in different settings.

w.a: Some sentences are simply better written than others, no matter where they appear.
w.why: ignores that the rhetorical situation defines effectiveness

w.a: A sentence is effective whenever it uses strong rhetorical devices.
w.why: devices have no effect independent of purpose and audience

cards.q: Explain why a writer's identity can change how an audience receives the same message.
cards.a: The writer is one component of the situation: who speaks shapes what the audience assumes about motive and expertise. A plea for safer crosswalks from a parent whose child was struck carries lived authority; the same words from a paving contractor invite suspicion of profit, so the audience weighs them differently.
cards.h: → writer's identity → audience infers motive and expertise → credibility → acceptance
cards.n: Saying 'the writer is credible' without naming the trait and the audience's inference is a label, not an explanation.
o: Audiences judge a message partly by its source, so a writer's experience, stake, or role can lend or cost credibility.
The writer's relationship to the audience, insider or outsider, sets how much trust the message starts with.

w.a: The identity of the writer does not matter because a good argument stands on its own.
w.why: ignores that audiences weigh credibility and motive

w.a: A famous writer is always more persuasive than an unknown one.
w.why: overgeneralizes; fit to this audience, not fame, matters

cards.q: Define exigence.
cards.a: The exigence is the part of a rhetorical situation that inspires, stimulates, provokes, or prompts a writer to create a text: a specific event, problem, or condition, such as a new policy, a crisis, or a published attack, that makes the writer respond now.
cards.n: Exigence is the trigger, not the topic: 'education' is a subject; 'the board's vote to cut the arts budget' is an exigence.
x: the reason the text was written
what prompts the writer to write

cards.q: Contrast exigence and occasion.
cards.a: The exigence is what prompts the text (a problem, event, or condition demanding a response); the occasion is the specific event, time, and place where the text is delivered, part of its context. A town's grief and anger after a factory fire is the exigence; the memorial service where the mayor speaks is the occasion.
cards.n: Students collapse these; on an MC question asking for the exigence, the choice naming the ceremony or venue is usually the trap.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to apologize (atone).
cards.a: To acknowledge a wrong, accept responsibility, and express regret in order to repair damaged trust. It is the purpose most directly dictated by its exigence, a specific harm the writer caused, which the apology must name precisely for the audience to accept it.
cards.n: A 'mistakes were made' apology hedges responsibility; analysis asks whether the apology's choices answer the specific harm that prompted it.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to justify.
cards.a: To give reasons or evidence that make a past or proposed action appear reasonable, necessary, or fair. Its exigence is usually a challenge (criticism, an investigation, a controversial decision), so the text defends a decision already made rather than winning readers to a new position.
cards.h: → definition + the exigence that calls for it
cards.n: Calling a justification simply 'persuasive' is too loose; name what was challenged and how the reasons answer that challenge.
x: give reasons an action was fair

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to warn.
cards.a: To alert an audience to a danger or likely consequence so that they change course before it arrives. Its exigence is a threat the writer perceives as near and preventable (a flood forecast, a budget shortfall), which is why warnings stress time and consequence.
cards.n: A warning with no preventable outcome is only lament; say what the audience can still do and why the writer thinks the time is now.

cards.q: Identify the exigence of this passage and the words that signal it: 'Last Tuesday, for the third time since March, the Elm Street bridge flooded and a school bus carrying twenty-two children had to turn back through rising water. I am writing to the county commission because the repair it postponed in January can no longer wait.' (a parent's letter to the county commission)
cards.a: The exigence is the third flooding of the Elm Street bridge last Tuesday, which forced a bus of children to turn back, after the commission had postponed the repair. 'Last Tuesday, for the third time since March' marks the prompting event; 'can no longer wait' marks the urgency that makes the parent write now.
cards.n: Answering 'bridge safety' names the subject, not the exigence; the answer must name the specific event that prompted this letter.

cards.q:
Identify the most likely exigence of each text:
1. A principal's letter to parents two days after a student's allergic reaction in the cafeteria
2. An op-ed titled 'Keep the Pool Open,' published the week the parks board posts its budget cuts
3. A graduation speech to nursing students in a year of severe hospital staffing shortages
4. A company statement issued the morning after its app exposed customers' home addresses
5. A scientist's letter to a newspaper after a viral post misreported her study
6. A eulogy for a town's mail carrier of forty years
7. A student editorial after the district eliminated the late bus
8. A mayor's radio address the morning after a flood
9. A coach's email to players after the team's third forfeit for low attendance
10. A petition circulated the day after a popular teacher's contract was not renewed
cards.a:
1 → the allergic reaction, which made parents fear for their children's safety at lunch
2 → the proposed cut that threatens to close the pool
3 → the staffing shortage the graduates are about to enter (the ceremony is only the occasion)
4 → the exposure of customer data and the loss of trust it caused
5 → the misreporting of her findings spreading online
6 → the carrier's death and the town's grief
7 → the elimination of the late bus
8 → the flood's damage and residents' fear and need for information
9 → the third forfeit caused by low attendance
10 → the non-renewal of the teacher's contract
cards.n: For item 3, 'graduation' is the occasion, not the exigence; the exigence is the condition that makes this speech's message necessary.

cards.q: Identify the best description of the writer's exigence: 'When the council voted last night to sell Harmon Field to a developer, it did so without a single public hearing. Families who have played there for sixty years learned of the sale from a sign on the fence this morning.' (A) The rising cost of housing in the city (B) The council's sale of Harmon Field without public input (C) The history of youth sports in the city (D) A sign posted on the fence this morning
cards.a: (B). The prompting event is the council's vote to sell the field without a hearing; the passage opens with it, and every detail (sixty years, a sign on the fence) sharpens its unfairness. (A) is a context the passage never names, (C) is background, and (D) is how families learned of the sale, a detail rather than the cause of writing.
cards.n: Exigence distractors often name a real detail from the passage; the exigence is the event that makes the text necessary, not any fact it mentions.

cards.q: Apply SOAPSTone: explain why it has no separate letter for exigence.
cards.a: SOAPSTone folds the prompting event into Occasion, so it blurs the trigger with the setting. The CED separates them: exigence is what provokes the text, while occasion is part of its context. A reader using SOAPSTone must add exigence deliberately, since the exam asks for it directly.
cards.h: → acronym merges trigger into Occasion → CED separates exigence from context → add it yourself
cards.n: SOAPSTone is a classroom mnemonic, not CED language; the CED's first sample multiple-choice question asks for the writer's exigence.
o: The acronym tracks what is visible on the surface (speaker, occasion, subject), while exigence often has to be inferred from why the text appeared when it did.
Its Occasion slot is meant to cover both the event and the setting, which hides the difference between what prompted the text and where it was delivered.

w.a: SOAPSTone has no letter for exigence because exigence is the same thing as the subject.
w.why: confuses the trigger with the topic

w.a: Exigence does not matter much for analysis, so SOAPSTone leaves it out.
w.why: false; exigence explains why the text and its choices exist

cards.q: Explain why a writer responding to a crisis often names the prompting event in the first sentence.
cards.a: Naming the event states the exigence the audience already feels, so the text's relevance is immediate and the writer shows awareness of what readers are living through. It also makes the call to act timely: the sooner the event is on the page, the sooner the demand seems urgent rather than abstract.
cards.h: → name the event → shared exigence → relevance + urgency → the audience keeps reading
cards.n: 'To grab the reader's attention' is generic; say what naming this event does for an audience already shaken by it.
o: Opening on the event proves the writer is responding to the audience's situation, not delivering a prepared lecture.
Stating the exigence first frames everything that follows as a response to it, so the audience reads each claim as part of a solution.

w.a: Writers name the event first because every essay should start with a hook.
w.why: a formula, not a reason tied to exigence and audience

w.a: Naming the event first is just a way to summarize what happened.
w.why: misses the effect on the audience and the purpose

cards.q: Explain why 'climate change' is a weak answer to the question 'What is this op-ed's exigence?'
cards.a: It names a broad subject, not the specific event that prompted this text. An exigence explains why the writer wrote now: a heat wave that closed schools, a vote to repeal a regulation. Only a specific trigger lets analysis connect the writer's choices to what the audience is reacting to.
cards.h: → subject ≠ trigger → exigence must be specific → only a trigger explains the choices
cards.n: Any answer that could describe a thousand texts on the same subject has not found this text's exigence.
o: The exigence is time-bound and particular, while a subject like climate change could prompt texts in any year.
Analysis needs the trigger because choices such as urgency or a call to act respond to that event, not to the subject in general.

w.a: Climate change is the exigence because it is the main topic of the op-ed.
w.why: equates the topic with the prompting event

w.a: Any major issue in the news counts as an exigence for an op-ed.
w.why: too broad to explain any specific choice

cards.q: Define purpose in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The purpose of a text is what the writer hopes to accomplish with it, and a writer may have more than one purpose in a text. State it as a verb aimed at the audience: to persuade voters to reject the bond, to reassure parents, to shame a board into acting.
cards.h: → CED definition + purpose stated as a verb
cards.n: 'To use rhetorical devices' or 'to inform people about the topic' is not a purpose; name what the writer wants this audience to think, feel, or do.
x: what the writer hopes to accomplish

cards.q: Contrast purpose and message.
cards.a: The message is what the text says, its central claim; the purpose is what the writer wants that message to do to the audience. 'Public libraries are democracy's classrooms' is a message; to persuade council members to restore library funding is the purpose the message serves.
cards.n: A thesis that only restates the message ('she says libraries matter') summarizes; one naming the purpose and the choices that serve it analyzes.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to critique.
cards.a: To evaluate a subject by exposing its flaws or limits against a standard, stated or implied, that the subject fails to meet. A critique judges rather than merely describes, and its audience must accept the standard for the judgment to land.
cards.n: Name the standard the writer measures by; 'she criticizes the policy' leaves out what makes the critique persuasive to this audience.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to satirize.
cards.a: To ridicule a person, institution, or practice through irony, exaggeration, or mockery in order to expose folly or vice and imply the need for reform. The speaker's surface proposal differs from the author's real purpose, the critique the absurdity exposes.
cards.n: Borrows irony from Style: satire has a corrective target; if you cannot name what the author wants changed, you have not found the purpose.

cards.q: Apply the correct purpose verb: a senator recounts a factory closure, then urges passage of a retraining bill.
cards.a: Two purposes, one serving the other: to move the audience by making the closure a human loss, and ultimately to persuade them to support the retraining bill. The anecdote serves the persuasive purpose by turning an abstract policy into consequences for real workers, which the call to pass the bill then answers.
cards.h: → primary + secondary purpose, then how they connect
cards.n: Naming only 'to inform' misses the call to act; a text may have more than one purpose, and the strongest answer ranks them.

cards.q: Contrast a text's stated purpose and its functional purpose.
cards.a: The stated purpose is what a text claims to be doing, such as 'simply presenting the facts'; the functional purpose is what its choices actually accomplish, such as persuading through selected facts and loaded words. Analysis tests the claim against the choices.
cards.h: → claimed aim vs what the choices do
cards.n: A text that announces neutrality while loading its diction is a classic analysis target; quote the loaded words as evidence of the functional purpose.

cards.q: Decide the purpose: a CEO's memo after a data breach names exactly what happened, states who is responsible, and outlines concrete remedies.
cards.a: The dominant purpose is to restore trust by accepting responsibility (an apology in substance), with secondary purposes to inform readers of what happened and to reassure them that remedies are under way. Naming the failure precisely and listing remedies serve all three, since vague language would read as evasion.
cards.n: Real texts blend purposes; name the dominant one and the secondary ones, then show which choice serves which.

cards.q: Identify the writer's purposes in this passage: 'Our doors will close for renovation on June 1. We know this is hard news for the families who visit every Saturday, and we are sorry for the long wait. But the new wing will double the space for children's exhibits, and every gift made this month will be matched by the Harlow Foundation.' (a museum director's letter to members)
cards.a: Three purposes: to inform members of the closure date; to console or apologize to regular families ('we are sorry for the long wait'); and, dominantly, to persuade members to donate, which the 'But' pivot, the promised benefit, and the matching gift serve. The apology comes first so readers are receptive before the request.
cards.h: → each purpose + the words that serve it
cards.n: Stopping at 'to inform' misses the pivot at 'But'; the EK's point is that a text may carry several purposes, one usually dominant.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to persuade.
cards.a: To move an audience to accept a claim, adopt an attitude, or take a specific action by giving them reasons and motives to do so.
cards.n: Persuade is the default guess and the weakest answer; a sharper verb such as warn, unify or mobilize almost always scores better.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to inform.
cards.a: To convey facts or explain a subject clearly to an audience without primarily arguing a contested position, though the selection of facts can still carry a slant worth noticing.
cards.n: Calling a text purely informative is a common misread, so check what the writer chose to leave out before settling on that label.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to inspire.
cards.a: To move an audience toward hope, ambition, or renewed commitment by appealing to shared ideals rather than by presenting new evidence or arguing a contested claim.
cards.n: Inspire and persuade differ in what they ask for: inspire seeks a change in feeling and commitment, persuade a change in position.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to mobilize.
cards.a: To move an audience from agreement to action, giving them a specific, immediate step to take rather than simply changing what they believe.
cards.n: Mobilize goes further than persuade - the audience may already agree; the text asks them to act now.
x: move an audience to act now

cards.q: Explain why a rhetorical analysis thesis must name the writer's purpose, not just restate the topic.
cards.a: Row A rewards a thesis that analyzes the writer's choices, and choices can only be analyzed as means to an end. Naming the purpose (to persuade graduates to take risks) gives the essay a defensible claim and gives each body paragraph a job: showing how a choice serves that purpose.
cards.h: → choices are means to an end → name the end → a defensible claim + a job for each paragraph
cards.n: A device-list thesis fails the same way: it names the tools the writer reached for without naming the goal those tools serve.
o: A topic ('this speech is about perseverance') restates the prompt, which the rubric says earns no thesis point.
Without a purpose, commentary cannot explain why a choice works, so the essay slides into listing devices.

w.a: The thesis should list three devices the writer uses so the reader knows what paragraphs are coming.
w.why: a device list without a purpose is not analysis of choices

w.a: The writer uses many rhetorical strategies to convey her message to the audience.
w.why: restates the prompt, which earns no thesis point

w.a: Naming the purpose is optional as long as the thesis mentions the audience.
w.why: audience without purpose leaves the choices unexplained

cards.q: Explain why stating a purpose with a precise verb ('to shame the board into acting') makes better commentary than 'to persuade.'
cards.a: Nearly every argument aims to persuade, so the general verb explains no particular choice. A precise verb names the effect sought on this audience, which lets commentary show why a specific choice fits: public shame explains why the writer lists the board's broken promises by date.
cards.h: → 'persuade' fits everything → precise verb names the intended effect → choices can be matched to it
cards.n: 'The purpose is to persuade the audience' is true of almost every passage, so it cannot explain why this writer made this choice.
o: A precise purpose verb turns commentary into cause and effect: this choice produces this reaction, which advances this aim.
Readers score commentary that ties a choice to purpose; a vague purpose gives the choice nothing specific to tie to.

w.a: It does not matter which verb you use as long as you mention the purpose once.
w.why: a vague purpose cannot explain specific choices

w.a: 'To persuade' is always the best purpose because arguments persuade.
w.why: true of everything, so it explains nothing

cards.q: Explain why a writer might pursue two purposes at once, such as consoling and calling to action.
cards.a: Audiences often need one thing before they can accept another. Grieving listeners must feel their loss acknowledged before a call to act seems respectful, so the consoling purpose earns the hearing that the persuasive purpose then uses; the first purpose prepares the audience for the second.
cards.h: → audience's immediate need → first purpose meets it → trust → second purpose lands
cards.n: Treating two purposes as the writer being 'unfocused' misreads the text; say how one purpose prepares the audience for the other.
o: Mixed audiences may need different things, so one purpose can serve some listeners while the other serves the rest.
A secondary purpose can remove an obstacle (grief, anger, confusion) that would otherwise block the primary one.

w.a: Writers use two purposes so the essay will be longer and more detailed.
w.why: no link to the audience's needs

w.a: A good writer should only ever have one purpose in a text.
w.why: contradicts the EK, which says writers may have more than one

cards.q: Define audience in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The audience is the readers or listeners a writer intends to reach. In the CED's words, an audience has shared as well as individual beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds, so describe an audience by what it believes, values, and needs, not only by who is present.
cards.n: 'The audience is the people listening' earns nothing; name what they believe, value, or need that the writer's choices address.

cards.q: Contrast primary and secondary audience.
cards.a: The primary audience is the group the writer directly addresses and most wants to move; the secondary audience is anyone else who will receive the text, such as the press, opponents, or later readers. The two may hold different beliefs and needs, so a choice aimed at one can be read differently by the other.
cards.n: Public speeches often argue past the room: the graduates are primary, the parents and press secondary; say which audience a choice is aimed at.

cards.q: Explain what is meant by audience assumptions.
cards.a: Audience assumptions are the beliefs, knowledge, and attitudes a writer takes for granted that the audience already holds, so the text builds on them without arguing for them. They are the shared beliefs and values the EK describes, and a writer who misjudges them leaves the argument resting on ground the audience does not accept.
cards.n: Naming an unstated assumption and showing the argument depends on it is a strong Row B move, and sometimes a Row C one.

cards.q: Identify King's stated audience in Letter from Birmingham Jail based on its opening line, and note who else was really listening.
cards.a: The stated audience is the eight white Alabama clergymen who had published a statement calling his demonstrations 'unwise and untimely'; 'My Dear Fellow Clergymen' addresses them as peers. King wrote knowing a far wider public, including white moderates across the nation, would read the letter, so his choices answer both.
cards.n: Writing to a named audience while expecting a wider one is itself a choice; say which audience a given passage of the letter is aimed at.

cards.q: Define the invoked audience in rhetoric.
cards.a: The invoked audience is the audience a text constructs within itself through its assumptions, address, and references ('fellow parents,' 'those of us who remember the old mill'), whether or not every actual reader fits that profile. Invoking an audience invites readers to adopt the beliefs and values attributed to it.
cards.n: Not a CED term and never asked by name; use it to explain how a writer invites readers into shared values.

cards.q: Contrast the invoked audience and the actual audience of a text.
cards.a: The invoked audience is whom the text's language and assumptions address, such as 'concerned parents'; the actual audience is whoever really reads or hears it, which may be broader and hold individual beliefs the invoked profile ignores. The gap explains why a text can unite some readers and alienate others.
cards.n: A published letter can invoke one small audience while being read by everyone; check whose beliefs each choice assumes.

cards.q: Define the universal audience as a rhetorical concept.
cards.a: An imagined audience of all reasonable people, used as a standard: an argument aimed at it relies on reasoning any thoughtful reader would accept rather than on the particular beliefs of one group. It sits at the opposite end from an audience defined by individual beliefs and backgrounds.
cards.n: Not a CED term; use it to judge whether an appeal persuades broadly or plays only to one group's shared assumptions.

cards.q: Identify one belief the audience likely shares and two individual differences the writer must anticipate: a school board member will speak to a meeting of parents about replacing paper textbooks with tablets next fall.
cards.a: Shared: the parents want their children to learn well and to have fair access to materials. Individual differences: some families lack reliable home internet, so tablets could widen gaps; some parents worry about screen time; some focus on cost as taxpayers. The speaker must honor the shared value while answering each concern.
cards.h: → one shared value + two individual differences
cards.n: Describing the audience as 'parents' is demographics; the EK asks for beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds, shared and individual.

cards.q: Explain why describing an audience only by demographics ('adults in 1963') weakens a rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: Choices work on what an audience believes, values, and needs, not on age or date. 'Adults in 1963' cannot explain why an appeal to religious duty would move them; 'churchgoing moderates who value order' can, so commentary needs the audience's beliefs to connect a choice to its effect.
cards.h: → choices act on beliefs and values → demographics name neither → commentary cannot link choice to effect
cards.n: Rubrics reward understanding of the rhetorical situation; a census description of the audience shows none.
o: The EK defines audience by beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds, so an analysis that omits them has not described the audience.
Two audiences of the same age can hold opposite values, so demographics cannot predict how a choice will land.

w.a: Describing the audience's age and location is enough to show you understand it.
w.why: names who, not what they believe or need

w.a: The audience does not matter much in rhetorical analysis; the devices matter.
w.why: devices have effects only on a particular audience

cards.q: Explain why a writer addressing a divided audience often appeals first to a value the whole audience shares.
cards.a: A shared value (children's safety, fairness) is ground no listener will dispute, so it earns a hearing from both sides before the contested claim. Starting there frames the claim as an application of what everyone already believes, which lowers the resistance of those who disagree.
cards.h: → shared value → no one objects → both sides keep listening → claim framed as following from it
cards.n: 'To connect with the audience' is too vague; name the shared value and why it matters that the whole audience holds it.
o: Opening on common values shows the writer sees the audience as one community, not as allies and enemies.
Disagreement usually concerns means, not ends, so beginning with the shared end narrows the dispute.

w.a: Writers start with shared values because it is polite to agree with people.
w.why: politeness is not the rhetorical effect

w.a: Appealing to shared values means the writer has no real argument.
w.why: the shared value is the premise the argument builds on

cards.q: Explain why a writer addressing an audience with individual differences might acknowledge those differences openly.
cards.a: Naming differences ('some of you drive an hour to work, some of you walk') shows the writer sees each reader's situation, which builds goodwill. It also keeps readers whose needs differ from the majority's from feeling ignored and dismissing the argument as not meant for them.
cards.h: → name the differences → readers feel seen → goodwill + no one opts out
cards.n: Claiming the writer 'relates to everyone' misses the mechanism: specific acknowledgment of individual needs.
o: Acknowledging differences lets the writer answer each group's likely objection before it forms.
An audience that feels its variety is recognized is more willing to accept a common solution.

w.a: Acknowledging differences weakens an argument by showing the audience is divided.
w.why: ignores the goodwill it builds

w.a: Writers mention differences to show off how much they know about the audience.
w.why: no link to acceptance or purpose

cards.q: Define context in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: Context is the set of circumstances in which a writer creates a text, which the CED says includes the time, place, and occasion. It also takes in the historical, cultural, and political conditions of that moment, which shape what the audience already knows and expects, and so which choices will work.
cards.n: Context is a lever, not background filler: use it to explain why a choice would land with this audience at this moment.

cards.q: Define occasion in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The occasion is the specific event or setting at which a text is delivered or published (a commencement, a eulogy, a council hearing, an op-ed page the day after a verdict), part of the text's context along with time and place. Each occasion carries conventions the audience expects.
cards.n: Occasion sets genre expectations; a speaker who breaks them (a warning at a celebration) is making a choice worth analyzing.

cards.q: Define genre as it functions within the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: Genre is the recognized form a text belongs to (eulogy, op-ed, open letter, commencement address, memo), which carries expectations about length, tone, and structure set by the occasion. Readers judge a text against those expectations before they weigh its argument.
cards.n: A writer who breaks genre conventions is making a choice, not an error; name the convention broken and what the break achieves.

cards.q: Contrast constraints and resources within the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: Constraints are elements of the context that limit a writer's choices, such as a five-minute time limit, a formal occasion, or a hostile audience; resources are elements a writer can draw on, such as shared history, a timely event, or existing credibility. The same fact, like a recent tragedy, can be either.
cards.h: → limits vs advantages, with one example each
cards.n: The CED's teaching notes ask how choices reflect 'the constraints and the available means of persuasion'; use the terms to explain a choice, not as labels.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to commemorate.
cards.a: To honor a person, group, or event publicly, affirming shared values and fixing the subject's meaning in collective memory. It is the purpose an occasion such as a memorial, anniversary, or dedication calls for, which is why such texts are formal and communal in address.
cards.h: → definition + the occasions that call for it
cards.n: Commemorative texts are rarely only praise; many turn memory into a charge to the living, a second purpose worth naming.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to console.
cards.a: To comfort an audience experiencing grief or hardship by affirming shared feeling, meaning, or hope rather than arguing a claim. Occasions of loss (a funeral, a vigil, a message after a disaster) call for it, and timing matters: consolation offered too soon or too late misreads the audience's need.
cards.h: → definition + the occasions that call for it
cards.n: Consolation often turns partway through: it comforts first, then asks the grieving audience to carry something forward.

cards.q: Define an elegiac tone and give an example occasion.
cards.a: A mournful, reflective tone suited to loss, blending grief with tribute. Example occasion: a eulogy or a memorial dedication, where the audience expects the speaker to mourn publicly and to honor what the person or community gave.
cards.n: Borrows tone from Style: 'elegiac' is not simply sad; it carries the formal, commemorative quality an occasion of public mourning expects.

cards.q: Identify the time, place, and occasion in this headnote, and describe one choice the context would lead you to expect: 'At 7 a.m. on the first school day after a tornado closed the district for a week, the superintendent posted a two-minute video message on the district website for families.'
cards.a: Time: early morning on the first day back after a week-long closure. Place: the district website, a public online video. Occasion: an update to families as schools reopen after a disaster. Expect brevity and practical priority: the superintendent likely leads with safety and logistics (which buildings are open, where buses run) and brief reassurance, because anxious families need information before reflection.
cards.h: → time, place, occasion + one predicted choice
cards.n: Labeling the three is identification only; the point comes from linking the context to a choice this audience needs.

cards.q: Explain why a message delivered the day after a disaster makes different choices than one delivered on its anniversary.
cards.a: Time changes the audience's needs. The day after, listeners are frightened and need facts, instructions, and reassurance, so plain, brief language fits. A year later they need meaning and remembrance, so reflection, narrative, and a call to honor what was lost fit the occasion.
cards.h: → time changes needs → day after: facts, safety → anniversary: meaning, memory → different choices
cards.n: 'The writer adapts to the situation' names nothing; say what the audience needs at each moment and which choice meets it.
o: The occasion's conventions differ: an emergency update is expected to be practical, a commemoration to be reflective.
Emotion is raw the day after and settled a year later, so appeals that fit one moment would feel wrong at the other.

w.a: Both messages should say the same thing because the disaster is the same.
w.why: ignores that context includes time

w.a: The anniversary speech is longer because the speaker has had more time to write it.
w.why: a practical guess, not a rhetorical reason

cards.q: Explain why a speaker at a graduation can open with a personal anecdote while a writer of a formal report to regulators usually cannot.
cards.a: Each occasion carries conventions. A commencement invites personal reflection and warmth toward graduates, so an anecdote builds connection; a regulatory report is read by officials who expect data, precision, and impersonal register, so an anecdote there would seem unserious and weaken credibility.
cards.h: → occasion sets conventions → ceremony invites the personal → report demands the impersonal → credibility
cards.n: Saying 'reports are boring' misses the point; the occasion's conventions shape what the audience accepts as credible.
o: The graduation audience wants to know the speaker as a person, while regulators want to know the facts are reliable.
Genre expectations are part of context, and breaking them without reason costs the writer authority.

w.a: Anecdotes are always more engaging, so the report writer should use one too.
w.why: ignores the occasion's conventions and audience

w.a: Reports cannot contain stories because that is against the rules of grammar.
w.why: confuses convention with grammar

cards.q: Explain why a writer who breaks the conventions of an occasion may be making a deliberate choice.
cards.a: Audiences arrive with expectations set by the occasion, so a departure (a warning at a celebration, humor at a memorial) seizes attention and signals that something is urgent enough to override custom. The break itself becomes an argument that the situation is not ordinary.
cards.h: → occasion sets expectations → break surprises → audience attends → signals urgency
cards.n: Calling the break a mistake assumes the writer did not know the occasion; ask what the departure makes the audience notice.
o: Breaking convention can show independence and honesty, which builds ethos with an audience tired of ritual language.
The contrast between what the occasion expects and what the speaker says emphasizes the message by making it stand out.

w.a: Breaking conventions shows that the speaker did not prepare properly.
w.why: assumes error instead of analyzing a choice

w.a: Conventions do not matter because audiences only care about the message.
w.why: ignores the expectations occasions create

cards.q: Apply audience analysis: what four questions should you ask before analyzing a speaker's choices?
cards.a: Who is the intended audience? What do they already believe about the subject? What do they value and need? What might make them resist? Because writers' perceptions of these things guide their choices, each choice can then be explained as the writer's answer to one of these conditions.
cards.h: → four questions, then how they guide analysis
cards.n: This is the engine of Row B commentary: choice, the audience belief it answers, and the effect; a device without the audience condition earns little.

cards.q: Define a hostile audience and the adjustment it typically demands.
cards.a: An audience predisposed to reject the writer's claim. Because the writer perceives that resistance, the choices shift: establish common ground and goodwill early, concede what is true in the audience's view, keep a calm tone, and often delay the thesis until shared premises are in place.
cards.n: Analyzing a text for a hostile audience as if it preached to allies misreads its concessions as weakness; they answer perceived resistance.

cards.q: Contrast a sympathetic and an undecided audience in terms of what a writer must do.
cards.a: A sympathetic audience already agrees, so the writer mainly supplies energy, language, and a plan to act; an undecided audience needs information and reasons, so the writer builds the case from shared premises and answers doubts. The writer's perception of which audience is present guides evidence, tone, and structure.
cards.h: → what each needs + how choices change
cards.n: Misjudging this warps an essay: a rally speech to allies looks thin on proof if analyzed as though it were converting opponents.

cards.q: Define common ground in an argument.
cards.a: Common ground is the area of agreement a writer establishes with an audience, often a resistant one, before advancing a contested claim, so the disagreement looks narrower than it seemed. It shows the writer understands the audience's values and uses them as a starting premise.
cards.n: Common ground is not flattery; it earns credit in analysis only when tied to the specific value the writer shares with this audience.

cards.q: Identify the move: 'Some will say this policy asks too much of small towns. It asks exactly what fairness requires of everyone.'
cards.a: The writer anticipates an objection the audience is likely to hold (the policy burdens small towns), states it, and rebuts it by reframing the demand as fairness, a value the objectors share. The move shows the writer's perception of the audience's beliefs guiding the argument.
cards.h: → name the move + the audience belief it answers
cards.n: Borrows counterargument from Claims and Evidence; 'some will say' is the flag, but the point is that the writer answers this audience's likely belief.

cards.q: Identify the rhetorical move King uses throughout Letter from Birmingham Jail before answering each clergyman's objection.
cards.a: He restates each objection in the clergymen's own terms, often granting what is reasonable in it ('You are quite right in calling for negotiation'), then refutes it. Because he perceives his readers as sincere 'men of genuine good will,' answering their words directly and respectfully makes his refutations hard to dismiss as unfair.
cards.h: → the move + why it fits this audience
cards.n: Borrows concession and refutation from Claims and Evidence; 'he uses counterarguments' earns nothing without the reason the move fits these readers.

cards.q: Identify the primary appeal King builds by opening Letter from Birmingham Jail with his credentials and pastoral role.
cards.a: Ethos. King perceived that the clergymen saw him as an outsider stirring trouble, so he answers that view by citing his role as president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, the invitation from its Birmingham affiliate, and his calling as a minister, credentials his clergy readers respect, before he makes any demand.
cards.h: → appeal + the audience perception it answers
cards.n: Ethos is granted by the audience; the point is that King builds it in terms his clergy readers already accept, answering their 'outsider' charge.

cards.q: Write one sentence for a letter to retirees on fixed incomes who oppose a school tax increase, showing you understand their needs before you ask for their vote.
cards.a: Model: 'Many of you have paid school taxes for forty years without a child in the building, and on a fixed income every added dollar is a real choice between one need and another, so I will not ask for this increase lightly.' It names their situation (fixed income, long contribution) and their value (prudence) before the request, signaling respect instead of assuming support.
cards.h: → name their need + their value, then signal the ask
cards.n: A sentence praising education in general shows no understanding of this audience; 2.B credit requires naming their specific beliefs, values, or needs.

cards.q: Explain why a writer anticipates objections.
cards.a: Anticipating the objection an audience already holds shows the writer understands their beliefs and answers resistance before it hardens. Fair treatment of the other view also builds credibility, so readers are more willing to accept the claim that follows.
cards.h: → perceive the audience's doubt → answer it early → resistance falls + fairness builds trust
cards.n: Borrows counterargument from Claims and Evidence; the move pays off only if the objection is the strongest one this audience holds, not a straw man.
o: Raising the objection first lets the writer frame it on the writer's terms instead of leaving readers to raise it silently.
An audience that hears its own doubt stated fairly feels respected, which lowers defensiveness toward the claim.

w.a: Writers anticipate objections to make their essays longer and more complete.
w.why: no link to the audience's beliefs

w.a: Anticipating objections shows the writer is unsure of the argument.
w.why: misreads a strategic move as weakness

cards.q: Explain why a writer who misjudges an audience's values can lose the argument despite strong evidence.
cards.a: Evidence persuades only when the audience accepts the values it serves. Data showing a factory would add 400 jobs will not move residents who value the quiet of their valley over growth; misreading them, the writer answered a question they were not asking.
cards.h: → evidence serves a value → audience rejects that value → evidence misses → argument fails
cards.n: Blaming the audience for being 'irrational' misses the EK: the writer's perception of the audience is supposed to guide the choices.
o: Writers choose evidence based on what they think the audience cares about, so a wrong perception produces irrelevant evidence.
An argument aimed at the wrong values can even confirm the audience's fear that the writer does not understand them.

w.a: Strong evidence always wins an argument no matter who the audience is.
w.why: ignores that audiences weigh evidence through their values

w.a: The writer lost because the audience did not read the evidence carefully.
w.why: blames the audience instead of the writer's choices

cards.q: Explain why a writer might acknowledge an audience's legitimate concern before stating the claim.
cards.a: Acknowledgment shows the writer has perceived and respects what the audience fears or needs, which lowers defensiveness. Once readers feel heard, they are more willing to follow reasoning toward a claim they initially resisted, because the claim no longer seems to dismiss them.
cards.h: → name their concern → they feel heard → defensiveness drops → claim gets a hearing
cards.n: 'It makes the writer seem nice' is not an effect on the argument; say how it changes the audience's willingness to accept the claim.
o: Acknowledging a concern first proves the writer's claim was reached with the audience's interests in view.
It converts a potential objection into shared ground, so the claim reads as a response to the concern rather than a rejection of it.

w.a: Writers acknowledge concerns first because it is the correct order for an essay.
w.why: a formula, not a reason tied to audience

w.a: Acknowledging concerns lets the audience know the writer agrees with them completely.
w.why: acknowledgment is not full agreement

cards.q: Explain why a writer facing a hostile audience often delays the thesis until late in the text.
cards.a: Stated first, the thesis gives a resistant audience a reason to stop listening. By leading with shared values and evidence, the writer builds agreement step by step, so the thesis arrives as a conclusion the audience has partly reached itself.
cards.h: → thesis first → hostile readers tune out → shared premises first → thesis feels earned
cards.n: Borrows thesis placement from Reasoning and Organization; saying 'for suspense' misses the audience's resistance, which is the reason.
o: Delaying the claim keeps the audience's attention on premises it can accept before it meets the one it resists.
An inductive order lets readers weigh evidence without the defensiveness an opening claim would trigger.

w.a: Writers delay the thesis to create suspense and keep the reader interested.
w.why: entertainment, not the audience's resistance

w.a: A thesis should always come in the first paragraph, so delaying it is a mistake.
w.why: ignores the rhetorical situation

cards.q: Define pathos.
cards.a: Pathos is the appeal to the audience's emotions and values: choices (images, anecdotes, charged words) meant to make the audience feel something that makes the writer's position compelling. It enacts the EK's point that writers try to relate to an intended audience's emotions and values to achieve a purpose.
cards.n: 'The author uses pathos' earns nothing; name the specific emotion, the choice that produces it, and why that emotion serves the purpose.

cards.q: Explain four ways a writer establishes pathos.
cards.a: Vivid sensory imagery and concrete detail; anecdotes about particular people; connotative, emotionally charged diction; and appeals to shared values, hopes, or fears. Each relates the argument to what this audience already feels and cares about.
cards.n: Listing techniques is not analysis; in an essay, say which emotion a technique produces and why that emotion serves the writer's purpose.

cards.q: Decide which appeal dominates: 'Picture the empty chair at every table this disease has left behind.'
cards.a: Pathos. The imagined image of an empty chair at a family table turns an abstract death toll into a personal absence the audience can see, producing grief and urgency that move them toward the writer's measure.
cards.n: Name the emotion targeted, here grief for an absent person; 'this is emotional' is a label, not analysis.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to unify.
cards.a: To bind a divided or diverse audience into one group by invoking shared values, a common history, or a common threat. It works through the audience's values: the writer names what everyone already cares about so that differences seem smaller than the bond.
cards.h: → definition + how values do the work
cards.n: Watch for first-person plural: a shift to 'we' and 'our' is the grammatical machinery of unification; quote it.

cards.q: Define shared values in rhetoric.
cards.a: Principles the writer and audience already hold in common, such as fairness, family, safety, or sacrifice, which a writer invokes as agreed ground from which to argue. Relating a claim to them lets the audience feel the claim follows from what it already believes.
cards.h: → definition + how a writer uses them
cards.n: Shared values work as ethos (the speaker is one of us) and pathos (the audience feels it); name the specific value, not 'values' in general.

cards.q: Analyze how the writer relates to the audience's emotions and values: 'Our grandparents did not build this cooperative so that their grandchildren could sell it to the first company that waved a check. They pooled tractors and seed through drought years because they believed no farmer should stand alone.' (a member's letter in a farm cooperative's newsletter before a vote on a buyout)
cards.a: The writer ties the vote to members' reverence for their predecessors and their value of mutual aid. 'Our grandparents' and their sacrifice 'through drought years' stir pride and obligation, while 'the first company that waved a check' casts the buyout as a betrayal, so members feel that voting no honors their inheritance.
cards.h: → values invoked + emotion stirred + effect on the vote
cards.n: 'The writer uses pathos about grandparents' names without explaining; say which value (loyalty, solidarity) and how it pushes members to vote no.

cards.q: Decide which sentence better relates to an audience of volunteer firefighters' families at a fundraising dinner, and explain why. (A) 'Response times in the district improved 12 percent last year.' (B) 'Every one of you has sat up past midnight listening for the truck to come home; tonight we make sure it comes home with the gear it needs.'
cards.a: (B). It speaks to what these families have lived (waiting, worry) and to what they value (their firefighters' safety), turning a donation into protection for their own. (A) is accurate but aimed at a policymaker; for this audience it names no emotion or value, so it does little to move them to give.
cards.n: Choosing the statistic because 'logos is stronger' ignores the EK: the right choice relates to this audience's emotions and values.

cards.q: Write one sentence urging small-business owners who prize independence to join a shared delivery cooperative, relating the proposal to that value.
cards.a: Model: 'Joining the co-op does not mean answering to anyone: you keep your prices, your hours, and your name on the door, and you stop depending on a national carrier that can raise your rates overnight.' It recasts cooperation, which might seem to threaten their independence, as the way to protect it.
cards.h: → one sentence naming their value and reframing the ask
cards.n: A sentence praising teamwork works against this audience's value; the task is to connect the proposal to what they already care about.

cards.q: Explain how King's long catalog sentence about lynchings and daily humiliations builds pathos in Letter from Birmingham Jail.
cards.a: The long periodic sentence stacks concrete injuries ('when you have seen...') so readers endure the weight of waiting before the main clause arrives. By the time King writes 'then you will understand why we find it difficult to wait,' the clergy's advice to wait feels unbearable, which is his purpose.
cards.h: → clause after clause of lived injury → main clause delayed → reader feels the wait → 'wait' becomes unbearable
cards.n: Borrows periodic syntax from Style; name the effect on the reader, not just the pile-up of clauses, to earn credit for analysis.
o: The catalog makes white readers imagine injuries they have not lived, relating the argument to their own love for family.
Each 'when you' clause addresses the reader directly, so the grievances become the reader's imagined experience rather than a report.

w.a: King uses a long sentence to show that he is a sophisticated writer.
w.why: about the writer's image, not the effect on these readers

w.a: The sentence is long because King had a lot of examples to list.
w.why: describes length without explaining its effect

w.a: King uses pathos in this sentence to make the reader feel emotions.
w.why: names the appeal without the specific emotion or purpose

cards.q: Explain why an anecdote about one person can move an audience more than a statistic about thousands.
cards.a: A single named person gives the audience someone to imagine and feel for, while large numbers stay abstract. The anecdote relates the issue to emotions the audience already has (sympathy, fear for their own family), which motivates action a statistic alone often cannot.
cards.h: → one person → the audience imagines and feels → emotion motivates → numbers stay abstract
cards.n: 'Stories are more interesting' does not explain the effect; name the emotion and why it leads this audience to act.
o: Audiences identify with individuals, so a story makes the stakes personal in a way a total cannot.
The anecdote supplies the human meaning a statistic lacks, and writers often pair them so the number gains weight.

w.a: Anecdotes are always better evidence than statistics.
w.why: overgeneralizes; the fit to audience and purpose decides

w.a: People do not understand statistics, so writers use stories instead.
w.why: condescending and ignores the emotional mechanism

cards.q: Explain why an appeal to an audience's values tends to persuade more durably than an appeal to fear.
cards.a: Fear fades once a threat seems distant, and heavy fear can make an audience feel manipulated. An appeal to values the audience holds (fairness, duty to children) makes the action an expression of who they already are, so the commitment outlasts the moment of alarm.
cards.h: → fear fades + can feel manipulative → values are part of identity → action lasts
cards.n: Claiming fear 'never works' overgeneralizes; the point is durability and the audience's sense of being manipulated.
o: Values are stable beliefs, so an argument anchored in them keeps working after the news cycle moves on.
Fear invites resistance from audiences who notice it, while values invite them to act as themselves.

w.a: Fear appeals are unethical, so writers should never use them.
w.why: a moral judgment, not a rhetorical explanation

w.a: Values appeals work better because they are more logical.
w.why: confuses values with logos

cards.q: Explain why humor can help a writer relate to an audience that is anxious about a change.
cards.a: Humor eases tension and signals that the writer shares the audience's unease, so the writer seems an ally rather than an authority imposing change. Relaxed listeners are more willing to hear the reasons for the change than listeners braced for bad news.
cards.h: → anxiety → humor releases tension + shows shared feeling → writer seen as ally → reasons get heard
cards.n: 'Humor makes it entertaining' misses the target emotion (anxiety) and the effect on acceptance.
o: A joke at the writer's own expense lowers the writer's status to the audience's level, building goodwill.
Laughing together creates a brief shared experience, which makes the audience feel part of the change rather than subject to it.

w.a: Humor is always appropriate because audiences like to laugh.
w.why: ignores occasion and audience

w.a: Writers use humor to distract the audience from the real issue.
w.why: assumes manipulation instead of explaining the effect

cards.q: Define ethos.
cards.a: Ethos is the appeal to the credibility, authority, and character of the writer, one of the appeals (modes of persuasion) through which arguments persuade or motivate action. It persuades because the audience trusts the person making the claim, trust the text earns through expertise, fairness, and goodwill.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + how it is earned
cards.n: Ethos is granted by the audience, not asserted; 'the author uses ethos' earns nothing without evidence of how it is built and why it matters here.

cards.q: Define logos.
cards.a: Logos is the appeal to reason: evidence, data, examples, definitions, and a clear line of reasoning that make a claim rationally convincing. It persuades when the audience can follow and accept the steps from evidence to claim.
cards.n: Numbers alone are not logos; the appeal lives in the reasoning linking the data to the claim, which commentary must trace.

cards.q: Define kairos.
cards.a: Kairos is the appeal to timeliness: the sense that the argument is being made at the right moment, seizing an opening the situation has created. It links the exigence to action ('before Tuesday's vote,' 'while the lot is still empty').
cards.n: Kairos is not a CED term, but noting timeliness shows you understand the exigence; 'now' and 'we can no longer wait' are its markers.

cards.q: Explain four ways a writer establishes ethos.
cards.a: By citing relevant expertise or experience; by using accurate evidence and correct conventions; by treating opposing views fairly; and by showing shared values or goodwill toward the audience. Which one a writer leans on depends on what this audience needs before it will trust the writer.
cards.n: Conceding a point is an ethos move: fairness buys trust before the refutation lands.

cards.q: Explain four ways a writer establishes logos.
cards.a: By supplying statistics and data; by reasoning from cause to effect or from examples to a generalization; by defining terms and drawing distinctions; and by arranging claims in a visible, orderly line of reasoning. Each lets an audience check the argument's steps for itself.
cards.n: 'The statistic appeals to logos' earns nothing unless commentary says what the number proves and why this audience would accept it.

cards.q: Decide which appeal dominates when a speaker cites her thirty years as a nurse before arguing for staffing limits.
cards.a: Ethos. Thirty years as a nurse gives her firsthand authority on staffing, so the audience trusts her claim about limits before any data appears; the credential answers the question 'how would she know?'
cards.n: Several appeals often work at once; name the dominant one and explain what it does for the purpose, not just the label.

cards.q: Decide which appeal dominates: 'The CDC's own data show infection rates fell 40 percent after the mandate.'
cards.a: Logos, with a supporting layer of ethos from the cited authority. The statistic offers verifiable evidence of cause and effect (the mandate, then a 40 percent drop), while the agency's reputation makes a skeptical audience likelier to accept the number.
cards.n: Say which appeal dominates and which supports rather than forcing a single label onto a sentence.

cards.q:
Identify the dominant appeal (ethos, pathos, logos, or kairos) in each excerpt:
1. In twenty years as an ER nurse, I've seen this.
2. She was nine. She never came home from school.
3. Crashes fell from 31 to 6 after the light went in.
4. The council votes Thursday; then it's too late.
5. I opposed this plan too, so I get your doubts.
6. Four dollars a month per home grows the library budget by a third.
7. Imagine smoke at 3 a.m. and no ladder truck.
8. The matching grant expires this month.
9. Every major medical association endorses it.
10. This town has never turned away a neighbor.
11. Pipes this old fail twice as often; a break is coming.
12. After three terms on this board, I know what delay costs.
13. Think of the children who will walk these halls.
14. The storm hits Friday; the levee is already cracked.
15. Two of three course graduates found work in six months.
cards.a:
1 → ethos (firsthand professional experience)
2 → pathos (grief for a lost child)
3 → logos (before-and-after data)
4 → kairos (a deadline makes action urgent now)
5 → ethos (goodwill and fairness toward doubters)
6 → logos (cost weighed against benefit)
7 → pathos (fear through an imagined scene)
8 → kairos (a closing window of opportunity)
9 → ethos (borrowed authority of experts)
10 → pathos (pride in a shared value)
11 → logos (cause-and-effect reasoning from a failure rate)
12 → ethos (experience on the board)
13 → pathos (protective feeling for children)
14 → kairos (an imminent threat), with fear as support
15 → logos (comparative statistic)
cards.h: → one appeal + its trigger per line
cards.n: Several excerpts mix appeals (14 is timing plus fear); name the dominant appeal and the words that create it, as you would in an essay.

cards.q: Explain why a speaker with obvious expertise may still open by showing goodwill toward a suspicious audience.
cards.a: Expertise shows the speaker knows the subject, but a suspicious audience also asks whether the speaker is on its side. Goodwill (acknowledging the audience's worries, sharing its stake) answers that second question, so the credentials are heard as help rather than as pressure from an outsider.
cards.h: → expertise answers 'does she know?' → goodwill answers 'is she for us?' → both needed for trust
cards.n: 'Goodwill makes the speaker likable' is thin; say which doubt of this audience it answers that credentials cannot.
o: Ethos has more than one part: competence and character or goodwill, and a suspicious audience tests the second.
Leading with credentials to a wary audience can sound like pulling rank, so goodwill first keeps the expertise from backfiring.

w.a: Experts do not need to build ethos because their credentials speak for themselves.
w.why: ignores the audience's suspicion

w.a: The speaker shows goodwill to hide the fact that her evidence is weak.
w.why: assumes deception instead of explaining the choice

cards.q: Explain why statistics persuade an audience only when it trusts their source.
cards.a: Logos depends on the audience accepting the evidence as true. A number from a source the audience suspects (a company studying its own product) invites dismissal, so writers pair data with a credible source or explain the method, joining ethos to logos so the reasoning can work.
cards.h: → logos needs accepted evidence → distrusted source → number dismissed → pair data with credibility
cards.n: Treating appeals as separate boxes misses the point: logos rests on ethos when the audience cannot check the data itself.
o: Most readers cannot verify a figure, so they judge it by who produced it.
A trusted source lets the audience skip the question 'is this true?' and move to 'what does this prove?'

w.a: Statistics are facts, so they persuade everyone equally.
w.why: ignores the audience's judgment of the source

w.a: Audiences do not like math, so statistics rarely persuade.
w.why: a stereotype, not the source-trust mechanism

cards.q: Explain why an argument that persuades an audience may still fail to motivate it to act.
cards.a: Agreement costs the audience nothing, while action costs time, money, or risk. The EK separates persuading from motivating action: moving an audience to act usually needs an appeal to emotion, values, or timeliness (a deadline, a personal stake) on top of reasons, so belief becomes a decision.
cards.h: → belief is free, action is costly → reasons win belief → emotion, values, timing win action
cards.n: Assuming 'if they agree, they will act' misses the EK's distinction between persuading and motivating action.
o: A call to act needs a specific, doable step and a reason to do it now, which logic alone rarely supplies.
Audiences that agree in principle often wait for someone else to act, so writers must make the stake personal.

w.a: If the argument is logical enough, the audience will automatically act on it.
w.why: ignores the cost of action

w.a: Audiences never act on arguments, so persuasion is pointless.
w.why: overgeneralizes and ignores motivating appeals

cards.q: Explain why 'the author uses ethos' earns no credit in a rhetorical analysis essay.
cards.a: It names an appeal without evidence or commentary. Row B rewards the specific choice that builds credibility (her thirty years as a nurse), its effect on this audience (they trust her account), and the tie to purpose (so they back the staffing bill); the label alone does none of that.
cards.h: → label only → no evidence, no effect, no purpose → nothing for Row B to reward
cards.n: Swapping in 'establishes credibility' changes nothing; the missing parts are the quoted choice and its effect on this audience.
o: The rubric scores explanation of how evidence supports a line of reasoning, and a bare label explains nothing.
Every writer can be said to use ethos, so the sentence could describe any passage and proves nothing about this one.

w.a: Naming ethos shows the reader you know the rhetorical terms, which earns points.
w.why: the exam does not score term recall

w.a: It would earn credit if the essay named all three appeals in the thesis.
w.why: a longer list is still a list without analysis

cards.q: Define the work an argument's introduction does, in the CED's terms.
cards.a: The introduction introduces the subject and/or the writer of the argument to the audience, and it may present the argument's thesis. It may orient, engage, and/or focus the audience by presenting quotations, intriguing statements, anecdotes, questions, statistics, data, contextualized information, or a scenario.
cards.n: An introduction is judged by fit to purpose and audience, not by a formula; 'hook, background, thesis' is a habit, not the CED's rule.

cards.q:
Identify the strategy each introduction opens with (quotation, intriguing statement, anecdote, question, statistic, data, contextualized information, or scenario):
1. 'Last spring my brother waited four hours in an emergency room with a broken wrist.'
2. 'Nearly one in four of the county's bridges is rated structurally deficient.'
3. 'What would you give up to get an hour of your day back?'
4. 'Imagine waking to find your street's only grocery store boarded up.'
5. 'The most dangerous room in your house is not the kitchen.'
6. '"A town is only as strong as its oldest bridge," the county engineer told the board.'
7. 'Median rent here rose from 900 to 1,450 dollars in ten years, while wages rose 11 percent.'
8. 'In 2019 the state ended its rural clinic grants; since then, towns like ours have relied on volunteer ambulances.'
cards.a:
1 → anecdote (engages with a personal story)
2 → statistic (one figure that orients readers to the scale)
3 → question (engages by making readers answer for themselves)
4 → scenario (places readers inside a possible future)
5 → intriguing statement (a surprise that demands explanation)
6 → quotation (borrows a voice to frame the subject)
7 → data (a set of figures that orients by comparison)
8 → contextualized information (history that orients readers to the current problem)
cards.h: → strategy + its job, one per line
cards.n: Naming the strategy earns nothing on its own; say what it does for this audience. 'Statistic' (one figure) and 'data' (a set) overlap.

cards.q: Decide which sentence, placed first, would best capture the audience's interest and introduce the topic of a student's letter to the school board arguing for later start times. (A) 'The school board meets on the first Monday of each month.' (B) 'At 6:40 a.m., when our first bus pulls away, most teenagers' bodies are still producing the hormone that tells them to sleep.' (C) 'Sleep is important for everyone.' (D) 'There are many different opinions about school start times.'
cards.a: (B). It engages with a concrete, surprising image tied to the board's own schedule and orients readers to the conflict (biology versus bus times) the letter will develop. (A) is a fact unrelated to the issue, (C) states an obvious truth that engages no one, and (D) surveys opinions without focusing on anything.
cards.h: → letter + interest + orientation + why others fail
cards.n: Intro questions on the exam test interest and relevance together; a vivid choice that is off-topic fails as surely as a dull on-topic one.

cards.q: Describe how this introduction orients, engages, and focuses its audience: 'Every Saturday for eleven years, Mrs. Alvarez has opened the Eastside pantry at 6 a.m. Last month, for the first time, she turned families away. Donations to the county's food banks have fallen by a third since January, and unless the county council restores its emergency grant, Eastside will close by summer.' (an op-ed in a county newspaper)
cards.a: It engages with an anecdote about a named volunteer whose first refusal of families gives the problem a human face; it orients readers with contextualized data (donations down a third since January); and it focuses them on a specific demand by ending on the thesis: the council must restore the grant or the pantry closes.
cards.h: → engage, orient, focus, each tied to its sentence
cards.n: Saying 'it has a hook and a thesis' describes a template; name what each part does for county readers and the council.

cards.q: Write a two-sentence introduction for a letter to your city council arguing that the downtown library should stay open until 9 p.m., using contextualized information to orient the council and ending with your thesis.
cards.a: Model: 'Since the library began closing at 6 p.m. last year, the students and shift workers who make up much of its evening traffic have had no public place to study or search for work after their day ends. The council should restore hours until 9 p.m., because a library that closes before its patrons are free to use it is failing its purpose.' Context orients; the thesis focuses.
cards.n: Opening with 'Libraries have existed for centuries' orients no one to this council's decision; the context must be specific to the situation.

cards.q: Write a revision of this rhetorical analysis introduction so that it identifies the rhetorical situation and the writer's choices: 'Throughout history, people have given speeches to persuade others. In her speech, the speaker uses many rhetorical strategies to convey her message.' (The passage is a hospital CEO's address to nurses after a year of layoffs, urging them to stay.)
cards.a: Model: 'Addressing nurses who had watched colleagues laid off all year, a hospital's CEO set out to persuade them to stay. She admits the hospital's failures in plain, unguarded language and recalls her own years on night shifts, rebuilding enough trust that her final appeal to their loyalty to patients, not to the institution, can be heard.' It names situation, purpose, and choices.
cards.h: → situation + purpose + choices in a defensible claim
cards.n: The original restates the prompt ('uses many rhetorical strategies'), which the rubric says earns no thesis point; its sweeping opener orients to nothing.

cards.q: Evaluate this opening of an argument essay on whether cities should ban cars from downtown streets: 'Since the dawn of time, humans have moved from place to place. Cars are a big part of modern life, and there are many opinions about them.'
cards.a: Ineffective. It introduces neither the specific subject nor a position: 'since the dawn of time' orients the reader to nothing, 'cars are a big part of modern life' states an obvious fact, and 'many opinions' refuses to focus. A reader finishes it with no idea what the essay will argue about downtown streets.
cards.h: → verdict + how it fails to introduce, orient, focus
cards.n: A sweeping historical opener wastes the reader's first impression; the CED's introduction orients the audience to this subject.

cards.q: Decide which opening better suits a proposal to a hospital's finance committee for a night-shift shuttle, and explain why. (A) 'Picture a nurse walking to a dark parking lot at 3 a.m., keys laced between her fingers.' (B) 'In the past year, 14 night-shift staff resigned citing commute safety; replacing each costs the hospital about 40,000 dollars.'
cards.a: (B). A finance committee's need is cost and evidence, so opening with resignations and the 40,000-dollar replacement cost orients them in their own terms and frames the shuttle as a saving. (A) engages feeling but may read as unserious to this audience; it would suit a speech to staff or the public better.
cards.h: → letter + the audience's need + where the other fits
cards.n: No opening strategy is better in general; skill 2.A asks for the introduction that fits this purpose and this audience.

cards.q: Explain why an anecdote suits the opening of a commencement speech.
cards.a: Graduates and families expect warmth and reflection on this occasion, and a brief story engages them personally while introducing the speaker as a person rather than a title. The anecdote can also carry the message in miniature, so the audience meets the theme before hearing it stated.
cards.h: → occasion invites the personal → story engages + introduces the speaker → theme previewed
cards.n: 'Anecdotes are a good hook' is generic; tie the anecdote to the occasion's expectations and to what it introduces.
o: An anecdote introduces the writer, one of the jobs the CED gives an introduction, by showing who the speaker is rather than listing credentials.
