A story creates a shared moment in a large, mixed audience, focusing attention before the argument begins.

w.a: Speakers open with anecdotes because every speech is supposed to start with a story.
w.why: a formula, not a reason tied to the occasion

w.a: The anecdote is there to make the speech longer and more entertaining.
w.why: no link to purpose or audience

cards.q: Explain why an introduction that gives context before the thesis helps an audience unfamiliar with the issue.
cards.a: Readers new to a dispute cannot judge a claim until they know what is at stake. Contextualized information (what changed, who is affected, what decision looms) orients them, so the thesis arrives as a reasonable answer to a problem they now understand rather than as an assertion from nowhere.
cards.h: → unfamiliar audience → context orients → stakes understood → thesis reads as an answer
cards.n: 'Background helps the reader' is too vague; say what the context lets this audience understand that makes the thesis acceptable.
o: Orienting an audience is one of the CED's named jobs for an introduction, and an unfamiliar audience needs it most.
Context establishes the exigence for readers who did not feel it, which makes the thesis seem necessary.

w.a: Context should come first because the thesis always belongs at the end of the introduction.
w.why: a rule, not an audience-based reason

w.a: Giving context shows the writer did a lot of research.
w.why: about the writer's image, not the audience's understanding

cards.q: Explain why a scenario ('Imagine you...') can engage an audience at the start of an argument about a future risk.
cards.a: A future risk is abstract, so audiences discount it. A scenario places the reader inside the consequence (the empty shelf, the flooded basement), making the risk feel personal and present, which engages attention and prepares the reader to accept a thesis about preventing it.
cards.h: → future risk feels distant → scenario puts the reader inside it → risk feels real → thesis welcomed
cards.n: Calling the scenario 'creative' misses its job: turning a distant risk into something this audience can picture.
o: Second-person address makes the reader the subject of the story, so the stakes are theirs.
A scenario substitutes imagination for experience the audience does not yet have.

w.a: Scenarios are effective because readers like fiction more than facts.
w.why: ignores the risk-to-reader mechanism

w.a: The writer uses a scenario because there is no real evidence available.
w.why: assumes weakness instead of explaining the effect

cards.q: Explain why an intriguing statement can be an effective opening for a skeptical audience.
cards.a: A surprising claim ('The most dangerous room in your house is not the kitchen') opens a gap the reader wants closed, so even a skeptic keeps reading. The writer earns attention without asking for agreement yet, then uses that attention to deliver the evidence.
cards.h: → surprise opens a question → skeptic reads on → attention before agreement → evidence lands
cards.n: 'It hooks the reader' names the goal, not the mechanism; say why curiosity works on readers who would resist a claim.
o: A skeptical audience resists being told what to think but not being puzzled, so the statement engages without triggering resistance.
The intriguing statement focuses the audience on the exact question the argument will answer.

w.a: Intriguing statements work because they are shocking and shock always persuades.
w.why: overgeneralizes; shock is not persuasion

w.a: The writer opens with a surprise to show off a clever sentence.
w.why: about style for its own sake, not the audience

cards.q: Define the work an argument's conclusion does, in the CED's terms.
cards.a: The conclusion brings the argument to a unified end and may present the thesis. It may engage and/or focus the audience by explaining significance in a broader context, making connections, calling the audience to act, suggesting a change in behavior or attitude, proposing a solution, leaving a compelling image, explaining implications, summarizing the argument, or connecting to the introduction.
cards.h: → unified end + (maybe) thesis + engage or focus
cards.n: Summary is only one of the CED's options; a conclusion that merely repeats the introduction does no new work for the audience.

cards.q:
Identify the CED conclusion strategy each closing sentence uses:
1. 'Call your council member before Tuesday's vote.'
2. 'If the bridge closes, the east side loses its only route to the hospital.'
3. 'This is not just about one park; it is about whether a city keeps its promises.'
4. (essay opened with Mrs. Alvarez) 'Next Saturday, Mrs. Alvarez will unlock the pantry at 6 a.m. again, if we let her.'
5. 'A small fee on each ticket would cover the shuttle's cost within two years.'
6. 'Cheaper, safer, and faster: the case for the bus lane is complete.'
7. 'The last light in the old mill went out in 1994; the next one is up to us.'
8. 'Stop seeing recycling as a chore and start seeing it as a paycheck for the town.'
9. 'The same logic that saved the library can save the pool.'
cards.a:
1 → call to act (a specific step before a deadline)
2 → implications (what follows if the argument is ignored)
3 → broader significance (the local issue as a question of civic trust)
4 → connection to the introduction (returns to the opening anecdote)
5 → proposed solution
6 → summary (the three reasons in brief)
7 → compelling image (the dark mill waiting for a new light)
8 → change in attitude or behavior
9 → making connections (links this case to another the audience knows)
cards.n: Several lines do two jobs (7 is an image and an implied call); name the dominant strategy, and in an essay say what it does for the audience.

cards.q: Identify how this conclusion creates a unified end, given the letter's opening. Opening: 'The first thing a visitor notices at Pine Street Elementary is the buckets: three of them, catching rain on the gym floor.' Conclusion: 'Approve the roof repair this spring, and next fall the only thing that gym floor will catch is a basketball.' (a parent's letter to the school board)
cards.a: It connects to the introduction by returning to the gym floor and its catching, now transformed from rain to a basketball, which closes the frame the opening set up. It also calls the board to act ('approve the roof repair this spring') and leaves a compelling image of the result, so the ending both unifies the letter and makes the request vivid.
cards.h: → connection to the intro + call + image
cards.n: 'It restates the thesis' misreads this ending; returning to the opening image with a change is what makes it unified rather than repetitive.

cards.q: Decide which sentence would best conclude a speech to volunteers at a river cleanup by calling the audience to act. (A) 'Rivers have been important to human settlement for thousands of years.' (B) 'In summary, we discussed pollution, wildlife, and recreation.' (C) 'Sign up at the table by the boathouse for next month's cleanup, and bring one friend who has never seen this river up close.' (D) 'Some people think cleanups make little difference.'
cards.a: (C). It gives the volunteers a specific, immediate action (sign up at the table) and extends their reach (bring a friend), turning the speech's momentum into commitment. (A) drifts to a broad generalization, (B) summarizes mechanically, and (D) raises an objection without answering it, ending on doubt.
cards.h: → letter + why it meets the goal + why others fail
cards.n: On writing questions the right ending matches the stated goal (here, a call to act); endings that summarize or generalize fail it even when true.

cards.q: Write a concluding sentence for an argument essay claiming that high schools should require a course in personal finance, explaining the argument's significance in a broader context.
cards.a: Model: 'A generation that graduates able to read a loan contract is not only spared its own debts; it becomes the voters, parents, and business owners who decide whether a whole community's economy rests on credit it can repay.' It widens the stakes from individual students to civic and economic life, answering 'so what?' for the reader.
cards.h: → one sentence that widens the stakes
cards.n: 'In conclusion, personal finance is important' restates without significance; the broader context must reach beyond the essay's own examples.

cards.q: Write a revision of this conclusion so it does more than repeat the introduction: 'In conclusion, the town should build a skate park because it would give teenagers a place to go, reduce vandalism, and improve the town.' (The essay is a letter to the town council from a high school junior.)
cards.a: Model: 'The council can keep paying to repair benches and repaint walls every summer, or it can give the town's teenagers a place they will want to protect. Put the skate park on next month's agenda, and invite the students who will use it to help design it.' It explains implications in the council's terms, proposes a concrete next step, and calls the council to act.
cards.h: → implication + solution + call, not a list of reasons
cards.n: A conclusion that only lists the essay's reasons again adds nothing; the CED's options (implication, call, solution, image) each do new work.

cards.q: Contrast a conclusion that summarizes an argument with one that explains its implications.
cards.a: A summary restates the argument's main points so the audience retains them, useful in a long or technical text; an implications conclusion explains what follows if the argument is right (costs, consequences, what changes next), extending the argument's reach. Summary looks back; implications look forward.
cards.n: In a 40-minute AP essay a summary conclusion is rarely needed; one sentence of implication does more than a paragraph of review.

cards.q: Decide which ending better fits a eulogy for a longtime school crossing guard, and explain why. (A) 'Tomorrow, when the children cross Maple Street, let each of us be the one who watches for them.' (B) 'To summarize, Mr. Hale was punctual, kind, and dedicated for thirty-one years.'
cards.a: (A). A eulogy's audience needs to mourn and to carry the person's meaning forward; (A) leaves a compelling image of the crossing and asks mourners to continue his care, uniting grief with purpose. (B) summarizes like a performance review, which suits a report, not an occasion of loss.
cards.n: Summary is a legitimate strategy, but not for every occasion; the fit to purpose, audience, and occasion decides.

cards.q: Explain why a call to action suits the conclusion of a speech to volunteers.
cards.a: Volunteers already agree with the cause, so what they need is a next step. A conclusion that names a concrete action (sign up, show up Saturday) converts the energy the speech built into commitment while it is strongest, which is the speech's purpose.
cards.h: → audience already agrees → needs a step → concrete call at the end → energy becomes commitment
cards.n: 'It ends on a strong note' is vague; name the audience's readiness and the specific action that uses it.
o: The end of a speech is when the audience's motivation peaks, so the request lands best there.
For a sympathetic audience, more argument is wasted; the conclusion's job is to focus them on action.

w.a: Every conclusion should end with a call to action because that is the strongest ending.
w.why: overgeneralizes; the audience and purpose decide

w.a: The call to action summarizes the speech's main points.
w.why: confuses a call with a summary

cards.q: Explain why returning to the introduction's anecdote in the conclusion creates a unified end.
cards.a: The return closes the frame the opening set up, so the argument feels complete rather than merely stopped. Showing the anecdote changed (the pantry reopened, the child safe) lets the audience see the argument's result in the same human terms that first engaged them.
cards.h: → opening frame reopened → closure → changed anecdote shows the argument's result → unity
cards.n: Repeating the anecdote unchanged is not the move; the unity comes from showing what the argument would change.
o: Connecting to the introduction is one of the CED's named conclusion strategies because it makes the text read as one piece.
The echo rewards the audience's attention, and the change in the anecdote makes the stakes concrete one last time.

w.a: Returning to the anecdote reminds the reader of the introduction in case they forgot it.
w.why: treats unity as a memory aid, not an effect

w.a: The writer repeats the story because repetition is always persuasive.
w.why: overgeneralizes and ignores the change

cards.q: Explain why a conclusion that only restates the thesis wastes the essay's last chance with the reader.
cards.a: The reader already knows the thesis, so hearing it again adds nothing. The conclusion is the last point of contact, where the writer can show why the argument matters (implications, broader context, a call), so a restatement leaves the audience with less than the body already gave them.
cards.h: → thesis already known → restatement adds nothing → last contact is where significance belongs
cards.n: 'In conclusion' followed by the thesis is the phrasing that earns nothing; the CED gives a conclusion work beyond repetition.
o: The audience remembers endings best, so the final paragraph should carry the argument's strongest or widest point.
Restating signals the writer has nothing more to say, which weakens the impression the argument leaves.

w.a: Restating the thesis is the main job of a conclusion.
w.why: the CED lists many jobs; restatement is the weakest

w.a: A conclusion should never mention the thesis at all.
w.why: the CED says a conclusion may present the thesis

cards.q: Explain why a compelling image can end a eulogy more powerfully than a summary of the person's achievements.
cards.a: Mourners need to feel the loss and hold on to the person, not review a resume. An image (his lamp still lit in the shop window) gives them something to remember and share, uniting grief with tribute, which is what the occasion of a eulogy asks for.
cards.h: → occasion of loss → audience needs to feel and remember → image gives a lasting picture → grief + tribute
cards.n: Saying 'images are more emotional' names pathos without tying it to the occasion and the mourners' need.
o: A summary of achievements reads like an obituary or a report, which suits a different genre and audience.
An image leaves the audience with a scene they can carry out of the room, extending the tribute beyond the speech.

w.a: Images are always better than summaries in any conclusion.
w.why: ignores occasion and purpose

w.a: The speaker uses an image because the person had no real achievements.
w.why: assumes a deficit instead of explaining the choice

cards.q: State what the CED says writers' comparisons are for and what makes one effective.
cards.a: Writers may make comparisons (similes, metaphors, analogies, or anecdotes) in an attempt to relate to an audience. An effective comparison must be shared and understood by the audience to advance the writer's purpose: it works only if the audience knows the thing compared and draws the intended conclusion.
cards.h: → purpose of comparisons + the condition for success
cards.n: Naming 'metaphor' is Style labeling; the Rhetorical Situation point is whether this audience shares the reference and what it makes them see.

cards.q: Explain how the comparison relates to the audience: 'Asking a nine-year-old to play one sport year-round is like planting the same crop in the same field every season: the first harvest looks fine, and then the soil gives out.' (a youth-league coach speaking to parents in a farming county)
cards.a: The analogy draws on crop rotation, knowledge these farming parents share, to make an abstract risk (overuse injury, burnout) concrete and familiar. Because they already accept that one crop exhausts a field, they carry that judgment over to their children, which advances the coach's purpose of discouraging early specialization.
cards.n: 'The coach uses a simile to make it relatable' names the device; the point comes from saying what the audience knows and what conclusion it carries over.

cards.q: Decide which analogy better serves a nurse explaining the need for a booster shot to an audience of long-haul truck drivers, and explain why. (A) 'A booster is like a software patch for your immune system.' (B) 'A booster is like topping off your tank before a long haul: the first fill got you started, but it won't get you across the country.'
cards.a: (B). Topping off a tank is part of every trucker's routine, so the audience instantly grasps that protection runs down over distance and needs refilling. (A) relies on software updates, which may be less familiar to this audience and implies the body has a flaw rather than needing a routine refill.
cards.h: → letter + what the audience shares + what transfers
cards.n: Picking the analogy you find cleverer ignores the EK: an effective comparison must be shared and understood by this audience.

cards.q: Write an analogy for homeowners at a town meeting arguing that the town should repair its water mains now rather than wait.
cards.a: Model: 'Putting off the water main repair is like ignoring the slow drip under your kitchen sink: it costs nothing this month and a new floor next year.' Homeowners share the experience of small household leaks becoming expensive damage, so the comparison carries their own judgment (fix it early) over to the town's pipes.
cards.h: → one analogy from the audience's experience + why
cards.n: An analogy to ancient aqueducts may impress but fails if this audience does not share the reference; draw it from their experience.

cards.q:
Identify each comparison's type (simile, metaphor, analogy, or anecdote) and whether the audience named is likely to share and understand it:
1. To first-year teachers: 'Your first October will feel like running a marathon in someone else's shoes.'
2. To retirees: 'Streaming works like a DVR: the shows wait for you until you press play.'
3. To middle schoolers: 'The school budget is a zero-sum Nash equilibrium.'
4. To farmers: 'The tariff is a hailstorm the week before harvest.'
5. To parents: 'When my son was four, he chased a ball into the street; that is why I voted for the speed bumps.'
6. To a city council: 'Deferred maintenance works like a credit card: skip a payment and the bill grows.'
7. To tourists: 'Our harbor is the Venice of the Great Lakes.'
8. To nursing students: 'Triage is like the Battle of Cannae.'
cards.a:
1 → simile; works: teachers know exhaustion and the awkwardness of borrowed shoes
2 → analogy; works if these retirees know DVRs, bridging new technology to familiar technology
3 → metaphor; fails: middle schoolers do not know game theory, so it obscures
4 → metaphor; works: farmers know hail's sudden, uncontrollable loss at the worst moment
5 → anecdote; works: parents share the fear, so the story relates the writer's vote to their experience
6 → analogy; works: council members know how unpaid debt compounds
7 → metaphor; likely works: Venice's canals are a widely known travel ideal
8 → simile; likely fails: few nursing students know the ancient battle, so it relates to no one
cards.h: → type + works or fails + why, one per line
cards.n: Borrows device names from Style; the RHS point is the second half of each line, whether this audience shares the reference.

cards.q: Explain how the anecdote works as a comparison for the audience: 'When I started this job, I could not change a tire. Twenty years later I run the county garage. Every skill you think you lack is one you have simply not been taught yet.' (a fleet manager speaking to new apprentices on their first day)
cards.a: The manager compares her past self to the apprentices' present selves: she too began unskilled. Because they share her starting point, the anecdote relates her to them as a former beginner rather than a boss, and her rise becomes evidence that their gaps are temporary, which serves her purpose of encouraging them.
cards.h: → then-me = now-you + what the audience concludes
cards.n: The CED counts anecdotes among comparisons; calling this a mere 'personal story' misses that it invites the audience to see themselves in her.

cards.q: Contrast a metaphor and an analogy as tools for relating to an audience.
cards.a: A metaphor asserts an identity in a phrase ('the budget is a lifeboat'), giving the audience an image and an attitude at once; an analogy develops a comparison step by step ('just as a lifeboat can hold only so many...') to carry reasoning from a familiar case to an unfamiliar one. Both work only if the audience knows the thing compared.
cards.h: → image in a phrase vs reasoning by parallel
cards.n: Borrows terms from Style; for 1.B credit, say what each comparison lets this audience understand or feel, not only which figure it is.

cards.q: Decide which comparison the writer should add to best help an audience of high school athletes understand why sleep matters for performance. (A) 'Sleep is like the REM cycle of the mind.' (B) 'Skipping sleep before a game is like skipping warm-ups: you can still play, but you are asking for an injury.' (C) 'Sleep is to the brain what a thesis is to an essay.' (D) 'Sleep deprivation is a silent epidemic.'
cards.a: (B). Warm-ups are part of every athlete's routine, and athletes already believe skipping them invites injury, so the analogy carries that belief over to sleep. (A) is circular and technical, (C) draws on essay writing, which this audience does not link to performance, and (D) is a metaphor with no tie to their experience.
cards.h: → letter + the shared reference + why others fail
cards.n: The trap is choosing the most sophisticated-sounding option; the exam rewards the comparison this audience already understands.

cards.q: Explain why a comparison drawn from the audience's own experience persuades better than a more impressive but unfamiliar one.
cards.a: A comparison persuades by transferring what the audience already knows and believes to the new case. If the audience does not share the reference, nothing transfers: the impressive comparison needs explaining itself, while a familiar one works instantly and shows that the writer knows them.
cards.h: → comparison transfers existing belief → unfamiliar source transfers nothing → familiar one works + shows care
cards.n: 'Familiar comparisons are easier to read' misses the mechanism: the audience's own judgment is what the comparison carries over.
o: The EK sets the condition directly: an effective comparison must be shared and understood by the audience.
A familiar reference also builds goodwill, since it proves the writer has paid attention to the audience's world.

w.a: An impressive comparison shows the writer is educated, which always builds credibility.
w.why: ignores whether the audience understands it

w.a: Comparisons are decoration, so it does not matter which one the writer uses.
w.why: denies the comparison's persuasive work

cards.q: Explain why an analogy can make an abstract policy concrete for a general audience.
cards.a: A general audience lacks the technical frame to judge a policy directly. An analogy maps the policy onto a situation they manage every day (a household budget, a leaking roof), so they can reason about it with judgment they already trust, which advances the writer's purpose.
cards.h: → policy is abstract → analogy maps it onto daily life → audience reasons with its own judgment → purpose advanced
cards.n: 'The analogy simplifies it' is incomplete; say what familiar situation it borrows and what conclusion the audience carries over.
o: The analogy supplies a structure of reasoning the audience already accepts, so the conclusion feels like their own.
It spares the writer technical detail that would lose a general audience while keeping the logic intact.

w.a: Analogies prove the policy is correct.
w.why: an analogy illustrates reasoning; it is not proof

w.a: Analogies work because general audiences cannot understand real arguments.
w.why: condescending and ignores the transfer mechanism

cards.q: Explain why a comparison can alienate an audience when it trivializes their experience.
cards.a: Calling mass layoffs 'a speed bump' tells workers who lost jobs that their loss is minor, which shows the writer does not share their perspective. Because an effective comparison must be shared by the audience, one that contradicts their experience costs the writer credibility and goodwill.
cards.h: → comparison shrinks their loss → audience sees the writer as outside their experience → trust lost
cards.n: Calling the comparison 'insensitive' names a reaction; explain the gap between the comparison and the audience's experience.
o: The comparison reveals the writer's perspective, and an audience that sees it as distant rejects the rest of the argument.
A trivializing comparison fails the EK's test: the audience does not share the understanding it assumes.

w.a: Any comparison is fine as long as the writer means well.
w.why: ignores how the audience receives it

w.a: Comparisons alienate audiences only when they are grammatically incorrect.
w.why: confuses correctness with fit to audience

cards.q: Define diction.
cards.a: Diction is a writer's deliberate word choice, considered individually and as a pattern. Together with syntax it influences how the audience perceives the writer (expert or outsider, peer or superior, sincere or evasive) and so how readily the audience accepts the argument.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + its effect on perception
cards.n: Borrows the term from Style; analyze diction in clusters and say what the pattern makes this audience think of the writer.

cards.q: Define register.
cards.a: Register is the level of formality and the variety of language a writer selects for a situation, from intimate and casual to formal and ceremonial. It sets the relationship the writer claims with the audience, which shapes how the writer is perceived and whether the argument is welcomed.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + the relationship it sets
cards.n: A shift in register mid-text is worth quoting; it usually signals a change in the relationship the writer wants with the audience.

cards.q: Contrast formal and informal register and state what each does to writer-audience distance.
cards.a: Formal register (elevated diction, complete constructions, no slang) creates distance and projects authority and seriousness; informal register (contractions, colloquialism, short forms) closes distance and signals solidarity. The choice shapes whether the audience perceives the writer as an expert above them or a peer beside them.
cards.h: → two registers + what each does to distance
cards.n: Distance is the payoff; 'the language is informal' earns nothing until you say what closeness does for this writer's purpose with this audience.

cards.q: Define persona.
cards.a: A persona is the constructed identity a writer adopts within a text (the humble neighbor, the outraged citizen, the seasoned expert), built through diction, syntax, and detail. It is how the writer asks to be perceived, and it may differ from the real author.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + how it is built
cards.n: Persona is a choice: ask why this mask would make this audience more willing to accept the argument.

cards.q: Define plain style and give an example.
cards.a: A style of simple, direct, largely concrete diction and short declarative sentences without ornament, e.g. 'The dam is old. The river is high. Leave tonight.' Its bareness makes a writer seem candid and urgent, which can raise an audience's trust where ornament would sound like spin.
cards.n: Borrows from Style: plain style is a choice, not an absence of style; explain how it shapes the audience's view of the writer (honest, urgent).

cards.q: Explain how the syntax shapes the audience's perception of the speaker: 'The bridge is safe. I have inspected it. My own children cross it every morning.' (a county engineer answering residents at a town meeting after rumors that a bridge is failing)
cards.a: Three short declaratives, each a flat statement of fact, make the engineer sound certain and unhedged, and the escalation to 'my own children' ties her credibility to personal stake. Anxious residents perceive a confident expert with nothing to hide, which makes them more likely to accept her claim that the bridge is safe.
cards.n: Borrows syntax from Style; 'she uses short sentences for emphasis' stops short of the EK: how syntax changes the audience's view and acceptance.

cards.q: Decide which revision makes a student writer more credible to the school board, and explain why. Original: 'Honestly, the new phone policy is kind of ridiculous and nobody likes it.' (A) 'The new phone policy is super unfair and literally everyone hates it.' (B) 'In a survey of 312 students, 71 percent said the new phone policy has made it harder to reach family during emergencies.'
cards.a: (B). Measured diction and a specific survey result present the student as a careful reporter rather than a complainer, so board members perceive a credible advocate and weigh the claim. (A) keeps the casual intensifiers ('super,' 'literally') and the sweeping 'everyone,' which lead adult readers to dismiss the writer as exaggerating.
cards.h: → letter + how each version makes the writer seem
cards.n: Choosing (A) because it 'shows passion' ignores the EK: diction shapes how the board perceives the writer, and so whether it accepts the claim.

cards.q: Write a revision of this sentence so a panel of engineers would take the writer seriously: 'The new bridge design is totally awesome and way safer than the old one.'
cards.a: Model: 'The proposed design distributes load across four cable stays rather than two, reducing peak stress on each anchor, which makes it measurably safer than the current bridge.' Precise technical diction and a subordinate clause explaining the mechanism signal expertise, so specialist readers perceive a writer who understands the subject.
cards.h: → one revised sentence + why it changes perception
cards.n: Swapping 'awesome' for 'excellent' keeps the problem; engineers need precise terms and reasons, not a more formal adjective.

cards.q: Explain the rhetorical effect of Lincoln opening with 'Four score and seven years ago' rather than 'eighty-seven years ago.'
cards.a: The biblical cadence of 'four score' gives the dedication a solemn, scriptural register, so listeners hear the speaker voicing a sacred national moment rather than reporting a date. Counting back to 1776 also grounds the nation in the Declaration's equality claim, which the speech goes on to renew.
cards.h: → archaic, biblical phrasing → solemn register → speaker heard as the voice of the occasion → sacred framing accepted
cards.n: Borrows diction from Style; naming 'archaic diction' without its effect on the audience at a cemetery dedication earns nothing.
o: 'Eighty-seven years ago' would sound like arithmetic; 'four score and seven' sounds like scripture, matching a cemetery dedication.
Dating the nation from the Declaration rather than the Constitution makes equality, not law, the founding principle the audience is asked to honor.

w.a: Lincoln said 'four score' because that is how everyone talked in 1863.
w.why: a factual guess that ignores the choice's effect

w.a: The phrase is an example of archaic diction.
w.why: names the device without its effect on the audience

w.a: Lincoln wanted the speech to sound old-fashioned so people would remember it.
w.why: vague; no link to occasion or purpose

cards.q: Explain why a writer's shift from 'you' to 'we' can change how an audience perceives the writer.
cards.a: 'You' places the writer outside and above the audience, as someone assigning blame or tasks; 'we' places the writer among them, sharing the burden. The shift makes the writer seem an ally rather than a critic, so the audience is more willing to accept the demand that follows.
cards.h: → 'you' = outside, judging → 'we' = inside, sharing → writer seen as ally → demand accepted
cards.n: 'It makes the audience feel included' is half the answer; say how the pronoun changes the audience's view of the writer and the demand.
o: First-person plural turns a demand into a shared commitment, which lowers the audience's resistance to being told what to do.
The pronoun shift can mark a turn in the text from diagnosis to solution, and the writer's inclusion signals willingness to share the cost.

w.a: Writers switch to 'we' because 'you' is grammatically incorrect in formal writing.
w.why: false and not a rhetorical reason

w.a: Using 'we' always makes an argument more persuasive.
w.why: overgeneralizes; it can seem presumptuous to an audience that sees the writer as an outsider

cards.q: Explain why grammatical errors in a complaint letter can reduce a reader's acceptance of an otherwise valid argument.
cards.a: Readers judge the writer as well as the claim. Errors suggest carelessness, and a reader who perceives the writer as careless extends that doubt to the facts and demands, so a valid complaint is discounted before it is weighed.
cards.h: → errors → writer seen as careless → doubt spreads to facts and demands → complaint discounted
cards.n: Borrows conventions from Style; 'errors are distracting' misses the EK's point about the writer's perceived credibility.
o: A company reading many complaints uses surface signals to decide which writers are reliable, and errors lower the writer's standing.
Correct conventions show respect for the reader, and a reader who feels respected is more willing to act.

w.a: Grammar does not matter as long as the complaint is true.
w.why: ignores how audiences perceive writers

w.a: Readers reject letters with errors because they cannot understand them.
w.why: most errors do not block meaning; the effect is on credibility

cards.q: Explain why elevated, formal diction suits a speaker at a memorial ceremony.
cards.a: The occasion asks the speaker to voice a community's grief and honor, and formal diction signals that the speaker takes the loss as seriously as the mourners do. Casual language would make the speaker seem to shrink the moment, costing the trust needed to comfort or charge the audience.
cards.h: → solemn occasion → formal diction shows seriousness → speaker trusted to voice grief → comfort lands
cards.n: 'Formal language sounds more professional' ignores the occasion and the mourners' perception of the speaker.
o: Formal diction marks the speech as ceremony, separating the moment from everyday talk as the audience expects.
Elevated words lend the dead the dignity the audience wants for them, which the audience credits to the speaker.

w.a: Formal diction is always better than informal diction.
w.why: ignores the rhetorical situation

w.a: Speakers use big words at memorials to show how educated they are.
w.why: about self-display, not the audience's need

cards.q: Define loaded diction and give an example.
cards.a: Word choice selected for strong emotional connotation to sway judgment rather than merely describe, e.g. calling a proposal a 'scheme' rather than a 'plan.' It can reveal the writer's bias: readers who share the bias are energized, while neutral or opposed readers may discount the writer as unfair.
cards.n: Test a loaded word by swapping in a neutral synonym and noting what shifts; then say how it affects credibility with this audience.

cards.q: Define connotation and give an example.
cards.a: Connotation is the emotional, cultural, and evaluative association a word carries beyond its literal meaning, e.g. 'thrifty,' 'frugal,' and 'stingy' all denote careful with money but connote praise, neutrality, and blame. Connotation lets a writer's bias show through apparently neutral description, which affects credibility with readers who notice it.
cards.n: Borrows connotation from Style; for RHS credit, tie the connotation to the writer's bias and to how this audience will judge it.

cards.q: Define euphemism and give an example.
cards.a: A mild or indirect expression substituted for a harsh or blunt one, e.g. 'downsizing' for firing workers, 'collateral damage' for civilian deaths. It can show tact toward a grieving audience, but when it hides responsibility, readers who see through it judge the writer evasive and credibility falls.
cards.n: Ask what the softer word protects the audience from noticing, and whether this audience will accept or resent the softening.

cards.q: Define bias as it applies to a source or speaker.
cards.a: Bias is a predisposition, interest, or perspective that shapes what a writer notices, includes, and omits. Word choice may reveal it, and a writer whose bias shows through unfair or one-sided language may lose credibility with an audience that does not share it.
cards.h: → definition + how word choice reveals it
cards.n: In synthesis, naming a source's stake and how it shapes its evidence is stronger than dismissing the source as 'biased.'

cards.q: Contrast ethos and credibility.
cards.a: Ethos is the appeal to the writer's character and authority; credibility is the trustworthiness an audience actually grants. A writer can attempt ethos (list credentials) and still lose credibility with an audience if the word choice seems biased, condescending, or careless.
cards.n: Credibility is earned or lost in the text, word by word, with a particular audience; ethos names the kind of appeal.

cards.q: Identify the textual markers that signal a writer is building credibility.
cards.a: First-person experience with the subject, credentials named or implied, precise and fairly cited evidence, measured and qualified language, fair summaries of opponents, and vocabulary or values shared with the audience. Each is a word-level choice an audience reads as a sign of an unbiased, trustworthy writer.
cards.n: Spotting a marker is identification; commentary must say why this audience would trust the writer more because of it.

cards.q: Analyze how the word choice affects the writer's credibility with undecided readers: 'The so-called developers have cooked up yet another scheme to bulldoze the wetlands, and their paid cheerleaders on the council are already lining up to rubber-stamp it.' (a letter to a town newspaper before a zoning vote)
cards.a: Loaded words ('so-called,' 'cooked up,' 'scheme,' 'bulldoze,' 'paid cheerleaders,' 'rubber-stamp') reveal the writer's bias against the project and imply corruption without evidence. Readers who already oppose it may cheer, but undecided readers are likely to see the writer as unfair and discount the letter's real concern about the wetlands.
cards.h: → loaded words + bias revealed + effect on this audience
cards.n: 'The writer uses loaded language' is identification only; the EK asks how the words affect credibility with a particular audience.

cards.q: Write a revision of this sentence that keeps its position but would preserve credibility with readers who support the project: 'The greedy developers want to destroy our wetlands for a quick buck.'
cards.a: Model: 'The development would fill twelve acres of wetland that absorb floodwater for the east side, a cost the proposal's projected tax revenue does not account for.' It keeps the opposition but replaces motive-attacking words ('greedy,' 'quick buck') with a specific, checkable consequence, so supporters must answer the argument instead of dismissing the writer.
cards.h: → one revised sentence + what changed and why
cards.n: Merely deleting 'greedy' leaves no argument; the revision needs specific, neutral language that carries the claim.

cards.q: Explain why a writer who uses neutral language about opponents often gains credibility with undecided readers.
cards.a: Undecided readers watch how a writer treats the other side as a test of fairness. Neutral language shows the writer is not driven by bias, so readers trust the writer's facts and judgment; name-calling signals that the conclusion came before the evidence.
cards.h: → undecided readers test fairness → neutral words pass the test → facts trusted → claim considered
cards.n: 'Neutral language is more polite' misses the mechanism: fairness toward opponents is evidence the writer's judgment can be trusted.
o: Fair wording lets undecided readers imagine agreeing without joining a side that insults people they know.
Loaded words give opponents an easy reason to dismiss the whole argument, which neutral wording denies them.

w.a: Writers should use neutral language so they do not hurt anyone's feelings.
w.why: politeness, not credibility

w.a: Neutral language is weaker because it shows the writer does not care.
w.why: confuses restraint with indifference

cards.q: Explain why the same loaded word can strengthen a writer's credibility with one audience and weaken it with another.
cards.a: A loaded word signals whose side the writer is on. Readers who share that bias hear it as honest conviction and trust the writer more; readers who do not hear it as prejudice and trust the writer less. As the EK says, credibility depends on the particular audience.
cards.h: → loaded word shows the writer's side → allies hear conviction → others hear bias → credibility splits
cards.n: Judging a word 'good' or 'bad' in the abstract ignores the EK's phrase 'with a particular audience.'
o: Word choice is read through the audience's own values, so the same connotation lands as insight or insult.
A rally audience rewards shared language as loyalty, while a mixed audience punishes it as partisanship.

w.a: Loaded words always damage a writer's credibility.
w.why: ignores audiences who share the bias

w.a: Loaded words are persuasive because they are emotional.
w.why: names pathos without the audience-dependent effect

cards.q: Explain why a euphemism in a corporate apology can cost the company credibility.
cards.a: An apology's audience wants the harm named plainly. Calling layoffs 'a realignment of resources' signals that the company is shielding itself, so readers perceive the apology as evasive and doubt its promises; blunt words would show the accountability the audience demands.
cards.h: → audience wants the harm named → euphemism shields the company → apology seems evasive → promises doubted
cards.n: 'Euphemisms are vague' is true but thin; say what this audience needs from an apology and how the softening denies it.
o: The euphemism reveals a bias toward protecting the company, which contradicts the apology's stated purpose.
Readers who were harmed recognize the softened term as spin, and spin is the opposite of the candor an apology promises.

w.a: Euphemisms make an apology sound more professional.
w.why: ignores the audience's need for accountability

w.a: The company used a euphemism so the apology would be shorter.
w.why: no link to credibility or audience

cards.q: Define a straw man rebuttal and explain why it damages ethos even when it wins the exchange.
cards.a: A straw man rebuttal attacks a weakened or distorted version of the opposing view instead of the view itself. Even when it seems to win, readers who hold or know the real position see the misrepresentation as unfair and biased, so the writer loses credibility with exactly the audience the argument needed to move.
cards.h: → distort the opposing view → easy win → informed readers see unfairness → credibility lost where it mattered
cards.n: Borrows refutation from Claims and Evidence; 'it is a logical fallacy' names the flaw but not its cost with this audience.
o: Undecided readers judge a writer's fairness by how accurately the other side is summarized, so a caricature signals bias.
Readers who hold the opposing view hear it misstated, conclude the writer never understood it, and stop listening.

w.a: A straw man is effective because it makes the other side look weak.
w.why: ignores how informed readers judge the distortion

w.a: A straw man only hurts the writer if the opponent points it out.
w.why: readers can recognize the distortion themselves

cards.q: Apply audience analysis: a price-hike memo will reach both loyal customers and industry regulators. What adjustment does this demand?
cards.a: The writer must adapt one text for two audiences with different perspectives and needs: loyal customers need reassurance and a sense of continued value, conveyed through tone and plain language, while regulators need factual justification, costs, and compliance detail. Evidence, organization, and language must serve both without contradicting either.
cards.h: → each audience's need + the adjustment it demands
cards.n: With a mixed audience no single appeal can carry the whole text; name which part addresses which audience's need.

cards.q: Define a captive audience and explain how it changes rhetorical strategy.
cards.a: An audience that must receive a message regardless of interest, such as students at a mandatory assembly. Because their attention is not self-selected, the writer must earn engagement by choosing evidence, examples, and language drawn from their perspective rather than assuming interest.
cards.n: A captive audience is not automatically hostile, only not self-selected; the needed adjustment is engagement, not concession.

cards.q: Define jargon and give an example.
cards.a: Specialized vocabulary of a profession or field, e.g. 'amortization,' 'titrate,' 'tort.' With specialists it signals expertise and saves time; with a general audience it excludes and confuses, so a writer considering the audience's context must define it or replace it.
cards.n: Borrows the term from Style; jargon is never good or bad in itself, only fitted or unfitted to this audience's background.

cards.q: Define colloquial diction and give an example.
cards.a: Informal, conversational word choice from everyday speech, e.g. 'kind of a mess,' 'no big deal,' 'y'all.' With a peer audience it closes distance and signals sincerity or shared identity; with a formal audience, such as a hearing board, it can cost the writer authority.
cards.n: Borrows from Style; judge colloquial language by the audience's context and expectations, not by a rule that informal is wrong.

cards.q: Define appeal to authority.
cards.a: Support drawn from the testimony of an expert, institution, or respected figure, borrowing that source's credibility for the writer's claim. It persuades only when the audience recognizes and respects the authority, so writers choose authorities from the audience's own perspective (a coach for athletes, a pediatrician for parents).
cards.n: Borrows expert opinion as evidence from Claims and Evidence; an authority this audience distrusts, or one irrelevant to the claim, adds nothing.

cards.q: Identify how the writer changed evidence, organization, and language for each audience. Version 1, to the city council: 'Adding a crossing guard at Fifth and Main would cost 14,000 dollars a year; the intersection saw nine pedestrian injuries last year, and the city's liability for one serious injury exceeds 200,000 dollars.' Version 2, to parents in a school newsletter: 'Last spring, a second-grader was clipped by a turning truck at Fifth and Main. A crossing guard there would mean one more adult watching for our kids. Come to Tuesday's council meeting.'
cards.a: Evidence: the council gets cost, injury counts, and liability, matching its budget perspective; parents get one child's near miss, matching their fear. Organization: the council version reasons from cost to benefit; the parent version moves from story to image to a call to act. Language: impersonal and numerical for officials, personal ('our kids') for parents.
cards.h: → evidence, organization, language, one line each
cards.n: Noticing only that 'one version is more emotional' misses two of the EK's three levers: evidence and organization change too.

cards.q: Decide which evidence would best persuade an audience of rural county commissioners to fund a mobile health clinic. (A) A national report on the rising cost of urban emergency rooms (B) A statement from a celebrity health advocate (C) The county's own data showing residents drive an average of 48 miles to the nearest clinic, and a neighboring county's figures after its mobile clinic cut ambulance calls by a fifth (D) A description of a hospital's new surgical wing
cards.a: (C). It uses the commissioners' own county data and a comparable rural county's result, evidence drawn from their context that answers their need to justify spending. (A) addresses cities, not their county; (B) relies on an authority they have no reason to trust on local needs; (D) is irrelevant to a mobile clinic.
cards.h: → letter + fit to the audience's context + why others fail
cards.n: The trap is the most impressive-sounding source; the exam rewards evidence drawn from this audience's perspective and needs.

cards.q: Write the same claim, that the town should build a dog park, twice: once for the parks budget committee and once for dog owners in a neighborhood newsletter.
cards.a: Committee: 'A fenced dog park on the unused lot at Birch Road would be a one-time capital cost and would reduce the off-leash complaints that now take up much of park staff's time.' Newsletter: 'Imagine a place where your dog can run full speed off the leash, and you can stop apologizing to joggers. Help us build it at Birch Road.' Each matches its audience's needs: cost versus daily life.
cards.h: → two versions + the need each serves
cards.n: Writing the same sentence with different adjectives misses the EK: evidence and organization, not just words, must change with the audience.

cards.q: Explain how a writer adapts diction for a specialist audience versus a general audience.
cards.a: For specialists, the writer uses technical terms undefined and skips steps, which signals competence and respects their time. For a general audience, the writer defines or replaces jargon and spells out the reasoning, because the audience's background, not the subject, sets how much must be explained.
cards.h: → audience background sets the level → specialists: terms + skipped steps → general: definitions + explained steps
cards.n: Borrows diction from Style; overexplaining to experts is as much a misstep as underexplaining to a general reader.
o: The same content needs different language because audiences differ in the contexts and needs they bring.
Undefined jargon tells a general reader the text is not for them, while defined terms invite them in.

w.a: A writer should always use simple words so that everyone can understand.
w.why: ignores that specialists expect precision

w.a: Using technical terms always makes the writer more credible.
w.why: true only with an audience that shares them

cards.q: Explain why an appeal can backfire with a particular audience.
cards.a: An appeal backfires when it assumes beliefs, knowledge, or trust the audience lacks. Heavy pathos can feel manipulative to a skeptical audience, and dense data can alienate a general one; because audiences are unique, an appeal that moves one group can harden another against the writer.
cards.h: → appeal assumes what the audience lacks → mismatch → reader resists → writer's position weakens
cards.n: Judging fit to audience, not just naming the appeal, separates analysis from labeling.
o: The same appeal meets different perspectives, contexts, and needs, so its effect depends on who receives it.
An appeal that feels like pressure to the wrong audience reveals the writer's misreading of them, which costs credibility.

w.a: Appeals only backfire when the writer uses them incorrectly.
w.why: ignores that fit depends on the audience

w.a: Pathos always backfires because emotional arguments are weak.
w.why: overgeneralizes about one appeal

cards.q: Explain why a writer speaking to the same audience a second time, after a failed vote, should change the argument.
cards.a: Audiences are dynamic: after the vote they know the first argument and have already rejected it. Repeating it invites the same result, so the writer must address the reasons they voted no (cost, trust), perhaps with new evidence or a revised proposal, meeting the audience where it now stands.
cards.h: → audience changed by the vote → old argument already rejected → answer their reasons → new evidence
cards.n: 'Try harder' or 'say it louder' ignores the EK's word 'dynamic': the audience's perspective has moved since the first argument.
o: The vote revealed the audience's real objections, so the writer now knows which needs the second argument must meet.
An unchanged argument signals the writer did not listen, which costs goodwill with an audience that has already said no.

w.a: The writer should repeat the same argument because persistence eventually wins.
w.why: ignores the audience's changed perspective

w.a: The writer should find a completely different audience instead.
w.why: evades the task of adapting to this audience

cards.q: Define a claim in argumentation.
cards.a: A claim is a statement of the writer's position that a reasonable reader could dispute, so it requires a defense: evidence and/or reasoning the audience needs before accepting it. Writers convey their positions through one or more such claims. A statement no informed reader would dispute is a fact, and it can serve as evidence but not as a claim.
cards.n: 'A claim is the writer's opinion' earns nothing; the CED's test is whether the statement requires a defense, not whether it is personal.
x: a statement that requires a defense

cards.q: Define burden of proof in argumentation.
cards.a: Burden of proof is the obligation, carried by whoever makes a claim, to supply enough evidence and reasoning for the audience to accept it. It follows from the CED's point that claims require a defense: stating a position creates the duty to defend it, and the burden is heaviest for a claim that asks readers to change what they believe or do.
cards.h: → who carries it + why it follows from claims
cards.n: Not a CED term (flagged as helpful). 'Prove me wrong' tries to shift the burden to the reader and defends nothing.

cards.q: Define a claim of fact and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of fact asserts that something is, was, or will be the case, and it is defended with verifiable evidence. It counts as a claim only if it is disputable: 'Most Ridgeview students sleep fewer than seven hours on school nights' needs survey data to defend, while 'Ridgeview's first bell rings at 7:25' is a checkable fact that needs no defense.
cards.n: Fact, value, policy and cause are a classroom taxonomy, not CED terms; a 'claim of fact' nobody disputes fails the CED test of requiring a defense.
x: that something is or was true

cards.q: Define a claim of value and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of value judges something as good or bad, better or worse, right or wrong, and is defended by naming a standard and showing that the subject meets or fails it. Example: 'The new library is a better public space than the one it replaced, because it serves more kinds of people.' The standard, serving more people, is part of what the writer must defend.
cards.n: A value claim with no stated standard ('The library is great') reads as taste; naming the criterion is what makes it defensible.

cards.q: Define a claim of policy and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of policy argues that a specific action should or should not be taken, usually with 'should' or 'must.' Example: 'The district should move high school start times to 8:30.' Its defense has two parts: that a problem exists, and that this action would address it at an acceptable cost.
cards.n: Showing only that the problem exists skips half the burden; readers also need a reason to think this remedy works and is worth its cost.

cards.q: Define a claim of cause and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of cause asserts that one thing produces another. Example: 'Closing the downtown grocery store has pushed older residents toward cheaper, less healthy food.' Its defense needs evidence of the link and of how it works, and it must rule out other explanations; showing that the two things happened together is not enough.
cards.h: → definition + example + what its defense needs
cards.n: Correlation offered as proof of cause is the classic overreach: two things moving together is a reason to look for a cause, not proof of one.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'Requiring a civics course should not be optional for graduation.'
cards.a: A claim of policy: it urges a specific action (making a civics course a graduation requirement), signaled by 'should.' Its defense must show both that students lack what the course teaches and that requiring it would supply that, not merely that civics matters.
cards.h: → type + the signal word + its burden
cards.n: Calling it a value claim because it implies civics is good misses the action it demands; classify a claim by what the reader is asked to accept or do.

cards.q: Identify the claims in this excerpt from a volunteer coach's letter to a school board, and state which sentence is not a claim: '(1) The middle school fields flooded eleven times last spring. (2) Those closures cost our teams more practice time than weather, holidays, and testing days combined. (3) The board should fund drainage before it funds new bleachers. (4) A district that lets its fields rot has stopped taking students' health seriously.'
cards.a: Sentences 2, 3, and 4 are claims, because each requires a defense: 2 is a claim of cause and comparison that needs practice records, 3 is a claim of policy, and 4 is a claim of value. Sentence 1 is a fact anyone can check in the maintenance log, so it needs no defense; it serves as evidence for the claims that follow.
cards.h: → the claim sentences + what each needs; the fact's role
cards.n: Picking sentence 1 because it comes first confuses evidence with position; a number that can simply be looked up needs no defense.

cards.q: Explain why writers convey their positions through claims that require a defense rather than through statements everyone already accepts.
cards.a: Only a disputable statement marks where the writer stands and gives readers something to be moved on. A claim sets up the evidence and reasoning that follow as a defense with work to do; a statement everyone accepts changes no one's mind and leaves the writer's position unstated.
cards.h: → disputable claim → marks the position → evidence has something to prove → readers can be moved
cards.n: 'Claims make an essay more interesting' is too vague; say that only a disputable statement gives the evidence something to prove.
o: An accepted statement leaves readers unsure what the writer wants them to believe or do, so the argument has no direction.
Stating a claim sets the terms on which readers will judge the argument, so the writer chooses the ground of the dispute.

w.a: Writers use claims because every essay is required to have a thesis.
w.why: a formula, not a reason tied to moving an audience

w.a: Claims persuade better than facts because opinions are more convincing than facts.
w.why: confuses claims with opinions; claims depend on facts as evidence

cards.q: Contrast inductive and deductive reasoning.
cards.a: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general conclusion that is probable, never certain; deductive reasoning moves from a general premise to a specific conclusion that must be true if the premises are true. Both defend claims with reasoning: induction gathers cases, deduction applies a principle the audience accepts.
cards.n: Not CED terms (flagged as useful). 'Induction is specific, deduction is general' blurs the direction of each move and earns nothing.

cards.q: Define a syllogism and give an example.
cards.a: A syllogism is a three-part deductive argument: a major premise (a general rule), a minor premise (a case that falls under it), and a conclusion that follows. Example: every district bus must pass a yearly safety inspection; Bus 14 is a district bus; so Bus 14 must pass a yearly inspection. It defends a claim through reasoning rather than new evidence.
cards.n: A syllogism can be valid and still fail to persuade: if the audience rejects the major premise, the form proves nothing to them.

cards.q: Define an enthymeme.
cards.a: An enthymeme is a syllogism with one premise left unstated because the writer assumes the audience already accepts it. 'She should chair the budget committee; she has never missed a deadline' leaves out the premise that people who meet deadlines manage money well. Naming the missing premise shows what the writer assumes this audience believes.
cards.n: Calling any short argument an enthymeme earns nothing; name the specific premise left out and why this audience would supply it.
x: a syllogism with an unstated premise

cards.q: Decide the type of reasoning: 'Every bridge inspected this year showed rust damage, so the county's bridges are likely deteriorating faster than reports admit.'
cards.a: Inductive reasoning: it generalizes from the bridges inspected this year to all the county's bridges, so the conclusion is probable, as 'likely' concedes. Its strength depends on how many bridges were inspected and whether they were typical.
cards.h: → type + the move + what its strength depends on
cards.n: 'Likely' is a clue, not the reason; the reason is the move from sampled cases to the whole category.

cards.q: Decide the type of reasoning: 'All published city audits must be reviewed by the comptroller. This audit was published. Therefore this audit must be reviewed by the comptroller.'
cards.a: Deductive reasoning: a general rule (major premise) is applied to a specific case (minor premise), so the conclusion must follow if both premises are true. It is a complete syllogism with no premise left unstated.
cards.n: The conclusion keeps 'must be reviewed'; concluding that the comptroller did review it would not follow, since a rule is not evidence it was obeyed.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'This painting is a masterpiece because a true genius made it, and we know she's a genius because look at this masterpiece.'
cards.a: Circular reasoning (begging the question): the claim that the painting is a masterpiece is defended by the painter's genius, and her genius is defended by the painting. No independent evidence or reasoning ever enters, so the claim receives no defense at all.
cards.h: → fallacy + why the defense never starts
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). On an essay, describe the loop in your own words; the label alone earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify which sentences of this excerpt from a nurse's op-ed are evidence and which are reasoning, and state the claim they defend: '(1) Our county has one school nurse for every 2,100 students. (2) The state health department recommends one for every 750. (3) A nurse who covers three buildings cannot reach an asthma attack in its first minutes, when treatment matters most. (4) Every school needs a nurse of its own.'
cards.a: The claim is sentence 4: every school needs its own nurse. Sentences 1 and 2 are evidence, a statistic and the standard it falls short of. Sentence 3 is reasoning: it explains why the gap matters, linking the ratio to a danger, so the numbers defend the claim instead of sitting beside it.
cards.n: Calling sentence 3 evidence misses its job: it adds no new fact, only the inference that connects the numbers to the claim.

cards.q: Explain why writers use enthymemes rather than full syllogisms.
cards.a: Leaving a premise unstated lets the audience supply it, so the shared belief feels obvious rather than argued and readers half persuade themselves; it is also efficient. The risk is that readers who do not share the premise see a gap, so the choice reveals whom the writer assumes they are addressing.
cards.h: → premise left out → audience supplies it → belief feels obvious → quicker, more intimate persuasion
cards.n: 'Enthymemes are shorter' is true but earns little; the rhetorical point is what supplying the premise does to the audience.
o: An enthymeme treats the audience as insiders who already know the rule, which flatters them and builds goodwill.
Stating the premise would expose it to challenge; leaving it implicit shields it from scrutiny.

w.a: Writers use enthymemes because full syllogisms are too complicated for most readers.
w.why: condescends to readers and ignores what the unstated premise does

w.a: Enthymemes are used to trick the audience into accepting false conclusions.
w.why: treats an ordinary rhetorical choice as deception by default

cards.q: Explain why an inductive argument can be strong even though its conclusion is never certain.
cards.a: Its strength comes from its evidence: the more numerous, varied, and representative the cases, the more probable the conclusion. Certainty is the wrong standard for most claims about people, policy, or the future, so a writer defends such claims by making the conclusion probable enough to act on.
cards.h: → many representative cases → conclusion probable → probable enough to act on → strong without certainty
cards.n: 'It uses lots of evidence' is half the answer; name representativeness, since many unrepresentative cases still make a weak induction.
o: Deduction's premises are themselves usually reached by induction, so probable conclusions underlie even 'certain' arguments.
An inductive writer can qualify the conclusion honestly ('likely,' 'in most districts'), which makes it harder to refute than an absolute.

w.a: Inductive arguments are strong because statistics never lie.
w.why: overstates evidence; samples can be biased

w.a: An inductive argument is strong only if there are no counterexamples at all.
w.why: confuses probable support with proof

cards.q: Define evidence and state what it must do in an argument.
cards.a: Evidence is the material a writer offers to support a claim; the CED lists facts, anecdotes, analogies, statistics, examples, details, illustrations, expert opinions, personal observations, personal experiences, testimonies, and experiments. It must be relevant to the claim, credible to the audience, and sufficient, and commentary must explain how it supports the claim.
cards.h: → definition + the CED's types + what it must do
cards.n: Reciting the list earns nothing; a paragraph scores when the evidence is specific and the commentary says how it proves this claim.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of analogy as evidence.
cards.a: An analogy makes an unfamiliar or abstract case understandable by mapping it onto one the audience already knows, and it can carry the audience's attitude from the known case to the new one. Its limit: it proves nothing by itself and fails when the two cases differ in the respect that matters, so writers pair it with other evidence.
cards.n: Treating an analogy as proof invites the reply 'the cases are different'; say which likeness carries the argument and why it holds.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of textual evidence.
cards.a: Quoted or paraphrased text lets readers check a claim against the source's own words, which makes it the core evidence of rhetorical analysis and synthesis. Its limits: a quotation can be pulled out of context, can crowd out the writer's own thinking, or can be left unexplained, and then it proves nothing.
cards.n: A long quotation with no commentary is the classic Row B ceiling; quote the few words that matter and explain them.

cards.q: Contrast quantitative and qualitative evidence.
cards.a: Quantitative evidence is numerical (statistics, measurements, survey percentages) and shows scale and pattern; qualitative evidence is descriptive (interviews, observations, testimonies, anecdotes) and shows experience and meaning that numbers miss. Arguments often pair them: the number shows how widespread, the account shows why it matters.
cards.n: Numbers are not automatically stronger; a claim about how people experience a policy may need testimony more than a percentage.

cards.q: Define a case study as a form of evidence and note its main limitation.
cards.a: A case study is an in-depth examination of one person, place, or event used to illustrate or test a broader claim; it bundles details, observations, and often testimony. Its main limitation is reach: one case, however vivid, may not be typical, so it cannot by itself establish a general pattern.
cards.n: 'Case study' is not on the CED's list; it combines several listed types. Generalizing from one case alone is the hasty-generalization trap.

cards.q:
Identify the CED evidence type in each excerpt (letters about city buses):
1. 'The route cuts took effect March 3.'
2. 'My neighbor, a night nurse, waited ninety minutes for a bus that never came.'
3. 'A city without buses is a body with blocked arteries.'
4. 'Forty-two percent of riders surveyed had missed work over a late bus.'
5. 'Consider Linden Street, where one added route halved commutes.'
6. 'The Fifth Street shelter has no roof, no bench, and a faded schedule.'
7. 'Picture a student with a trombone case in sleet for forty minutes.'
8. 'A university transit planner calls the map "designed for 1975."'
9. 'Each morning this month I counted more riders than seats.'
10. 'I rode the 14 for four years, late every week.'
11. 'A driver told the council she is ordered to skip stops.'
12. 'Two routes made free for three months gained 19 percent in riders; two unchanged routes, 2 percent.'
cards.a:
1 → fact (a checkable date)
2 → anecdote (a brief story about someone else)
3 → analogy (maps the city onto a body)
4 → statistic
5 → example (one representative case)
6 → details (specific features of one place)
7 → illustration (an imagined picture that makes the point concrete)
8 → expert opinion
9 → personal observation (what the writer saw)
10 → personal experience (what the writer lived)
11 → testimony (a witness's account)
12 → experiment (a comparison of changed and unchanged routes)
cards.n: Types overlap (an anecdote is also an example); name the closest type and what it does for the claim, which is what the exam asks.

cards.q: Explain why the CED counts analogies and personal experiences as evidence even though neither can prove a general claim on its own.
cards.a: Evidence supports a claim without having to prove it alone: an analogy makes the reasoning clear by linking a new case to a familiar one, and a personal experience shows what the claim means in a life. Writers combine types so each does the work it suits, and the argument as a whole carries the proof.
cards.h: → support is not proof → each type does different work → analogy clarifies, experience humanizes → combined they defend
cards.n: 'All evidence is equally valid' earns nothing; the point is that each type supports differently and few work alone.
o: Readers persuaded only by numbers are rare; types that make a claim vivid or understandable move readers statistics leave cold.
The exam's passages are argumentative prose in which writers routinely argue by analogy and experience, so readers must be able to explain how those support claims.

w.a: Analogies and personal experiences are on the list because they are the easiest evidence to find.
w.why: availability is not a reason a type supports a claim

w.a: Personal experience always proves a claim because the writer was actually there.
w.why: one person's experience cannot establish a general pattern

cards.q: Identify what makes a thesis statement NOT defensible.
cards.a: A thesis is not defensible when it restates the prompt, states an obvious fact that needs no defense, summarizes the issue or others' views without taking a position, or is too vague for any evidence to test. The CED's test: an effective claim provokes interest and requires a defense; if no reasonable reader could disagree, there is nothing to prove.
cards.n: 'It must be a strong opinion' misses the point: forceful wording does not help if the statement still requires no defense.

cards.q:
Decide whether each statement is an effective claim (it requires a defense) or an obvious fact (it requires none):
1. 'Many teenagers own smartphones.'
2. 'Phones should be locked away during class, not just silenced.'
3. 'Our town has two public pools.'
4. 'The town's second pool does more for public health than a third police cruiser would.'
5. 'Exercise is good for people.'
6. 'Gym class should be graded on effort, not athletic skill.'
7. 'Voting in local elections is legal for adult citizens.'
8. 'Local elections shape daily life more than national ones do.'
9. 'Libraries lend books.'
10. 'A library card is the most underused public benefit in this county.'
cards.a:
1 → obvious fact
2 → effective claim (a policy readers could reject)
3 → obvious fact
4 → effective claim (a comparison that needs evidence)
5 → obvious fact
6 → effective claim (a policy on grading)
7 → obvious fact
8 → effective claim (a comparative judgment)
9 → obvious fact
10 → effective claim (a superlative that must be defended)
cards.h: → one verdict per line, with what makes it disputable
cards.n: Topic is not the test: 5 and 6 are both about exercise, but only 6 takes a position a reasonable reader could dispute.

cards.q: Decide which opening claim better serves an op-ed arguing for a four-day school week, and explain why: (A) 'School schedules have changed many times over the past century.' (B) 'A four-day week would give students the one thing a fifth day of class cannot: time to recover.'
cards.a: (B): it takes a position a reader could dispute and provokes interest with a paradox (less school as a benefit) that readers will want tested, so it launches the argument. (A) is a known fact that needs no defense; a reader can accept it and still reject the four-day week.
cards.h: → letter + provokes interest + requires a defense
cards.n: Choosing (A) because it sounds balanced or factual misreads the EK: an opening that asks for no defense gives the op-ed nothing to argue.

cards.q: Write a claim that requires a defense, starting from this obvious fact: 'Many high school students have part-time jobs.'
cards.a: Model: 'A part-time job teaches high school students more about managing time than any study-skills class, as long as the job stays under fifteen hours a week.' It takes a position a reader could reject and sets a limit, so it would need evidence (grades, hours, testimony) to defend.
cards.h: → model claim + why it needs a defense
cards.n: 'Many students have jobs, which is interesting' still states the fact; the rewrite must assert something a reasonable reader could dispute.

cards.q: Identify the sentence that states the speaker's claim in this opening of a restaurant owner's remarks to a city council, and explain why the other sentences are not claims: '(1) Our block has four restaurants and one parking lot. (2) The lot has sixty spaces. (3) On Friday nights all sixty are full by six o'clock. (4) Your plan to turn that lot into a plaza will close at least one of us within a year.'
cards.a: Sentence 4 is the claim: it predicts a consequence of the council's plan that listeners could dispute and the owner must defend. Sentences 1 to 3 are facts anyone can check by walking the block; they need no defense and serve as evidence that parking is already scarce.
cards.h: → the claim sentence + why the rest are facts as evidence
cards.n: Choosing sentence 3 because it is the most vivid confuses striking evidence with the position the evidence is there to defend.

cards.q: Explain why an argument that opens with 'Technology has changed the way we live' loses readers' interest before it reaches its thesis.
cards.a: The sentence is an obvious fact every reader already accepts, so it provokes no interest and commits the writer to nothing; readers learn neither the position nor what is at stake. An effective claim raises a question readers want answered, which pulls them into the evidence.
cards.h: → obvious fact → nothing to dispute → no position, no stakes → no reason to read on
cards.n: 'It is too broad' is only part of it; the CED's point is that an obvious fact requires no defense and so gives readers nothing to weigh.
o: A sentence any essay on any subject could begin with signals that the writer has not yet decided what to argue.
Opening with a claim lets every later sentence read as support; opening with a truism delays the argument and wastes the reader's first attention.

w.a: The opening fails because it does not include a statistic.
w.why: a statistic would still be evidence, not a claim

w.a: The sentence is fine because it is true and nobody can argue with it.
w.why: being unarguable is exactly why it cannot serve as a claim

cards.q: Explain why a writer might open with an obvious fact and then state a claim that requires a defense.
cards.a: An agreed fact gives the audience common ground and context, so the claim that follows reads as a reasonable next step rather than an attack. The fact works as a starting point and as evidence, not as the claim; the problem arises only when the writing never moves past it.
cards.h: → shared fact → common ground and context → claim lands as a reasonable next step
cards.n: Saying 'the fact is a hook' names a label without the reason; explain what agreeing with the fact does for the audience's willingness to hear the claim.
o: Starting from a fact readers accept lets the writer lead them step by step to a conclusion they might resist if it came first.
The contrast between the settled fact and the disputed claim can itself create interest: this is known, but here is what it means.

w.a: Writers start with facts because facts are always more persuasive than claims.
w.why: facts cannot persuade anyone of a position no one has stated

w.a: Opening with a fact is always a mistake on the AP exam.
w.why: the problem is stopping at the fact, not starting from one

cards.q: Contrast quoting, paraphrasing, and summarizing as ways to embed a source's information in your own sentences.
cards.a: Quoting reproduces the source's exact words in quotation marks, best when the wording itself matters. Paraphrasing restates a specific passage in your own words and structure at about its original length. Summarizing condenses a longer passage to its main point. All three must be syntactically embedded in the writer's own ideas and attributed to the source.
cards.h: → three definitions + when each fits + shared rule
cards.n: A paraphrase that swaps a few synonyms into the source's sentence structure is neither your own words nor a quotation; restate it fully or quote it.

cards.q: Identify whether each sentence quotes, paraphrases, or summarizes this source, a city health office report: 'Blocks with under 10 percent tree cover recorded afternoon surface temperatures up to 12 degrees Fahrenheit higher than blocks with over 30 percent cover.' 1. 'On the city's barest blocks, afternoon pavement runs as much as 12 degrees hotter than on its leafiest ones.' 2. 'The health office found that the barest blocks run "up to 12 degrees Fahrenheit higher" in the afternoon.' 3. 'The health office's report shows that tree cover and heat are linked across the city.'
cards.a: 1 → paraphrase: the same specific finding restated in new words and structure. 2 → quotation: the exact phrase is in quotation marks, embedded in the writer's sentence. 3 → summary: it reduces the finding to its general point and drops the figures.
cards.h: → one label per sentence + the tell
cards.n: Sentence 1 still needs attribution in an essay; a paraphrase without a source reads as the writer's own finding.
