cards.q: Decide which version better embeds the source in the writer's argument, and explain why: (A) 'Trees cool neighborhoods. "Blocks with under 10 percent tree cover recorded afternoon surface temperatures up to 12 degrees Fahrenheit higher." This is important.' (B) 'Because the city's own health office found that the barest blocks run "up to 12 degrees Fahrenheit higher" in the afternoon, planting trees there is public health, not decoration.'
cards.a: (B): the quoted words sit inside the writer's own sentence and grammar, are attributed, and are put to work for the writer's claim in the same breath. (A) drops the quotation as a freestanding sentence and follows it with a comment that explains nothing.
cards.h: → letter + embedded, attributed, and used for the claim
cards.n: 'This is important' after a dropped quotation is the classic empty follow-up; say what the quotation proves.

cards.q: Write one sentence that embeds a short quotation from this source in your own claim. Source: a school counselor's survey report states, 'Two thirds of students who work more than 20 hours a week said they had fallen asleep in class at least once this month.'
cards.a: Model: 'If, as the counselor's survey found, "two thirds of students who work more than 20 hours a week" have fallen asleep in class this month, then a cap on student work hours protects learning, not just sleep.' The quoted phrase fits the sentence's grammar, is attributed, and serves the writer's claim.
cards.h: → model sentence + what makes it embedded
cards.n: Quoting the entire sentence and adding 'This shows that students are tired' embeds nothing; take only the words you need and make them part of your claim.

cards.q: Explain why embedding a quotation inside your own sentence is more effective than letting it stand as a sentence of its own.
cards.a: Embedding makes the source serve the writer's claim: the writer's syntax frames how the words are read, the attribution shows where they come from, and the sentence moves straight to what they prove. A freestanding quotation interrupts the line of reasoning and leaves readers to guess why it is there.
cards.h: → writer's syntax frames the words → source serves the claim → reasoning keeps moving
cards.n: 'It flows better' names a feeling, not a reason; say that embedding makes the source's words part of the writer's claim.
o: An embedded quotation can be trimmed to the few words that matter, which keeps the focus on the evidence the claim needs.
A dropped quotation hands control of the paragraph to the source; embedding keeps the writer's voice in charge.

w.a: Embedding quotations is just a formatting rule graders care about.
w.why: misses what embedding does for the line of reasoning

w.a: Standalone quotations are better because they let the source speak for itself.
w.why: sources do not explain their own relevance to your claim

cards.q: Explain why a writer might paraphrase a source's statistic rather than quote it.
cards.a: A statistic's exact wording rarely matters, so paraphrase lets the writer keep the number accurate while fitting it into the writer's own sentence and emphasis, keeping one voice and saving quotation for words whose phrasing carries the point. The paraphrase still needs attribution.
cards.h: → a number's wording rarely matters → paraphrase fits it to the writer's sentence → quote only telling phrasing
cards.n: 'Paraphrasing avoids plagiarism' is backwards: a paraphrase must still be attributed, so that is not the reason to choose it.
o: Quoting a dense sentence of data forces readers through the source's phrasing; a paraphrase can foreground the one figure the claim needs.
Too many quotations make an essay read as a collage of sources; paraphrase keeps the argument in the writer's voice.

w.a: Writers paraphrase statistics so they can round the numbers in their favor.
w.why: changing the figure misrepresents the source

w.a: Paraphrasing means you do not have to say where the number came from.
w.why: paraphrased information still requires attribution

cards.q: State the six purposes for which the CED says writers use evidence strategically, with a one-clause gloss of each.
cards.a: To illustrate (make an idea concrete by showing it), clarify (make a complex or abstract point understandable), set a mood (create an emotional atmosphere), exemplify (offer a representative instance of a general claim), associate (link the subject to something whose qualities transfer to it), and amplify (enlarge or intensify a point's importance).
cards.n: The CED lists the six without defining them; these glosses are working definitions. Naming a purpose earns credit only with its effect on this audience.
x: illustrate, clarify, set a mood, exemplify, associate, amplify

cards.q:
Identify the primary purpose (illustrate, clarify, set a mood, exemplify, associate, or amplify) of the evidence in each excerpt from speeches about a river cleanup:
1. 'The river carries 40 tons of trash a year, about the weight of four loaded school buses.'
2. 'At dawn the water is brown and still, and the only sound is plastic knocking against the pilings.'
3. 'Take the Marsh Road culvert: in March it was blocked by 300 bottles and flooded six basements.'
4. 'Cleaning this river is the same work our grandparents did when they built the levee by hand.'
5. 'It is not one bag of trash. It is ten thousand bags, from every street, every storm drain, every season, for thirty years.'
6. 'Imagine a heron lifting its head from the shallows with a six-pack ring around its beak.'
cards.a:
1 → clarify (turns an abstract tonnage into a size listeners can picture)
2 → set a mood (bleak stillness before the argument)
3 → exemplify (one representative case of litter causing floods)
4 → associate (links the cleanup to ancestral civic pride)
5 → amplify (repetition and accumulation magnify the scale)
6 → illustrate (a concrete image of harm to wildlife)
cards.h: → one purpose per line + what it does
cards.n: Illustrate and exemplify overlap: an example is one real case of a pattern, an illustration makes the idea visible; defend your label with the effect.

cards.q: Decide which sentence a speaker should add to amplify the claim that the county's rural roads are dangerous, and explain why: (A) 'Last year a school bus slid into the ditch on Miller Road.' (B) 'Last year: 212 crashes on rural roads, 212 phone calls to families, 212 times a deputy's car pulled into a driveway at night.'
cards.a: (B): repeating '212' across three escalating images enlarges the number into a toll on families, which intensifies the point's importance. (A) exemplifies the danger with one representative case, which is useful, but it narrows attention to a single event rather than magnifying it.
cards.h: → letter + what amplifying does + what the other does
cards.n: Picking (A) because a school bus is more emotional confuses exemplifying with amplifying; the task names the purpose, so match it.

cards.q: Write one sentence of evidence that clarifies this abstract point for an audience of eighth graders: 'The school's budget shortfall is large.' Use these figures: the shortfall is $180,000, and one teacher's salary and benefits cost about $90,000 a year.
cards.a: Model: 'The shortfall, $180,000, is what it costs to pay two teachers for a full year.' Converting an abstract sum into a unit eighth graders understand (their teachers) makes the size of the problem clear, which is what evidence that clarifies does.
cards.h: → model sentence + what it converts the number into
cards.n: Adding more numbers ('a 4.2 percent deficit') does not clarify for this audience; translate the figure into something they already know.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might use evidence to set a mood before presenting statistics.
cards.a: A mood prepares the audience to feel what is at stake, so the numbers that follow land as confirmation of something already felt rather than as abstractions. Evidence that sets a mood also signals the writer's attitude, framing how readers will interpret the data.
cards.h: → mood first → audience feels the stakes → numbers confirm the feeling → data read through the writer's frame
cards.n: 'To grab the reader's attention' is the generic answer; say what the mood does to how the statistics are read.
o: Statistics alone can feel distant; a scene first gives readers a reason to care about the scale the numbers reveal.
The order matters: a mood after the numbers can read as sentimental decoration, while a mood before them shapes their meaning.

w.a: Writers set a mood first because statistics are boring.
w.why: a dismissive generalization, not an effect on this audience

w.a: Setting a mood replaces the need for statistics.
w.why: mood supports the numbers; it does not prove the claim

cards.q: Explain why the same piece of evidence can serve different purposes in different arguments.
cards.a: Purpose depends on the claim the evidence is attached to and the audience it is meant to move: a flooded basement exemplifies a pattern in an engineer's report but sets a mood in a mayor's speech to residents. Explaining evidence means naming what it does here, not applying a fixed label.
cards.h: → purpose depends on claim + audience → same fact, different job → commentary names this job
cards.n: Assigning every statistic to 'logos' and every story to 'pathos' ignores how the context changes what the evidence does.
o: The writer's placement and framing (where the evidence sits, what words surround it) direct which purpose readers perceive.
A single detail can serve two purposes at once, clarifying for one reader and amplifying for another, so strong commentary names the dominant one for the intended audience.

w.a: Each type of evidence always has one purpose, like statistics always clarify.
w.why: purpose is set by use, not by type

w.a: The purpose of evidence is always just to prove the claim.
w.why: ignores the CED's other purposes, such as setting a mood

cards.q: Decide which evidence type best persuades a skeptical policy audience and explain why.
cards.a: Verifiable data and credentialed expert opinion: a skeptical policy audience weighs cost, scale, and risk, so evidence it can check strengthens the validity of the reasoning and the writer's credibility. A brief anecdote can follow to relate the numbers to the audience's values, but it should not carry the proof.
cards.h: → evidence type + what it does for this audience
cards.n: 'Pathos, because emotions persuade' ignores this audience; strategic selection starts from what these readers value and trust.

cards.q: Identify the three things the CED says strategically selected evidence does for an argument.
cards.a: It strengthens the validity and reasoning of the argument, relates to the audience's emotions and values, and increases the writer's credibility. One well-chosen piece can do all three: a local, checkable figure supports the reasoning, touches what readers care about, and shows the writer did the work.
cards.h: → three effects + how one piece can do all three
cards.n: Mapping the three effects onto 'logos, pathos, ethos' and stopping there labels without explaining; say how this evidence does it.

cards.q: Identify what each sentence of evidence does for the argument (validity and reasoning, emotions and values, or credibility) in this excerpt from a pharmacist's letter urging her town to install a drug take-back box: '(1) In fourteen years behind the counter, I have been asked every week where to throw away old pills. (2) The sheriff's office reports that most of the painkillers it seized from teenagers last year came from a family's medicine cabinet. (3) Every one of those cabinets belongs to a family that thought it was being careful.'
cards.a: (1) builds credibility: her firsthand experience makes her an informed witness to the need. (2) strengthens validity: an official record links leftover pills to misuse, supporting the reasoning for a take-back box. (3) relates to emotions and values: it turns the record into careful families like the readers' own, so the risk feels close and blameless.
cards.h: → one effect per sentence + how it achieves it
cards.n: Calling sentence 1 'pathos' because it is personal misses its job: fourteen years of questions make her credible, not merely sympathetic.

cards.q: Decide which evidence a student should use to persuade a school board of parents that the new later start time is working, and explain why: (A) 'Sleep experts recommend eight to ten hours of sleep a night for teenagers.' (B) 'Since the change, first-period tardies at our school have fallen from 41 a week to 12.'
cards.a: (B): it is local and checkable and answers the board's actual question, whether the change is working here, so it strengthens the reasoning and relates to parents' concern for their own children. (A) is accurate but general; it shows why the change was made, not that it worked.
cards.h: → letter + fit to the board's question + what (A) lacks
cards.n: Choosing (A) because experts sound authoritative ignores the claim; evidence must support this claim for this audience, not the topic in general.

cards.q: Write a two-sentence paragraph opening: a claim that the town should build a skate park, then evidence chosen to relate to the values of retirees who worry about teenagers loitering downtown.
cards.a: Model: 'A skate park on Mill Street would give downtown back to everyone who uses it. When a neighboring town opened one two years ago, its merchants' association reported that complaints about skateboarders on shop steps fell by more than half within a year.' The evidence answers the retirees' concern (order downtown) rather than the skaters' wishes, so it relates to their values.
cards.h: → claim sentence + evidence aimed at this audience's value
cards.n: Evidence about how much teenagers love skating serves the wrong audience; strategic selection starts from what these readers fear or value.

cards.q: Explain why pairing a statistic with a brief anecdote often persuades better than either alone.
cards.a: The statistic shows scale and supports the validity of the reasoning; the anecdote gives that scale a face and relates it to the audience's emotions and values. Together they answer both the skeptic who asks 'how many?' and the reader who asks 'why should I care?'
cards.h: → statistic: scale, validity → anecdote: a face, values → together answer both kinds of doubt
cards.n: Labeling the pair 'logos plus pathos' is a start, not an answer; say what doubt each piece removes for the reader.
o: An anecdote alone invites the charge that it is one unusual case; the statistic shows it is typical.
A statistic alone can numb readers; the anecdote makes one of the numbers a person, so the scale becomes felt.

w.a: Using two kinds of evidence is always better because more evidence is better.
w.why: quantity alone is not the reason; each piece does different work

w.a: The anecdote is there to make the essay more interesting to read.
w.why: misses how it relates the claim to the audience's values

cards.q: Explain why a writer's choice of evidence can raise or lower the writer's credibility, not just the claim's.
cards.a: Readers judge writers by what they cite: accurate, current, fairly represented evidence from sources the audience respects signals care and honesty, while a dated, one-sided, or sensational source signals carelessness or bias and makes readers doubt even the sound parts of the argument.
cards.h: → evidence reveals the writer's care → good sources build trust → weak sources spread doubt to the whole argument
cards.n: 'Good evidence makes you sound smart' is vague; name what the choice shows about the writer (care, fairness, honesty).
o: Evidence the audience already trusts lets the writer borrow that trust.
A single misrepresented figure, once caught, turns readers into skeptics of every other claim.

w.a: Credibility comes only from the writer's credentials, not the evidence.
w.why: the CED says strategic evidence increases credibility

w.a: Any evidence at all increases credibility because it shows research.
w.why: poorly chosen evidence lowers credibility

cards.q: Define sufficient evidence in the CED's terms.
cards.a: Evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality provide apt support for the argument: enough instances, and instances that are relevant, credible, specific, and representative, to support the claim as stated. Sufficiency is measured against the claim, so a broad or absolute claim needs more and better evidence than a narrow, qualified one.
cards.n: 'Sufficient means a lot of evidence' misses quality: ten unrepresentative anecdotes are not apt support for a claim about a whole population.
x: quantity and quality provide apt support

cards.q: Decide the stronger evidence for a claim that a new policy is effective nationwide: one detailed case study, or a smaller statistic drawn from many locations.
cards.a: The statistic drawn from many locations: a nationwide claim needs evidence whose quality includes breadth, and results from many sites show the effect is not one place's accident. The case study can clarify how the policy works, but by itself it is insufficient for a national claim.
cards.n: Picking the case study because it is more detailed confuses vividness with sufficiency; match the evidence to the scope of the claim.

cards.q: Decide which evidence type best supports a claim about a long-term historical trend, and explain why.
cards.a: Evidence drawn from many points across the period, such as several historical examples or a data series: a trend is a pattern over time, so sufficient evidence must show the pattern repeatedly. A single anecdote or one year's statistic cannot distinguish a trend from a one-time event.
cards.h: → evidence type + why a trend needs repetition
cards.n: One dramatic historical example feels decisive but shows only that something happened once; a trend claim needs the pattern.

cards.q: Define a spurious (false) correlation and give an example.
cards.a: A spurious correlation is a statistical association between two things that are not causally connected, produced by coincidence or a hidden third factor. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer because of hot weather, not because one causes the other. Correlation alone is insufficient evidence for a claim of cause.
cards.h: → definition + example + the hidden third factor
cards.n: Treating 'these rose together' as proof of cause is the error; name the third factor or the coincidence that could explain both.

cards.q: Identify why the evidence in this paragraph from a student editorial is insufficient: 'Our cafeteria food is making students sick. Last Tuesday my friend Dana ate the chicken wrap and went home with a stomachache. Clearly, the district needs a new food vendor.'
cards.a: Both quantity and quality fall short: one anecdote about one student on one day cannot support a claim about all students, and it does not rule out other causes of Dana's stomachache. Nurse-visit records across a semester or health inspection reports would begin to be apt support for a claim as large as replacing the vendor.
cards.h: → quantity problem + quality problem + what would suffice
cards.n: 'It needs more evidence' is only half the answer; say what kind (representative, checkable) and why this claim demands it.

cards.q: Write two sentences of evidence that would make this claim sufficiently supported, naming the kinds of sources you would cite: 'The town's new crosswalk signal has made Main Street safer for pedestrians.'
cards.a: Model: 'In the eighteen months before the signal, police recorded nine collisions with pedestrians at Main and Fourth; in the eighteen months since, they have recorded one. The town engineer's counts show that traffic at the crossing rose over the same period, so the drop is not explained by fewer cars.' Comparable counts from an official source supply quantity; ruling out the obvious alternative supplies quality.
cards.h: → two evidence sentences + why they are sufficient
cards.n: 'Everyone feels safer now' is testimony without scope; a safety claim needs comparable counts before and after.

cards.q: Explain why a claim of cause needs stronger evidence than a claim of value to be defensible.
cards.a: A claim of cause asserts that one thing produces another, so sufficient evidence must show the link and rule out other explanations; correlation alone is not apt support. A claim of value is defended by showing its subject meets a stated standard, which requires relevant evidence but not ruling out rival causes.
cards.h: → cause asserts a mechanism → must rule out alternatives → value needs only a standard met → cause's bar is higher
cards.n: 'Cause claims are more scientific' is vague; name the extra burden, ruling out other explanations.
o: Two things can rise together by coincidence or because of a third factor, so a causal claim must address those possibilities; a value claim faces no such rivals.
Readers can accept a value judgment on shared criteria, but they accept a cause only when the evidence shows how it works.

w.a: Claims of cause always need statistics, while claims of value never need evidence.
w.why: value claims need evidence too

w.a: A claim of cause is proven once you show the two events happened one after the other.
w.why: that is the post hoc error

cards.q: Explain why a broad claim needs more evidence than a narrow one to be sufficiently supported.
cards.a: Sufficiency is measured against the claim: a claim about 'all students' or 'every city' must hold across every case it covers, so a few instances cannot support it, while a claim about one school can rest on that school's records. Narrowing a claim is often a faster route to sufficiency than finding more evidence.
cards.h: → scope of claim sets the bar → broad claim covers more cases → needs more and wider evidence
cards.n: 'Big claims are harder to prove' restates the question; explain that evidence must be apt to the scope of the claim.
o: A broad claim can be defeated by one counterexample from any corner it covers, so its evidence must reach those corners.
The same three examples can be sufficient for 'in our district' and insufficient for 'across the country.'

w.a: Broad claims are better because they cover more ground.
w.why: covering more ground raises the burden of proof

w.a: Any claim is supported once it has three pieces of evidence.
w.why: sufficiency depends on the claim, not a fixed number

cards.q: Contrast a claim, a thesis, and an assertion.
cards.a: A claim is any statement that requires a defense; a thesis is the main, overarching claim the writer is seeking to defend or prove, the one every other claim serves. An assertion is a statement put forward without support; it functions as a claim only once evidence and reasoning back it.
cards.n: Calling every claim in an essay 'the thesis' misreads its structure; the thesis is the one claim all the others serve.

cards.q: Define a defensible thesis.
cards.a: A defensible thesis is an overarching claim that a reasonable reader could dispute and that available evidence could support; it takes a clear position rather than restating the prompt, stating an obvious fact, or summarizing both sides. On the exam, Row A awards the point for a thesis that presents a defensible position (in rhetorical analysis, one that analyzes the writer's choices).
cards.h: → definition + what it is not + the Row A link
cards.n: Defensible does not mean correct or certain; a thesis that equivocates ('some say good, some say bad') takes no position and earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain the role of a subclaim in an essay.
cards.a: A subclaim is a supporting claim that advances one step toward the thesis, usually as a body paragraph's topic sentence. Each subclaim needs its own evidence and commentary, and together the subclaims form the line of reasoning that defends the overarching claim.
cards.h: → what it is + where it sits + how subclaims add up
cards.n: Borrows line of reasoning (reo). A subclaim that only restates the thesis in new words adds no step to the argument.

cards.q: Identify the thesis of this paragraph from a hospital volunteer's essay, and state how the other sentences relate to it: '(1) Every Thursday I push the book cart through the fourth floor. (2) Patients who ask for a book rarely want the book. (3) They want a stranger who stops for five minutes and asks what they like to read. (4) A hospital that measures care only in medications and minutes is missing the part patients remember. (5) Last week a man in room 410 told me about every mystery novel he had read since 1970.'
cards.a: Sentence 4 is the thesis: the overarching claim that care has a human dimension hospitals fail to measure. Sentence 1 gives the writer's vantage point, sentences 2 and 3 are observations that lead to it, and sentence 5 is anecdotal evidence that patients value the conversation more than the book.
cards.h: → the thesis sentence + the job of each other sentence
cards.n: Choosing sentence 2 because it sounds like a general statement confuses a supporting observation with the claim the whole paragraph defends.

cards.q: Write a defensible thesis for this prompt: 'Write an essay that argues your position on whether cities should make public transit free to ride.'
cards.a: Model: 'Cities should make public transit free, because fares keep off the buses the very riders who depend on them most, and a city that funds roads without charging drivers at each intersection can fund buses the same way.' It takes a position readers could dispute and indicates the reasoning the essay will defend.
cards.h: → model thesis + why it is defensible
cards.n: 'Free transit has pros and cons' takes no position; 'Buses carry passengers' states a fact. Neither requires a defense.

cards.q: Explain why the thesis of a rhetorical analysis essay is a claim about the writer's choices rather than about the passage's subject.
cards.a: A thesis is the overarching claim an essay defends with evidence; in rhetorical analysis the evidence is the writer's choices, so the claim must be about how those choices serve the writer's purpose. A thesis about the subject itself would need outside evidence and turn the analysis into a different argument.
cards.h: → thesis = claim the evidence defends → evidence is the writer's choices → claim must be about those choices
cards.n: Agreeing or disagreeing with the speaker in a Q2 thesis is the classic misread; the task is to analyze choices, not take a side on the issue.
o: The rhetorical analysis rubric awards Row A for a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices, which a claim about the subject cannot do.
Only a claim about choices can be defended entirely from the passage, which is all the evidence the task provides.

w.a: The thesis should say whether the writer is right, because every essay needs a position.
w.why: that is the argument task, not rhetorical analysis

w.a: A good thesis summarizes what the passage is about in one sentence.
w.why: a summary is not a claim that requires defense

cards.q: Explain why every body paragraph of an argument should be traceable back to its thesis.
cards.a: The thesis is the overarching claim the whole essay exists to defend, so each paragraph's claim, evidence, and commentary must advance it. A paragraph that proves something else, however true, spends the reader's attention without adding support and blurs what the essay argues.
cards.h: → thesis = the claim the essay defends → each paragraph must advance it → off-thesis proof dilutes the argument
cards.n: 'So the essay stays organized' is vague; say that a paragraph earns its place only by defending the overarching claim.
o: Readers use the thesis to decide what each paragraph is for; a paragraph they cannot connect reads as a digression.
A line of reasoning is a chain toward one claim, and a paragraph aimed elsewhere breaks the chain.

w.a: Every paragraph should repeat the thesis word for word so the reader remembers it.
w.why: repetition is not advancement

w.a: Body paragraphs can argue anything related to the topic.
w.why: related to the topic is not the same as supporting the thesis

cards.q: Contrast a thesis and a thesis statement.
cards.a: A thesis is the main claim a text defends, whether or not it is stated; a thesis statement is that thesis directly expressed in words. A writer's thesis is not necessarily a single sentence or an explicit statement and may take a thorough reading of the whole text to identify.
cards.h: → the claim vs its direct expression
cards.n: Saying a text 'has no thesis' because no single sentence states it confuses the thesis with the thesis statement.

cards.q: Write a thesis statement for this passage, which never states its thesis directly: a retired lineman's letter to his town's newspaper reads, 'Forty years I climbed poles for the power company. I have been up a pole in an ice storm at two in the morning, the town dark below me and the wires singing. Last month the company announced it will close the Millbrook repair yard and send crews from the city, ninety minutes away. On the night of the 2009 ice storm, we had the hospital's lights back in forty minutes. I have been doing the arithmetic on ninety minutes ever since.'
cards.a: Model: 'Closing the Millbrook yard will leave the town dark for hours in exactly the storms when power matters most, so the company should keep its crews here.' It states what the letter implies through the contrast between forty minutes and ninety.
cards.h: → one-sentence thesis statement + the details implying it
cards.n: 'The lineman worked for forty years' restates a detail; a thesis statement names the claim the details add up to.

cards.q: Decide which sentence best states the implied thesis of this passage from a nurse's essay, and explain: 'When I started on nights, there were six of us for thirty beds. Now there are four. The woman in bed 12 pressed her call button for twenty minutes before anyone could come. She was not in danger. She was frightened, and she was alone.' (A) 'Nurses work long hours at night.' (B) 'A patient in bed 12 waited twenty minutes for help.' (C) 'Cutting night nurses from six to four has cost patients the comfort of care, not only its safety.' (D) 'Hospitals are dangerous places.'
cards.a: (C): the details build toward a claim the passage never states, that the staffing cut costs patients care even when they are safe ('She was not in danger. She was frightened'). (A) is an obvious fact, (B) repeats one detail, and (D) generalizes far beyond what the passage argues.
cards.h: → letter + how the details imply it + what the rest are
cards.n: Picking (B) because it is 'in the passage' confuses evidence with the claim the evidence implies; an implied thesis is never quoted.

cards.q: State where a thesis may appear in an AP essay and whether it must be a single sentence.
cards.a: The thesis may appear anywhere within the response and may be more than one sentence, provided the sentences are close together, according to the CED's scoring notes. What the exam requires is clear communication of the thesis; a position the reader must infer does not earn the point.
cards.h: → where + how many sentences + the requirement
cards.n: An essay whose position emerges only across the body, never stated, risks the point: the notes accept any location, not an implied thesis.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might withhold a direct statement of the thesis until the end of a text.
cards.a: Leading readers through the evidence first lets them reach the conclusion almost on their own, which suits a skeptical or hostile audience that would resist the claim if it came first. The delayed thesis then reads as the result of reasoning rather than as a demand.
cards.h: → evidence first → readers reason toward it → resistance lowered → thesis lands as a conclusion
cards.n: Borrows REO-1.A (reasoning that arrives at a thesis). 'For suspense' names a feeling without explaining what the delay does for this audience.
o: A thesis stated early gives resistant readers a target to argue against as they read; a delayed thesis gives them nothing to resist until the evidence is in.
Ending on the thesis makes it the last and most memorable thing readers take away.

w.a: Writers delay the thesis because they have not decided what they think.
w.why: treats a deliberate choice as confusion

w.a: A thesis at the end means the text has no thesis.
w.why: the thesis is still there; its statement comes later

cards.q: Explain why the CED requires a clearly communicated thesis in exam essays even though published writers often only imply theirs.
cards.a: An exam reader must find the position to score it and to follow the line of reasoning, and an implied thesis risks being read as summary. A published writer can count on patient readers and rich context; a timed essay cannot, so stating the thesis clearly is part of the task.
cards.h: → reader must locate the position → implied thesis may read as summary → timed context → state it clearly
cards.n: 'Because graders are strict' misses the reason: the reader needs the claim to judge whether the evidence defends it.
o: A stated thesis lets every body paragraph be read as support; an implied one leaves the reader reconstructing the argument.
Published texts that imply a thesis often rely on genre and occasion to signal it, which an exam essay lacks.

w.a: Implied theses are only allowed for professional writers.
w.why: the difference is context and purpose, not status

w.a: The thesis must be the first sentence of the essay.
w.why: the thesis may appear anywhere and span sentences in close proximity

cards.q: Contrast commentary and summary.
cards.a: Summary restates what the evidence says; commentary explains how it supports the claim, establishing the logical relationship between evidence and claim (why this detail makes that claim more believable). Summary answers 'what?'; commentary answers 'so what, and how?'
cards.h: → two definitions + the question each answers
cards.n: 'This shows that' followed by a restatement of the quotation is still summary; commentary adds the link the evidence does not state.

cards.q: Explain what a sentence of strong commentary must do.
cards.a: It must name the logical link between this evidence and this claim: what the evidence shows, why that makes the claim more believable, and how it moves the line of reasoning toward the thesis. It is specific to the evidence; a sentence that could follow any quotation is not commentary.
cards.h: → what it shows → why it supports → where it leads
cards.n: Stock phrases ('This shows how important this is') fit any evidence and so explain none; commentary uses the evidence's own specifics.

cards.q: Define a warrant.
cards.a: A warrant is the assumption, usually unstated, that connects evidence to claim: the principle that makes the evidence count as support. It is the logical relationship that commentary makes explicit. The term comes from the Toulmin model, not the CED.
cards.n: Not a CED term (flagged as useful). To find a warrant, ask what a reader must already believe for this evidence to prove this claim.
x: the assumption linking evidence to claim

cards.q: Identify the warrant: 'The bridge is 70 years old, so it should be replaced.'
cards.a: The warrant is that a bridge about 70 years old is likely unsafe or past its design life, and that unsafe infrastructure should be replaced. Commentary would have to defend that assumption, for instance with inspection data, since age alone does not prove danger.
cards.h: → the unstated assumption, in one sentence
cards.n: Restating the evidence ('the bridge is old') is not the warrant; the warrant is the rule that turns 'old' into 'should be replaced.'

cards.q: Contrast a warrant and its backing in the Toulmin model.
cards.a: The warrant is the assumption that links the data to the claim; the backing is further evidence or reasoning that supports the warrant when an audience might reject it. Example: the warrant 'bridges this old are unsafe' could be backed by engineering data on how long such bridges last.
cards.h: → the assumption vs the support for the assumption
cards.n: Backing supports the warrant, not the claim directly; supplying more data about this bridge adds evidence, not backing.

cards.q: Write one sentence of commentary that links this evidence to this claim. Claim: the school should keep its late bus. Evidence: of the 140 students who ride the late bus, 95 stay after school for tutoring or clubs.
cards.a: Model: 'Because 95 of the 140 riders use the late bus to stay for tutoring or clubs, cutting it would not just end a ride home; it would end after-school help for the students who most actively seek it.' It states the logical relationship: the bus is what makes the tutoring and clubs possible for these students.
cards.h: → model sentence + the link it states
cards.n: 'This shows the late bus is important' restates the claim; commentary must say why these numbers make cutting the bus costly.

cards.q: Explain why evidence cannot speak for itself in an argument.
cards.a: The same fact can support different claims, so readers need the writer to say which claim it supports and why. Without commentary, readers may draw a different conclusion or none, and the evidence sits beside the claim instead of defending it. Commentary establishes the relationship the evidence leaves open.
cards.h: → one fact, many possible meanings → writer must name the link → commentary turns data into support
cards.n: 'Evidence needs to be explained' repeats the question; say that a fact does not announce which claim it proves.
o: Readers bring their own assumptions to evidence; commentary replaces their guess with the writer's reasoning.
Two writers can cite the same statistic for opposite claims, which shows the argument lives in the commentary.

w.a: Evidence speaks for itself if it is strong enough.
w.why: even strong evidence can support different claims

w.a: Commentary is only needed when the reader is not very smart.
w.why: commentary is the argument, not a courtesy

cards.q: Explain why commentary that states an unstated warrant can strengthen an argument for a skeptical audience.
cards.a: A skeptic's doubt often lies in the assumption linking evidence to claim, not in the evidence itself. Stating that assumption lets the writer defend it with backing instead of leaving the gap for the skeptic to find and exploit, and it shows the writer knows exactly where the argument needs support.
cards.h: → doubt lives in the assumption → name it → defend it with backing → gap closed before the skeptic finds it
cards.n: 'It makes the argument clearer' is vague; say that skeptics attack the unstated link, so naming and backing it answers them in advance.
o: An audience that shares the warrant needs it left implicit, but one that does not will reject the evidence unless the warrant is argued.
Making the warrant explicit signals honesty about the argument's assumptions, which raises the writer's credibility.

w.a: Writers should always state every warrant, whatever the audience.
w.why: a shared warrant can be left implicit

w.a: Stating the warrant weakens the argument by admitting an assumption.
w.why: every argument has warrants; defending one strengthens it

cards.q: Identify the words that introduce the source and the words that integrate it into the writer's line of reasoning in this sentence from a synthesis essay: 'Even the bus company's own safety officer, who has every reason to defend the current schedule, admits that drivers "skip stops to stay on time" (Source D), which suggests the problem lies in the schedule, not the drivers.'
cards.a: 'Even the bus company's own safety officer, who has every reason to defend the current schedule, admits' introduces the source and tells readers why its testimony carries weight (a reluctant witness). 'Which suggests the problem lies in the schedule, not the drivers' is commentary that ties the quotation to the writer's claim.
cards.h: → introducing words + integrating words + what each does
cards.n: Pointing only to '(Source D)' names the citation, not the introduction; the commentary before and after the quotation does the integrating.

cards.q: Decide which version better integrates the source into the writer's line of reasoning, and explain: (A) 'Source B says that 30 percent of seniors in the county have no internet at home. Libraries are important.' (B) 'Libraries remain essential because, as the county survey in Source B shows, 30 percent of seniors have no internet at home, which makes the library their only door to online services.'
cards.a: (B): the writer's claim comes first, the source is introduced by what it is (a county survey), and the commentary after the figure explains how it supports the claim. (A) drops the statistic between a bare citation and a vague claim, so the reader must supply the connection.
cards.n: Preferring (A) because it is shorter misses the EK: integration requires commentary that places the source in the reasoning.

cards.q: Write a sentence that introduces and integrates this source for an essay arguing that the school should ban phones during class. Source C is an op-ed by a principal who opposes a ban; it includes the line 'phones follow students into every lesson.'
cards.a: Model: 'Even Principal Ortiz, who opposes a ban, concedes that phones "follow students into every lesson" (Source C), which is exactly why a rule, not willpower, is needed.' The introduction tells readers the source disagrees with the writer's position, which makes its concession strong evidence, and the commentary turns it toward the writer's claim.
cards.h: → model sentence + what the introduction and commentary do
cards.n: Quoting an opposing source without saying it opposes the writer wastes its best feature, the weight of an admission against interest.

cards.q: Explain what integrating source material into a line of reasoning requires beyond naming the source.
cards.a: Three moves: introduce the source (who it is and, when it matters, why readers should trust or weigh it), present the specific information, and add commentary on how it advances the paragraph's claim. A source that is named but not tied to the claim is present in the essay without being integrated into its reasoning.
cards.n: Parenthetical citations prove where evidence came from, not why it matters; integration is the commentary around them.

cards.q: Explain why telling readers who a source is before quoting it can change how much weight the evidence carries.
cards.a: A source's identity is part of the evidence: an expert, a firsthand witness, a reluctant witness, or an interested party each deserves different weight. Introducing the source lets readers judge the information as the writer intends and shows the writer has weighed it, strengthening claim and credibility alike.
cards.h: → identity is part of the evidence → introduction sets its weight → readers judge it as intended
cards.n: 'It gives credit to the source' is attribution, not the reason; say how knowing who speaks changes what the words prove.
o: The same sentence proves more from a critic who concedes the point than from an ally who repeats it, and only the introduction tells readers which it is.
An unintroduced quotation forces readers to guess its authority, and many will assume the least.

w.a: Introducing sources is only a rule of citation style.
w.why: misses its effect on the evidence's weight

w.a: Readers can look up the source themselves, so introductions add nothing.
w.why: the argument must do that weighing for them

cards.q: Explain why a paragraph that opens with a source's quotation and ends with the writer's claim tends to read as summary.
cards.a: Without a claim or introduction to frame it, the quotation arrives before readers know what to look for, so they read it as information rather than support. The writer's point, coming last, seems drawn from the source rather than advanced with it, so the paragraph follows the source's thinking.
cards.h: → no frame first → quotation read as information → claim seems borrowed → source leads the reasoning
cards.n: 'The order is wrong' is not an explanation; say what readers can and cannot see when the quotation comes first.
o: Leading with the writer's claim tells readers why the quotation matters before they reach it.
Source-first paragraphs tend to chain into a tour of sources, the pattern graders read as summary.

w.a: Quotations should always come first because they are the strongest part of a paragraph.
w.why: evidence is strong only in relation to a claim

w.a: A paragraph reads as summary only if it has no quotations.
w.why: quoting without framing is exactly what reads as summary

cards.q: State the three things the CED says synthesis requires, and what each means.
cards.a: Consideration, explanation, and integration of others' arguments into one's own argument. Consideration means weighing others' positions, including opposing ones; explanation means saying what each argues and how it bears on the writer's position; integration means working them into the writer's argument as part of its line of reasoning.
cards.n: Synthesis is not 'using sources'; an essay that quotes three sources without explaining or integrating them has not synthesized.

cards.q: Contrast synthesizing sources and summarizing them.
cards.a: Summary reports what each source says, usually one after another; synthesis integrates the sources into the writer's own argument, using them as evidence, relating them to one another, and explaining how each advances the writer's claim. In summary the sources set the structure; in synthesis the writer's position does.
cards.h: → what each does with sources + who controls the structure
cards.n: A paragraph per source ('Source A says... Source B says...') is summary even when every source is accurately cited.

cards.q: Identify whether this paragraph synthesizes its sources or only summarizes them, and explain: 'Source A, a pediatrician, says young athletes who play one sport year-round get more overuse injuries. Source D, a travel-team coach, says year-round training builds elite skill. Source F is a chart showing that youth sports costs are rising. All of these sources discuss youth sports.'
cards.a: It only summarizes: each source is reported in turn, no claim of the writer's organizes them, and nothing explains how they relate (for instance, that the coach's recommended schedule is the one the pediatrician links to injury). The last sentence states the topic, not a position.
cards.h: → verdict + the missing claim + the missing relationships
cards.n: Accurate citation of three sources does not make synthesis; the test is whether the writer's argument uses and connects them.

cards.q: Write one sentence that synthesizes these two sources for an essay arguing that children should play more than one sport before high school. Source A: a pediatrician reports that children who play only one sport year-round suffer more overuse injuries. Source D: a travel-team coach argues that year-round training in one sport builds elite skill.
cards.a: Model: 'The travel coach in Source D credits year-round training with building elite skill, but that is the very schedule Source A's pediatrician links to overuse injuries, which suggests early specialization buys skill at the cost of the bodies that must last long enough to use it.' It considers both, explains their relation, and integrates them into the writer's claim.
cards.n: 'Source A and Source D disagree about sports' notes a relationship but makes no claim; synthesis puts the relationship to work for the thesis.

cards.q: Explain why synthesis requires the writer to consider arguments that disagree with the writer's position.
cards.a: Integrating only agreeing sources turns synthesis into a chorus that readers suspect is selective. Considering and explaining an opposing argument shows the writer's position survived a real test, and it lets the writer define the terms of the disagreement instead of leaving readers to raise it unanswered.
cards.h: → agreeing sources only → looks selective → opposing view considered → position tested and credible
cards.n: 'To show both sides' misstates the goal; synthesis considers opposing arguments in order to strengthen the writer's own position.
o: An opposing source often supplies the complication that makes a position precise, such as the condition under which it holds.
Readers who hold the opposing view will read on only if they see it represented fairly.

w.a: Synthesis means giving equal space to every side without taking a position.
w.why: synthesis serves the writer's own argument

w.a: Opposing sources should be avoided because they weaken the essay.
w.why: ignoring them weakens credibility more

cards.q: Explain why the writer's own claim, not the sources, should lead each paragraph of a synthesis essay.
cards.a: Synthesis integrates others' arguments into one's own; when sources lead, the essay becomes a tour of what others think and the line of reasoning disappears. Opening each paragraph with the writer's claim makes every source serve as evidence the writer then explains.
cards.h: → claim first → sources become evidence → commentary explains them → writer's reasoning stays in control
cards.n: 'It sounds more confident' is a style reason; the point is that the claim decides which source material belongs and why.
o: A paragraph that begins with its claim can draw on several sources at once, which is where synthesis happens.
Starting from a source lets that source's argument set the paragraph's direction, so the writer ends up summarizing it.

w.a: Each paragraph should cover one source so the grader can count the three required.
w.why: counting sources is not synthesis

w.a: The sources are the experts, so their points should come before the writer's.
w.why: the essay's task is the writer's position

cards.q: Contrast attribution, citation, and reference as ways to acknowledge another's work.
cards.a: Attribution names the source within the writer's sentence ('the county's health survey found'). Citation marks the source in a standard form, such as (Source C) on the exam or an author and page in a research paper. Reference points readers to a work or idea without quoting it ('as in Orwell's essay on language'). All three acknowledge others' words, ideas, images, or data.
cards.h: → three forms + an example of each
cards.n: The CED names the three without defining them; these distinctions are working ones. A citation alone does not tell readers why the source matters.

cards.q:
Decide whether each item in a student's synthesis essay needs acknowledgment:
1. A phrase quoted from Source A.
2. A figure from the chart in Source E, restated in the student's words.
3. 'Water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit.'
4. Source B's argument that fees punish poor families, restated in the student's words.
5. The student's own conclusion from comparing Sources B and C.
6. A description of the photograph in Source F.
7. 'The United States has fifty states.'
8. An idea from Source D's interview, reworded as a topic sentence.
cards.a:
1 → yes (another's exact words)
2 → yes (another's data, even paraphrased)
3 → no (common knowledge)
4 → yes (another's idea, even in new words)
5 → the conclusion is the student's own, but the sources it compares are cited
6 → yes (another's image)
7 → no (common knowledge)
8 → yes (an idea stays the source's when reworded)
cards.h: → one verdict per line + the reason
cards.n: Rewording is the trap: ideas, data, and images need acknowledgment just as quoted words do.

cards.q: Identify the problem in this sentence from a synthesis essay, given that the figure comes from Source C: 'Cities that plant trees on their hottest blocks can cut afternoon pavement temperatures by up to twelve degrees, which shows that trees are public health infrastructure.' Then fix it.
cards.a: The figure is presented as the writer's own knowledge: it has no attribution or citation, so readers cannot check it and the writer takes credit for another's data. Fix: 'According to the city health office's report (Source C), the barest blocks run up to twelve degrees hotter in the afternoon, which shows that trees are public health infrastructure.'
cards.h: → the missing acknowledgment + a corrected sentence
cards.n: The commentary is fine; the problem is ownership of the figure. Unacknowledged data is still borrowing even when paraphrased.

cards.q: Write a sentence that paraphrases and acknowledges this idea for a synthesis essay: in Source B, an op-ed, a farmer argues that a county ban on new wells protects the aquifer only if existing wells are metered too.
cards.a: Model: 'A ban on new wells may be a half measure: as the farmer writing in Source B points out, the aquifer is protected only if the wells already pumping are metered as well.' The idea is restated in the writer's own words, attributed ('the farmer writing in'), and cited (Source B).
cards.h: → model sentence + attribution and citation marked
cards.n: Paraphrasing an idea without naming its source presents someone else's argument as your own, whether or not any words are copied.

cards.q: Explain why acknowledging sources strengthens, rather than weakens, a writer's argument.
cards.a: Attribution lets readers check the evidence and weigh its source, which makes the claim more credible, and it separates the writer's reasoning from borrowed material so the writer's own contribution is visible. Unacknowledged borrowing, once noticed, discredits the whole argument.
cards.h: → acknowledged source → checkable, weighable evidence → writer's contribution visible → credibility gained
cards.n: 'It avoids plagiarism' names a rule, not the rhetorical benefit; say what acknowledgment does for the reader's trust.
o: Naming a respected source lends the argument that source's authority.
Clear acknowledgment shows the writer has done the work of finding and weighing evidence.

w.a: Citing sources shows you did not have your own ideas.
w.why: the writer's ideas are clearer when borrowed material is marked

w.a: Acknowledgment only matters in research papers, not in timed essays.
w.why: the synthesis task requires sources to be clearly indicated

cards.q: Decide which thesis previews a line of reasoning without listing points, and state what each of the others does: (A) 'Elementary schools should abolish homework for three reasons: stress, family time, and sleep.' (B) 'Elementary schools should abolish homework, because the hours it takes from young children buy almost no learning in return.' (C) 'This essay will discuss homework in elementary schools.'
cards.a: (B) previews the reasoning, a cost weighed against a benefit, without listing points, so readers know how the argument will move. (A) previews by listing three points, which is allowed but not required. (C) announces a topic and takes no position, so it is not a thesis at all.
cards.h: → letter + what each of the three does
cards.n: Thinking (A) is the only 'correct' model is the trap the CED warns against: a thesis need not list the points of an argument.

cards.q: Identify the line of reasoning this thesis previews: 'Although a curfew would reduce late-night crime downtown, it would do so by punishing the many teenagers who work late shifts, and better lighting and more patrols would protect them without treating them as suspects.'
cards.a: It previews three moves in order: a concession (the curfew would reduce crime), a counterclaim about its cost (it burdens teenagers who work late), and an alternative (lighting and patrols). The body should follow that sequence, ending on the alternative the writer favors.
cards.h: → the moves, in order + what the body should do
cards.n: Listing the thesis's topics (curfew, crime, teens) misses the relationships 'although,' 'by,' and 'without' set up between them.

cards.q: Write a thesis that previews its line of reasoning without listing three points, for this prompt: 'Write an essay that argues your position on whether high school students should be required to complete community service in order to graduate.'
cards.a: Model: 'Requiring service risks turning generosity into a chore, but a requirement that lets students choose their cause and reflect on the work could build the civic habit the policy is meant to create.' It signals the essay's path, a concession, then a turn to a qualified proposal, without enumerating body paragraphs.
cards.h: → model thesis + the path it previews
cards.n: 'Community service should be required for three reasons' promises a list but not a line of reasoning; the preview should show how ideas connect.

cards.q: State what the CED says a thesis statement may do about an argument's structure, and what it need not do.
cards.a: A thesis statement may preview the line of reasoning of an argument. It need not list the points of the argument, the aspects to be analyzed, or the specific evidence to be used; a thesis that takes a clear, defensible position is complete without a map.
cards.n: The 'three-prong thesis' is a classroom habit, not a CED requirement; a list of devices can even lock an analysis into device-hunting.

cards.q: Explain why a thesis that lists three rhetorical devices can weaken a rhetorical analysis essay.
cards.a: A device list previews a sequence of labels, not a line of reasoning, so the essay tends to march device by device without saying how the choices work together toward the writer's purpose. Previewing the writer's moves or the effect they build gives the essay a direction its paragraphs can advance.
cards.h: → device list → paragraphs follow labels → no account of purpose → analysis becomes identification
cards.n: 'Devices are boring' is not a reason; say that the list previews labels instead of reasoning about the writer's purpose.
o: A preview of what the writer does to the audience (disarms, then proves, then rallies) gives each paragraph a claim to defend rather than a device to find.
The CED says a thesis need not list aspects to be analyzed, and a list often invites summary of each device's appearances.

w.a: A thesis should always list three devices so the grader knows what is coming.
w.why: the CED says listing is not required and it often hurts analysis

w.a: Listing devices shows the grader you know rhetorical terms.
w.why: term recall is not what the rubric rewards

cards.q: Explain why a writer might choose a thesis that previews the line of reasoning over one that only states a position.
cards.a: A preview tells readers how the argument will unfold, so each paragraph reads as a planned step and readers can track how it advances the claim. It also commits the writer to an order, which keeps a timed essay on course. A position alone is acceptable but leaves readers to discover the structure.
cards.h: → preview shows the path → paragraphs read as planned steps → readers follow → writer stays on course
cards.n: 'It makes the thesis longer and more detailed' misses the function; say what the preview lets the reader do.
o: Complex arguments with a concession or a turn benefit most, since the preview warns readers that the argument will change direction.
A previewed structure helps readers hold a long argument in mind, which matters more as the essay grows.

w.a: Every thesis must preview the essay's structure to earn the point.
w.why: the CED says a preview is optional

w.a: Previewing the reasoning gives away the argument, so good writers avoid it.
w.why: it guides readers; the defense still has to be made

cards.q: Decide which detail from this source is most relevant to the claim that the town should fund a summer lunch program for children, and explain. Source E, a county report on child nutrition, states: (A) the county has 14 public schools; (B) 38 percent of the county's students qualify for free school lunch, and visits to the food bank by families with children rise by half in July; (C) the report's authors interviewed cafeteria managers in the spring.
cards.a: (B): it shows the need directly, many children rely on school lunch, and their families' need jumps when school is out, which is exactly what a summer program answers. (A) is background and (C) describes the report's method; neither supports the claim.
cards.h: → letter + how it fits this claim
cards.n: Choosing (A) because numbers look strong confuses a statistic with relevant evidence; select what bears on this claim.

cards.q: Identify the weakness in how this synthesis paragraph uses its sources: 'Source A talks about the importance of sleep. Source C also discusses teenagers and school. Source F has a graph about start times. These sources show that schools should start later.'
cards.a: The sources are referred to by topic, not used: no specific, apt material is selected (no finding, figure, or quotation), and nothing explains how each supports the claim. Drawing on multiple sources means choosing the most relevant information from each, such as the graph's key figure, and combining it in the writer's argument.
cards.h: → what is missing (specific material + commentary) + a fix
cards.n: Counting three cited sources is not synthesis; references to what a source 'talks about' supply no evidence.

cards.q: Write one sentence that combines specific material from these two sources to support the claim that the city should add protected bike lanes. Source B, a city traffic report: collisions involving cyclists on Harbor Street rose from 11 to 19 in two years. Source E, an interview with a delivery rider: 'I ride on the sidewalk on Harbor because the street feels like a dare.'
cards.a: Model: 'Harbor Street's rise from 11 to 19 cyclist collisions in two years (Source B) explains why one delivery rider now takes the sidewalk because the street "feels like a dare" (Source E): without protected lanes, the street fails both the riders who stay on it and the pedestrians they are pushed toward.'
cards.h: → one sentence joining both sources to the claim
cards.n: Stating the two facts in separate sentences with 'Also' leaves the connection to the reader; combining them is where the argument happens.

cards.q: State the three things the CED says writers do when synthesizing sources.
cards.a: They draw upon arguments from multiple sources, strategically select the most relevant information, and combine apt and specific source material as part of their own argument. Selection and combination are the writer's work; the sources supply material, not the structure.
cards.n: 'Use at least three sources' is the exam's minimum, not the CED's description; selection of the most relevant material is the skill.

cards.q: Explain why quoting a source's most relevant sentence is usually stronger than summarizing the whole source.
cards.a: Selection is where the writer's thinking shows: the relevant, specific sentence supports this claim directly and leaves room for commentary, while a summary spends space on material the argument does not use and blurs what the source actually proves for this claim.
cards.h: → select the apt sentence → direct support + room for commentary → summary dilutes and blurs
cards.n: 'Quotes are more exact' is only part of it; say that selecting the relevant part shows how the source serves this claim.
o: A precise quotation lets readers see the exact evidence the commentary is about.
Summarizing a whole source often imports points that complicate or distract from the writer's claim.

w.a: Summarizing the whole source is better because it proves you read it.
w.why: the task rewards use, not proof of reading

w.a: The longer the quotation, the more evidence it provides.
w.why: length adds material the argument must then explain or ignore

cards.q: Explain why combining two sources in one sentence can support a claim better than citing them in separate paragraphs.
cards.a: Placed together, sources can do what neither does alone: one supplies the number and the other its human meaning, or two independent sources confirm the same point. The combination shows the writer weighing them against each other, while separate paragraphs leave the relationship for readers to find.
cards.h: → sources side by side → each supplies what the other lacks → relationship explicit → stronger support
cards.n: 'It saves space' is a practical side effect, not the reason; say what the combination proves that each source alone does not.
o: Corroboration from sources with different perspectives is stronger than either alone.
Combining a source that supports with one that complicates lets the writer qualify the claim precisely.

w.a: Combining sources is just a way to meet the three-source requirement faster.
w.why: reduces synthesis to counting

w.a: Sources should always be kept separate so the reader is not confused.
w.why: keeping them apart is what reads as summary

cards.q: Contrast a primary and a secondary source.
cards.a: A primary source is firsthand material: original data, a speech, an eyewitness account, a document from the time. A secondary source analyzes or reports on primary material, such as a news article about a study. Neither is automatically more reliable: a primary source can be biased or partial, and a good secondary source can supply context the original lacks.
cards.h: → two definitions + neither is automatically more reliable
cards.n: Assuming primary means reliable is the trap; judge any source by its expertise, interests, evidence, and date.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of expert testimony.
cards.a: Expert opinion lends credibility on questions an audience cannot judge alone. It is only as reliable as its fit: it weakens when the expert speaks outside their field, has a stake in the outcome, is out of date, or is contradicted by other experts.
cards.n: 'Experts say' with no name or field is a claim of credibility with nothing to check; name who, and why they know.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'This diet must work - a famous actor swears by it in every interview.'
cards.a: Appeal to authority (the fallacious kind): the actor's fame is offered as proof, but fame gives no expertise in nutrition, so the source is not credible on this claim. A registered dietitian or a clinical trial would be.
cards.h: → fallacy + why this source lacks credibility here
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Citing experts is legitimate; the flaw is authority that does not match the claim.

cards.q: Decide which source is more reliable for the claim that a new reading program raised a district's third-grade scores, and explain: (A) the program publisher's website, which says 'schools using our program see dramatic gains'; (B) the district's annual report, which gives third-grade reading scores for the three years before and the two years after the program began, noting that the test did not change.
cards.a: (B): it gives specific, checkable figures, compares before and after on the same test, and comes from a source with less stake in the program's success. (A) is an interested party making a vague claim with no data, so it cannot establish the result.
cards.h: → letter + evidence, method, and interest compared
cards.n: Choosing (A) because it is more confident mistakes certainty for credibility; the publisher profits if readers believe it.

cards.q: Identify the factors a reader should check to judge whether a source is reliable and credible for a particular claim.
cards.a: The author's expertise on this claim; the publisher or venue and whether the work was reviewed; its date; its purpose and interests (who benefits if readers believe it); the evidence and methods it shows; and whether other credible sources agree. Reliability is judged claim by claim, not once for the whole source.
cards.n: A professional-looking website is not a factor; ask who wrote it, what they know, and what they gain.

cards.q: Explain why a source can be credible on one claim in a synthesis essay and unreliable on another.
cards.a: Credibility follows expertise and interest: a teachers' union survey of its members is strong evidence of teachers' experience but weak evidence on budget costs, where the union has a stake and no special expertise. A writer weighs each claim against what the source knows and what it stands to gain.
cards.h: → credibility tied to expertise + interest → varies claim by claim → weigh each use separately
cards.n: 'Some sources are biased' is too general; say how the same source's authority changes with the claim it is used for.
o: A source's firsthand knowledge makes it authoritative on what it witnessed, not on what it predicts or recommends.
Dismissing a whole source for one weakness throws away evidence it is well placed to provide.

w.a: A source is either credible or not credible, and that never changes.
w.why: credibility depends on the claim

w.a: Any source with an author's name and a date is credible.
w.why: those are signs to check, not proof of reliability

cards.q: Explain why a writer might still use a source that has an obvious interest in the outcome.
cards.a: An interested source can be the best witness to facts only it has, such as a company's own sales data, and it is especially powerful when it admits something against its interest. The writer uses it for what it can reliably show and says so, which turns a weakness into a sign of the writer's care.
cards.h: → interested source has unique facts → admissions against interest are strong → use it with its interest named
cards.n: 'Every source is biased anyway' dismisses the question; say what the source can still reliably show and how the writer signals its interest.
o: Avoiding every interested source would leave out the people most affected by an issue.
Naming the interest up front prevents readers from discovering it later and doubting the writer.

w.a: Writers should never use a source that benefits from the outcome.
w.why: it may hold unique or damaging-to-itself evidence

w.a: An interested source is fine as long as you do not mention its interest.
w.why: hiding it undermines credibility when noticed

cards.q: Contrast a position and a perspective.
cards.a: A position is the stance a source takes on an issue: for, against, or a qualified view. A perspective is the vantage point it argues from, shaped by its background, interests, and expertise. Sources may share a position on a subject yet each come from a different perspective.
cards.h: → stance vs vantage point + the CED's key point
cards.n: Using the words interchangeably ('the doctor's position is medical') blurs the distinction the CED draws.

cards.q: Identify the shared position and the different perspectives of these three sources on a proposal for a bike lane on Harbor Street: Source A, a pediatric ER doctor, supports it because of the injuries she treats; Source B, a bike-shop owner, supports it because more riders mean more customers; Source C, a retired traffic engineer, supports it because separated lanes reduce all kinds of crashes.
cards.a: Position: all three support the lane. Perspectives: medical (injuries treated), commercial (business interest), and technical (traffic-safety expertise). The difference matters for weighing them: B has a financial interest, while C's expertise bears directly on the safety data.
cards.h: → one position + three perspectives + why it matters
cards.n: Reporting 'all three sources agree' and stopping throws away what the different perspectives add to the argument.

cards.q: Decide which sentence better uses the three sources on the Harbor Street bike lane (a pediatric ER doctor, a bike-shop owner, and a retired traffic engineer, all in favor) in a synthesis essay, and explain: (A) 'Sources A, B, and C all say the same thing: the city needs the bike lane.' (B) 'A doctor who treats injured riders, a shop owner who sells to them, and an engineer who studied crash data all reach the same conclusion from different directions, which suggests the lane serves health, business, and safety at once.'
cards.a: (B): it shows the sources share a position from different perspectives and turns that agreement into evidence of the lane's broad value. (A) treats three perspectives as one voice and wastes the strength of independent agreement.
cards.n: 'All the sources agree' is a summary, not synthesis; say why agreement from different vantage points strengthens the claim.

cards.q: Identify the position and the perspective of this source: a dairy farmer who has served twelve years on the county water board argues, in the farm bureau's newsletter, that the county should limit new lawn irrigation during droughts.
cards.a: Position: in favor of limiting new lawn irrigation in droughts. Perspective: agricultural and administrative, as a farmer whose livelihood depends on the same water and a board member who knows the county's supply data. Both shape what she emphasizes and how readers should weigh her.
cards.n: Calling her perspective 'pro-limits' repeats the position; perspective is where she stands, not what she concludes.

cards.q: Explain why noticing that sources share a position but not a perspective can strengthen a synthesis essay.
cards.a: Agreement from different vantage points is stronger evidence than agreement from one: if a doctor, a shop owner, and an engineer reach the same position for different reasons, the claim holds across interests. It also lets the writer weigh each source's interest and expertise rather than treating them as one voice.
cards.h: → same position, different perspectives → independent confirmation → claim holds across interests
cards.n: 'It shows the writer used many sources' counts sources; say what independent agreement proves.
o: Different perspectives supply different kinds of evidence, so the writer can build a paragraph on each without repeating the same point.
Naming perspectives shows readers the writer has weighed who says what and why.

w.a: If sources agree, it does not matter who they are.
w.why: who agrees, and why, is what makes agreement meaningful

w.a: Sources with different perspectives cannot be used in the same paragraph.
w.why: combining them is where synthesis happens

cards.q: Explain why two sources with opposite positions can share a perspective.
cards.a: Perspective comes from background, interests, and expertise, not from conclusions: two economists may both argue from cost data yet disagree about whether a tax helps. Seeing the shared perspective shows the real disagreement lies in evidence or values within that frame, which tells the writer where to aim.
cards.h: → perspective = vantage point, not conclusion → same frame, different verdicts → locate the real disagreement
cards.n: 'Because people disagree' repeats the premise; explain that perspective and position are different things.
o: Two parents can both argue from a parent's perspective, one for and one against a later start time, because they weigh different needs.
A shared perspective can make a disagreement more useful to the writer, since both sides speak to the same concerns.

w.a: Opposite positions always mean opposite perspectives.
w.why: confuses stance with vantage point

w.a: If two sources share a perspective, one of them must be wrong about the evidence.
w.why: they may weigh the same evidence or values differently

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of statistical evidence.
cards.a: Statistics show scale and pattern beyond a single case and persuade data-minded audiences. Their limits: the sample may be small or biased, a figure may be cherry-picked or stripped of context, and a correlation does not show cause. Strong arguments say where the number comes from and what it can and cannot show.
cards.h: → strength + limits + how strong writers account for them
cards.n: Treating a statistic as unanswerable proof is the trap; name its source and scope, as the CED's 'account for limitations' asks.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of anecdotal evidence.
cards.a: An anecdote is concrete and memorable and relates an abstract claim to the audience's emotions and values. Its limit is that one story is a sample of one: it cannot show a pattern and may be unrepresentative. Strong arguments acknowledge that and pair the anecdote with broader evidence.
cards.h: → strength + limit + how to account for it
cards.n: Defending a general claim with a single story invites the charge of hasty generalization; say what the story illustrates, not proves.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of historical example as evidence.
cards.a: A historical example shows that something has actually happened and supplies a precedent the audience recognizes. Its limit is that circumstances change, so the writer must show that the past case resembles the present one in the respect that matters, and acknowledge where it does not.
cards.n: 'History repeats itself' is not an argument; the writer must say why this past case is parallel enough to guide this decision.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of personal experience as evidence.
cards.a: Personal experience gives firsthand authority and immediacy, especially about how a policy or event is lived. Its limits: others cannot check it, it may not be typical, and readers may dismiss it as one person's view. It is strongest when the writer acknowledges that and uses it to illustrate a pattern other evidence shows.
cards.h: → strength + limits + how to use it well
cards.n: The argument essay accepts personal evidence, but a vague 'I have seen this happen' is neither specific nor accounted for; say what it shows.

cards.q: Write a sentence that acknowledges this source's limitation and accounts for it in your reasoning. Your claim: the school should keep its later start time. Source B: a survey of 200 students at one high school found that 70 percent reported feeling more alert in first period after the change.
cards.a: Model: 'Source B's survey covers one school and relies on students' own reports, so it cannot show that a later start raises alertness everywhere; but because it measures the very students this decision affects, it is apt evidence for keeping the change here.' It names the limits (one school, self-report) and adjusts the claim's scope to fit them.
cards.h: → model sentence: limit named + reasoning adjusted
cards.n: Naming a limitation and then ignoring it ('although it is small, it proves...') acknowledges without accounting; adjust the claim.

cards.q: Explain why acknowledging a limitation of your own evidence can make an argument stronger.
cards.a: Naming the limit shows the writer has tested the evidence, which builds credibility, and it lets the writer define how much the evidence proves before an opponent overstates the weakness. Accounting for the limit, by narrowing the claim or adding evidence, keeps the reasoning honest and harder to dismiss.
cards.h: → limit named → writer seen as careful → weakness framed on the writer's terms → claim sized to the evidence
cards.n: 'It shows both sides' misstates the move; acknowledging a limitation is about your own evidence, not the opposing position.
o: Readers who spot an unacknowledged weakness distrust the whole argument; readers told about it trust the rest more.
Accounting for a limitation often produces a more precise claim, which is easier to defend.

w.a: Admitting a limitation gives the opponent free ammunition.
w.why: the opponent can find it anyway; naming it first controls its impact

w.a: Every piece of evidence should be presented as flawless.
w.why: overclaiming invites refutation

cards.q: Explain why a writer using a statistic from an advocacy group should say who produced it.
