cards.a: Readers who later learn that a figure came from an interested group will doubt both the figure and the writer. Naming the source up front, and noting whether independent data agree, accounts for its possible bias within the reasoning and shows the writer has weighed the evidence rather than hidden its origin.
cards.h: → source's interest is part of the evidence → named up front → bias accounted for → credibility kept
cards.n: 'To avoid plagiarism' confuses attribution rules with the reasoning point: the source's interest affects how much the figure proves.
o: An advocacy group's figure may still be accurate; naming it lets the writer argue why it can be trusted, for instance because it matches government data.
Hiding the source's interest treats readers as marks rather than judges, which the CED's strongest arguments avoid.

w.a: Statistics from advocacy groups should never be used.
w.why: they can be accurate and useful when their bias is acknowledged

w.a: Numbers are objective, so it does not matter who produced them.
w.why: who collected them affects which numbers were chosen and how

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'She wants schools to teach media literacy, which just means she thinks students are too dumb to think for themselves.'
cards.a: Straw man: it replaces her actual proposal, teaching students to evaluate media, with a distorted version (she thinks students are stupid) and attacks that. A source that treats opposing positions this way reveals its bias: it has not considered the other position as its holders actually state it.
cards.h: → fallacy + the distortion + what it shows about the source
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Quote the distortion ('just means') and state the actual proposal; the label alone earns nothing.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of cherry picking and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Cherry picking is citing only the evidence that supports a claim while leaving out evidence that contradicts it. Example: 'Sales rose in March and June, proving the campaign worked,' when sales fell in the other four months. A source that cherry-picks has not considered other positions or data, which signals bias.
cards.n: Every fact cited can be true while the picture is false; check what the source leaves out, not just what it includes.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of straw man and give a one-line example.
cards.a: A straw man misrepresents an opposing position as weaker or more extreme than it is, then refutes the distorted version. Example: 'My opponent wants to trim the arts budget, so apparently she thinks music is worthless.' It shows how far a source is from fairly considering other positions.
cards.n: Refuting a caricature proves nothing about the real position; a fair source states the opposing view in terms its holders would accept.

cards.q: Decide which source is less biased, judging by how each treats other positions, and explain. Both oppose a school-uniform policy. Source A: 'Supporters say uniforms reduce bullying; a district study did find fewer reported incidents, but the drop coincided with a new anti-bullying program, so uniforms may not be the cause.' Source B: 'Only control freaks want uniforms; they care more about neat rows than about kids.'
cards.a: Source A: it states the supporters' strongest argument and evidence fairly, then responds with a reason, so it considers the other position. Source B dismisses supporters with a caricature and never engages their reasons, which reflects heavy bias even though both sources take the same position.
cards.h: → letter + how each treats the other side
cards.n: Judging bias by the position taken misses the CED's test: two sources on the same side can differ greatly in how far they consider others.

cards.q: Identify two signs of bias in this passage from a flyer opposing a new dog park: 'The so-called dog park would hand our quiet neighborhood to barking, mess, and strangers. Every neighbor we asked is against it. No one has explained why dogs deserve land our children need.'
cards.a: First, it never states or answers the supporters' reasons (exercise, safety, a place for dog owners to meet), and 'so-called' dismisses the idea instead of engaging it. Second, 'every neighbor we asked' reports only agreeing voices from an unexplained sample. The less a source considers other positions, the more biased it is.
cards.h: → two signs, each tied to the text
cards.n: 'It is one-sided' names bias without evidence; quote the words that show which positions the flyer ignores or dismisses.

cards.q: Explain why a source that never mentions opposing views should be used with caution in a synthesis essay.
cards.a: The CED ties a source's bias to how far it considers other positions; one that ignores them has likely selected only favorable evidence, so its facts may be accurate but incomplete. A writer can use it for what it verifiably reports while checking its claims against a source that weighs both sides.
cards.h: → ignores other positions → likely selective → facts may be true but incomplete → use with a check
cards.n: 'It is biased so do not use it' overcorrects; say what the source can still supply and how the writer compensates.
o: A one-sided source is useful evidence of what its side believes, even when it is weak evidence of what is true.
Relying on it without comment would import its bias into the writer's own argument.

w.a: Sources that only argue one side are the strongest because they are confident.
w.why: confidence without consideration of others signals bias

w.a: Any source that takes a position is biased and should be avoided.
w.why: taking a position is not the test; ignoring others is

cards.q: Write a revised thesis that accounts for this new evidence. Original thesis: 'Later school start times improve students' grades.' New evidence: a district study finds that a later start improved attendance and sleep but found no change in grades.
cards.a: Model: 'Later start times give students more sleep and better attendance, gains that justify the change even though the district's study found no rise in grades.' The claim now rests on what the evidence shows, and it answers the finding that contradicts the original thesis instead of ignoring it.
cards.h: → model thesis + what changed and why
cards.n: Adding 'although some studies disagree' to the old thesis acknowledges the evidence without revising the claim it contradicts.

cards.q:
Decide, for each piece of new evidence, whether it calls for revising the thesis, changing the line of reasoning, or simply adding it as evidence. Thesis: 'The town should replace its aging library with a new building downtown.'
1. An engineer finds the old building can be repaired for a third of the cost of a new one.
2. A survey shows residents value the library mainly for children's programs, not the book collection your second paragraph emphasizes.
3. A census count confirms the population growth your first paragraph argues.
4. The only available downtown site turns out to be in a flood zone.
5. The old building's roof proves sound, but it can never be made fully accessible to wheelchair users.
cards.a:
1 → revise the thesis: replacement over repair needs rethinking, perhaps to 'repair and expand'
2 → change the line of reasoning: keep the position, rebuild paragraph 2 around children's programs
3 → add as evidence: it confirms an existing step
4 → revise the thesis: 'downtown' no longer holds
5 → change the line of reasoning: the reason for replacement shifts from the roof to accessibility
cards.n: Treating every new fact as a threat to the thesis is the overreaction; ask whether it changes the claim, a reason for it, or neither.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of no true Scotsman and give a one-line example.
cards.a: No true Scotsman rescues a generalization from a counterexample by redefining the category to exclude it. Example: 'No serious scientist doubts this.' 'Dr. Vance does.' 'Then he is not a serious scientist.' It is the opposite of what new evidence should prompt: instead of revising the claim, the writer redefines its terms so that no evidence could count against it.
cards.h: → definition + example + what should happen instead
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). The tell is a definition that shifts only when a counterexample appears.

cards.q: Identify what changed between these two outlines after the writer found new evidence, and whether the thesis changed. Draft 1 thesis: 'Cities should ban gas-powered leaf blowers because they are too loud.' Paragraphs: neighbors' complaints; workers' hearing; quiet as quality of life. New evidence: a state study finds the machines expose their operators to heavy exhaust. Draft 2 thesis: 'Cities should phase out gas-powered leaf blowers, which harm the workers who use them through both noise and exhaust.' Paragraphs: workers' hearing; workers' breathing; a phase-out with rebates for landscapers.
cards.a: Both changed. The thesis was revised: the harm now includes exhaust, the focus moved from neighbors to workers, and 'ban' became 'phase out.' The line of reasoning changed to match: the neighbors' paragraph was replaced by one on exhaust, and a new final step proposes rebates, because a phase-out needs a plan for the workers it affects.
cards.h: → thesis changes + reasoning changes + why they fit
cards.n: Noting only that a paragraph was added misses the point of the EK: new evidence can reshape the claim and the path to it together.

cards.q: Explain why revising a thesis in light of new evidence is a strength rather than an admission of failure.
cards.a: A thesis is the claim the evidence can defend; when the evidence changes, a thesis that stays the same is defending something the writer now knows is overstated or wrong. Revising keeps claim and support aligned, which is what makes the argument credible to readers who know the evidence too.
cards.h: → thesis must match its evidence → new evidence shifts what is defensible → revision keeps them aligned → credibility
cards.n: 'Changing your mind shows open-mindedness' is a virtue claim; say why an unrevised thesis becomes indefensible.
o: Readers who know the new evidence will dismiss an argument that ignores it.
The revised thesis is usually more precise, which makes it both truer and harder to refute.

w.a: A strong writer picks a thesis and sticks to it no matter what.
w.why: a thesis that ignores contrary evidence is not defensible

w.a: Revising the thesis means the first draft was worthless.
w.why: drafting is how the evidence gets tested

cards.q: Explain why new evidence might change a line of reasoning without changing the thesis.
cards.a: New evidence can confirm the claim while undercutting one of the reasons for it, or supply a stronger reason than the writer had. The writer then reorders, replaces, or adds a step so the reasoning rests on the best support, while the position itself stays the same.
cards.h: → evidence bears on a reason, not the claim → swap or reorder steps → same thesis, stronger path
cards.n: 'Because the thesis was already right' skips the mechanism; name what the evidence does to a particular step of the reasoning.
o: A new finding that a reason is weak removes that step, even if other reasons still carry the claim.
Stronger evidence for one reason may move it to the end of the essay, where the most persuasive step belongs.

w.a: If the thesis does not change, the essay does not need to change either.
w.why: the reasons and their order may still need revision

w.a: New evidence always requires a completely new essay.
w.why: often only one step of the reasoning is affected

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'I met two rude tourists from that city, so people from there must all be unfriendly.'
cards.a: Hasty generalization: a conclusion about everyone from a city is drawn from two encounters, and tourists are not even a representative sample of the people who live there. It is the kind of generalization the CED says a lack of understanding of a subject's complexity produces.
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Sample size is one problem; the leap from tourists to residents adds an unrepresentative sample.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Either we privatize the water utility, or the whole system collapses within a year.'
cards.a: False dilemma: it reduces a complex choice to two options when others exist, such as new public funding, phased repairs, or a public-private partnership. The oversimplification makes the writer's option look like the only escape from disaster.
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Refute it by naming a specific third option, not just by saying 'there are other options.'

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'If we let students redo one quiz, soon every assignment will be optional and no one will learn anything.'
cards.a: Slippery slope: it claims that one allowance, a single quiz retake, will inevitably lead to total collapse without showing why each step must follow. The oversimplification is treating a chain of uncertain possibilities as a certainty.
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). A warning about consequences is not a fallacy in itself; it becomes one when the links are never shown.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'The team started winning right after they changed the mascot, so the new mascot must be the reason.'
cards.a: Post hoc ergo propter hoc: it assumes that because the winning began after the mascot changed, the mascot caused it. It oversimplifies causation by ignoring other explanations, such as new players, an easier schedule, or chance.
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). 'After' is not 'because'; a causal claim must rule out the other explanations.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of post hoc ergo propter hoc and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Post hoc ergo propter hoc ('after this, therefore because of this') assumes that because B followed A, A caused B. Example: 'Test scores rose after the school repainted its halls, so the paint improved learning.' Sequence alone oversimplifies causation; a causal claim must rule out other explanations.
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Timing is a reason to investigate a cause, never proof of one.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of composition and division and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Composition assumes that what is true of the parts is true of the whole; division assumes that what is true of the whole is true of each part. Examples: 'Every player is an all-star, so the team will win' (composition); 'The school is top-ranked, so every teacher there is excellent' (division). Both are generalizations that ignore how parts and wholes differ.
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Composition builds up from parts, division breaks down from the whole; both assume traits carry over.

cards.q: Write a revision of this claim that reflects the complexity of the issue instead of oversimplifying it, using these details: 'The new cafeteria menu has failed because students hate healthy food.' Details: sales of the new salads fell by half, but sales of fruit cups and grain bowls rose; lines are longer because the salad station is slow.
cards.a: Model: 'The new menu has struggled less because students reject healthy food than because of how it is served: fruit cups and grain bowls are selling, while salads, stuck at the slowest station, have lost half their buyers.' The revision accounts for the mixed evidence and names a more precise cause.
cards.h: → model revision + what complexity it accounts for
cards.n: Softening the wording ('students somewhat dislike healthy food') keeps the oversimplified cause; the revision must use the evidence that complicates it.

cards.q: Explain why oversimplifying an issue weakens a writer's credibility with an informed audience.
cards.a: Readers who know the issue see what the simplification leaves out and conclude that the writer either does not understand the subject or is hiding its complications; either way they discount the argument. Acknowledging complexity shows command of the subject and makes the claim harder to dismiss.
cards.h: → informed readers see what is missing → writer seems ignorant or evasive → argument discounted
cards.n: 'Simple arguments are boring' misses the reason; say what an informed reader concludes about a writer who ignores complexity.
o: A simplified claim is easy to refute with one counterexample the audience already knows.
An argument that engages the complications earns the right to its conclusion; one that skips them seems to assume it.

w.a: Simple claims are always stronger because they are easier to understand.
w.why: clarity is not the same as oversimplification

w.a: Informed audiences do not care about complexity as long as the argument is emotional.
w.why: ignores how informed readers judge credibility

cards.q: Decide whether this is a defensible claim or an unqualified overclaim: 'Homework should never be assigned on weekends.'
cards.a: An unqualified overclaim: 'never' makes the claim absolute, so a single reasonable exception (a long-term project, optional reading) defeats it. 'Homework should rarely be assigned on weekends, and never as busywork' keeps the position while making it defensible.
cards.h: → verdict + the absolute word + a defensible version
cards.n: Swapping 'never' for 'almost never' fixes the risk; deleting the position altogether ('homework is complicated') loses the claim.

cards.q:
Identify the absolute term in each claim and give a qualified version:
1. 'Homework never helps young children learn.'
2. 'Every teenager is addicted to their phone.'
3. 'This study proves that recess improves grades.'
4. 'Nobody reads newspapers anymore.'
5. 'The only way to reduce traffic is to raise parking fees.'
6. 'Online classes are always worse than in-person ones.'
cards.a:
1 → 'never': 'Homework does little to help most young children learn.'
2 → 'Every': 'Many teenagers use their phones compulsively.'
3 → 'proves': 'This study suggests that recess may improve grades.'
4 → 'Nobody': 'Far fewer people read printed newspapers than a generation ago.'
5 → 'The only way': 'Raising parking fees is one of the most direct ways to reduce traffic.'
6 → 'always': 'Online classes tend to work less well for students who struggle to manage their own time.'
cards.h: → absolute word + qualified version, per line
cards.n: Item 3 shows the EK covers evidence too: 'proves' states evidence in absolute terms even when the claim itself looks modest.

cards.q: Decide which claim better suits a writer entering the long-running debate over year-round school calendars, and explain: (A) 'Year-round school is always better for students than the traditional calendar.' (B) 'For students who lose the most ground over long summers, a year-round calendar with shorter breaks is likely to do more good than harm.'
cards.a: (B): it limits the claim to a group and a likelihood, acknowledging that the debate has produced mixed findings and staking out ground the writer can defend. (A) states an absolute that informed readers can defeat with a single counterexample, which ignores the ongoing discourse.
cards.h: → letter + how it fits an ongoing debate
cards.n: Choosing (A) because it sounds more confident confuses force with strength; in an ongoing debate, absolutes are the easiest claims to refute.

cards.q: Write a version of this thesis that avoids absolute terms while keeping a clear position: 'Every student benefits from taking a gap year before college.'
cards.a: Model: 'A gap year benefits most students who spend it working or serving with a clear plan, though students without a plan or support may do better to enroll directly.' It keeps the position (gap years are worthwhile) but limits it to the students the evidence can cover.
cards.n: 'Some students might possibly benefit from gap years' hedges away the position; the goal is a limited claim, not a vague one.

cards.q: Identify the kinds of words that express claims, reasoning, or evidence in absolute terms.
cards.a: Universal quantifiers (all, every, none, no one), absolute frequency (always, never), certainty markers (proves, undeniably, obviously, clearly), and exclusive or superlative claims stated as fact (the only, the best, the worst). Each claims more than evidence in an ongoing debate usually supports.
cards.h: → four families of words, with examples
cards.n: A word list is a starting point: 'clearly' in a sentence that is then defended is fine; the problem is the claim it inflates.

cards.q: Explain why arguments that are part of an ongoing discourse often avoid absolute terms.
cards.a: An ongoing conversation means informed readers already know counterexamples and competing arguments. An absolute claim invites them to produce one and dismiss the whole argument, while a qualified claim acknowledges the discussion and stakes out ground the writer can actually defend.
cards.h: → ongoing debate → readers know counterexamples → absolutes invite refutation → qualified claims hold
cards.n: 'Absolute words sound arrogant' is a tone point; the CED's reason is that arguments join a discourse where counterexamples are already known.
o: Qualified language signals that the writer knows the discussion and is adding to it, which builds credibility with readers who have followed it.
A claim that allows for exceptions can absorb a counterexample; an absolute claim collapses under one.

w.a: Good writers never use absolute words at all.
w.why: an absolute is fine when evidence truly supports it

w.a: Avoiding absolutes means the writer is not sure of the position.
w.why: qualification sets the claim's scope, not the writer's confidence

cards.q: Explain why 'proves' is a riskier verb than 'suggests' when a writer introduces evidence.
cards.a: 'Proves' claims the evidence settles the question, so any gap in it discredits the claim; 'suggests' matches what most evidence can actually do and signals that the writer knows the discussion continues, which makes readers more willing to accept the point.
cards.h: → 'proves' claims certainty → any gap discredits it → 'suggests' matches the evidence → readers accept more
cards.n: 'Suggests sounds more polite' is a style reason; the point is matching the verb to what the evidence can support.
o: One study rarely settles a question, so 'proves' overstates it for informed readers.
Choosing verbs that fit the evidence shows the writer understands the evidence's limits.

w.a: Writers should say 'proves' because it sounds more persuasive.
w.why: overstatement invites refutation

w.a: 'Suggests' makes evidence weaker, so it should be avoided.
w.why: it describes the evidence accurately, which strengthens trust

cards.q: Define a qualifier and give three examples.
cards.a: A qualifier is a word, phrase, or clause that limits the scope or certainty of a claim so it says no more than the evidence supports. Examples: 'usually' (word), 'in most rural districts' (phrase), 'unless the grant is renewed' (clause).
cards.h: → definition + a word, a phrase, a clause
cards.n: Qualifiers make a claim more defensible, not weaker; an unqualified absolute can be refuted with one counterexample.

cards.q: Contrast a qualifier that strengthens an argument and hedging language that weakens one.
cards.a: A qualifier names exactly where or when a claim holds ('in districts without buses,' 'for students under 14'), narrowing it to what the evidence supports and showing control. Hedging ('it could perhaps be argued') withholds commitment without naming any limit, so readers cannot tell what the writer believes.
cards.n: 'Under most circumstances' qualifies; 'it could maybe be said' hedges. The difference is whether a specific limit is named.

cards.q: Identify the problem: 'Some people might think that social media could possibly be somewhat harmful in certain cases.'
cards.a: Stacked hedges: 'some people might think,' 'could possibly,' 'somewhat,' and 'in certain cases' qualify the claim so heavily and vaguely that no position remains. A qualified version names the limit: 'Social media harms teenagers' sleep when they use it after midnight.'
cards.h: → the problem + the stacked words + a fix
cards.n: Hedging and qualifying look alike but do opposite work: a qualifier names the conditions, a hedge names none.

cards.q: Apply a qualifier to strengthen this claim: 'Standardized tests are unfair to low-income students.'
cards.a: 'Standardized tests are unfair to low-income students when test preparation is sold rather than provided by schools.' The clause limits the claim to the condition the evidence addresses, unequal access to preparation, which makes it harder to refute with a counterexample.
cards.h: → rewritten claim + what the modifier limits
cards.n: A vague qualifier like 'sometimes' does less work than naming the actual condition under which the claim holds.

cards.q: Define qualification of a claim.
cards.a: Qualification limits a claim's scope, certainty, or conditions with modifiers (words, phrases, or clauses) such as 'often,' 'in most cases,' or 'unless,' so the claim can withstand counterexamples. It is how writers limit the scope of an argument without abandoning the position.
cards.h: → definition + what it limits + example modifiers
cards.n: A qualified claim is harder to disprove, not weaker; qualifying is different from giving up the position.

cards.q: Identify eight qualifiers a writer can use to limit a claim.
cards.a: Often, usually, in most cases, tends to, may, largely, unless, and with few exceptions. Words (often, may), phrases (in most cases), and clauses (unless the funding lapses) all qualify; the right one names the limit the evidence actually supports.
cards.n: Scattering qualifiers through every sentence turns qualification into hedging; qualify the claims your evidence cannot fully cover.

cards.q:
Identify the modifier that qualifies each claim, whether it is a word, phrase, or clause, and what it limits:
1. 'Most teenagers need more sleep than they get.'
2. 'The tax will probably pass.'
3. 'In towns under 5,000 people, one library branch is enough.'
4. 'The ban works if parents enforce it at home.'
5. 'Remote classes suit students who already manage their time well.'
6. 'Before age ten, children pick up accents more easily.'
7. 'The plan will cut costs, although not in its first year.'
8. 'Recycling largely pays for itself.'
cards.a:
1 → 'Most' (word): limits scope from all teenagers
2 → 'probably' (word): limits certainty
3 → 'In towns under 5,000 people' (phrase): limits scope to small towns
4 → 'if parents enforce it at home' (clause): limits the claim to a condition
5 → 'who already manage their time well' (clause): limits scope to one group
6 → 'Before age ten' (phrase): limits scope in time
7 → 'although not in its first year' (clause): limits scope in time and concedes a cost
8 → 'largely' (word): limits degree
cards.h: → modifier + form + what it limits, per line
cards.n: Naming the modifier is half the task; the exam asks what it does, so state what the claim no longer covers.

cards.q: Explain why a rebuttal (reservation) makes a Toulmin argument stronger rather than weaker.
cards.a: A rebuttal (reservation) names the conditions under which the claim would not hold, which shows the writer has tested the argument's limits, so readers trust the claim where it does hold. It also limits the claim's scope before an opponent can, leaving less to attack.
cards.h: → exceptions named → limits tested → claim trusted where it holds → less left for opponents
cards.n: Toulmin's 'rebuttal' (an exception clause) differs from the CED's rebut (answering an opposing argument); keep the two apart.
o: The reservation turns a counterexample the audience might raise into part of the writer's own argument.
A claim with stated exceptions is more precise, and precise claims are harder to refute than sweeping ones.

w.a: A reservation weakens the argument because it admits the claim is not always true.
w.why: unqualified claims are easier to defeat

w.a: Writers add reservations only to reach a required length.
w.why: ignores what the limit does for credibility and scope

cards.q: Explain why a qualifying clause such as 'unless families opt out' can make a policy proposal more persuasive.
cards.a: The clause limits the proposal to cases the writer can defend and answers a likely objection before readers raise it, so the policy seems considered rather than sweeping. Readers who would reject a blanket rule can accept a qualified one.
cards.h: → clause limits scope → objection answered in advance → proposal seems considered → more readers can accept it
cards.n: 'It makes the claim less extreme' names the result, not the reason; say which objection the clause answers and for whom.
o: A qualified proposal gives resistant readers a way to agree without surrendering their concern.
Naming the condition shows the writer has thought about how the policy would work in practice.

w.a: Qualifying clauses make a proposal sound unsure, which weakens it.
w.why: a named condition shows control, not doubt

w.a: Adding 'unless' clauses is only a grammar choice with no effect on persuasion.
w.why: the clause changes what readers are asked to accept

cards.q: Define counterargument.
cards.a: A counterargument is a position or objection that opposes the writer's claim, which the writer states in the text in order to respond to it. Engaging the strongest counterarguments is how a writer enters an ongoing conversation instead of arguing as if no one had spoken before.
cards.n: Stating a feeble objection nobody holds is not engagement; the counterargument should be one an informed opponent would actually make.

cards.q: Define Rogerian argument.
cards.a: Rogerian argument, named for the psychologist Carl Rogers, seeks common ground: the writer first restates the opposing position fairly, grants the conditions in which it is right, names shared values, and only then proposes a position both sides can accept. It enters the conversation by treating positions already argued as partly valid.
cards.n: Not a CED term (flagged as useful). Its signature is a genuine concession before any proposal, not a token nod to the other side.

cards.q: Contrast Rogerian and classical (Aristotelian) argument.
cards.a: Classical argument states and proves the writer's position, then refutes opposing views, aiming to win over an undecided audience. Rogerian argument begins by fairly restating the opposing view and finding shared ground, aiming at a position a resistant audience can accept. Both engage positions already argued; they differ in when and how.
cards.n: Neither is a CED term (flagged as useful). Choosing between them is a choice about audience: how resistant are these readers?

cards.q: Decide which argument structure fits: a writer wants to find common ground with a skeptical audience before proposing any solution.
cards.a: Rogerian argument: it opens by restating the opposing view fairly and naming shared values, so a skeptical audience hears its own position acknowledged before any proposal. A classical structure puts the writer's case first, which a skeptical audience may resist before it reaches the evidence.
cards.h: → structure + why it fits this audience
cards.n: Borrows audience analysis (rhs). The skeptical audience, not the topic, decides the structure.

cards.q: Identify how the writer enters the ongoing conversation in this opening of a school librarian's essay: 'For a decade, the debate over school libraries has been framed as books versus screens: one side warns that devices are killing reading, the other that print is obsolete. Both sides assume a library is a room full of objects. I want to argue that a library is a teacher, and that the real question is who will teach students to find what is true.'
cards.a: She summarizes the two positions already argued (books versus screens), identifies an assumption both share (a library is a collection of objects), and redirects the debate with her own claim (a library teaches research). Engaging both sides first shows she knows the conversation and presents her claim as a new move within it.
cards.h: → positions summarized → shared assumption named → new claim
cards.n: Calling this 'a hook' names a function without the move; the key is that she challenges an assumption both existing sides share.

cards.q: Write a two-sentence opening for an argument essay on whether cities should close downtown streets to cars, one that engages the positions already argued before stating your own.
cards.a: Model: 'Downtown car bans are usually debated as a fight between shop owners who fear losing drivers and residents who want quieter streets. Both sides overlook the people who most need downtown to work, those who cannot drive at all, and their needs make a partial ban, limited at first to weekends, the better place to start.'
cards.h: → two sentences: positions engaged, then own claim
cards.n: 'Some people think cars should be banned and others do not' reports that a debate exists; entering it means saying what both sides miss.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might choose Rogerian argument over classical arrangement when addressing a hostile audience.
cards.a: A hostile audience stops listening when it feels attacked; restating its view fairly and naming shared values first lowers its defenses, so the proposal that follows is heard as a response to its concerns. Classical arrangement's early case for the writer's side can read as combative and shut such readers down.
cards.h: → hostile readers resist attack → fair restatement + shared values first → defenses lowered → proposal heard
cards.n: Borrows audience analysis (rhs). 'Rogerian is nicer' is not a reason; explain what the order does to a hostile audience's willingness to listen.
o: Rogerian structure lets the audience see its own position represented accurately, which is a precondition for trusting the writer.
Starting from common ground turns the argument into a shared problem instead of a contest the audience can lose.

w.a: Rogerian argument is better because it avoids taking any side.
w.why: it does take a position, after establishing common ground

w.a: Hostile audiences cannot be persuaded, so the structure does not matter.
w.why: structure is exactly what can change a resistant reader's response

cards.q: Explain why an argument that ignores what others have already said on its subject tends to persuade informed readers less.
cards.a: Informed readers carry the existing arguments with them, so they test each claim against objections the writer never mentions; the silence suggests the writer does not know the conversation or cannot answer it. Engaging prior positions shows where the new claim fits and why it improves on them.
cards.h: → readers know the debate → unanswered objections fill the silence → writer seems uninformed → engagement wins trust
cards.n: 'It seems one-sided' is vague; say that informed readers supply the missing objections themselves and hold them against the writer.
o: Engaging prior positions lets the writer frame them, rather than letting readers bring their strongest versions uninvited.
A claim positioned against earlier ones shows readers what is new about it, which gives them a reason to care.

w.a: Mentioning other arguments only gives readers reasons to disagree.
w.why: readers already know them; ignoring them looks evasive

w.a: An argument is stronger if it pretends the issue is settled.
w.why: an ongoing conversation is by definition not settled

cards.q:
Decide whether each source supports, complements, or contradicts this thesis: 'Our town should convert the vacant textile mill into a year-round public market.'
1. A county survey: 68 percent of residents say they would shop weekly at a downtown market.
2. An engineer's report: the mill's floors cannot hold crowds without $2 million in repairs.
3. A historian's essay on the mill's role in the town's founding.
4. A report that a similar market in a neighboring town closed within two years for lack of vendors.
5. A farmers' association letter: twenty growers want a year-round indoor place to sell.
6. A study finding that downtown foot traffic raises sales at nearby shops.
cards.a:
1 → supports (direct evidence of demand)
2 → contradicts (a cost the thesis must answer)
3 → complements (adds heritage value to reuse without proving the market would work)
4 → contradicts (evidence the model can fail)
5 → supports (evidence of vendor supply)
6 → complements (extends the benefit beyond the market to the whole downtown)
cards.n: The CED names the three relations without defining them; a working test: supports proves the claim, complements adds a related angle, contradicts cuts against it.

cards.q: Define concession.
cards.a: A concession accepts all or a portion of a competing position or claim as correct, agrees that it is correct under a different set of circumstances, or acknowledges the limitations of the writer's own argument (the CED's three forms). Writers concede to show fairness, which enhances their credibility, before returning to their own position.
cards.h: → the CED's three forms + why writers concede
cards.n: Signal words (admittedly, granted, it is true that) mark a concession; a concession with no turn back to the writer's claim reads as surrender.

cards.q: Define refutation.
cards.a: Refutation shows that all or part of a competing position or claim is invalid, using evidence and reasoning against its evidence, its logic, or its assumptions. Along with rebutting and conceding, refuting opposing arguments is one of the moves the CED says enhances a writer's credibility.
cards.n: Attacking the person who made the argument is ad hominem, not refutation; refutation targets the argument's evidence, logic, or assumptions.

cards.q: Define rebuttal.
cards.a: A rebuttal offers a contrasting perspective on an argument and its evidence, or provides alternative evidence, to propose that all or a portion of a competing position or claim is invalid (the CED's definition). It answers the opposing argument without having to disprove it outright.
cards.h: → the CED's definition + how it differs from refuting
cards.n: Students use rebut and refute interchangeably; in the CED's terms, a rebuttal proposes invalidity with a contrasting view or other evidence.

cards.q: Contrast concession and refutation.
cards.a: A concession accepts that an opposing point is correct in whole or in part, or under some circumstances, or admits a limit of the writer's own case; a refutation shows that an opposing point is invalid. Writers often pair them: conceding what is true earns trust, and refuting what is not reclaims the ground.
cards.h: → accept vs invalidate + why they pair
cards.n: Label the pair and explain the sequence's effect on a skeptical reader; naming 'concession' alone earns nothing.

cards.q: Contrast counterargument and rebuttal.
cards.a: The counterargument is the opposing position or objection itself, stated in the writer's text; the rebuttal is the writer's response, offering a contrasting perspective or alternative evidence to show that all or part of it is invalid. One raises the objection, the other answers it.
cards.n: A counterargument left standing with no rebuttal reads as a concession the writer never meant to make.

cards.q: Identify the move: 'Cutting the budget will save money short term - but it guts the programs that prevent costlier crises later.'
cards.a: Concession followed by rebuttal: the writer accepts a portion of the competing claim as correct (the cut saves money in the short term), then pivots on 'but' to offer a contrasting perspective (long-term costs) showing that the case for cutting is incomplete.
cards.h: → the two moves + the pivot word
cards.n: Quote the pivot: 'but' marks the exact point where the writer takes the ground back, which is what an analysis should point to.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Senator Cole wants stricter emissions limits, but why listen to someone who just bought a second house?'
cards.a: Ad hominem: it attacks Cole's personal purchase instead of the emissions proposal, so it rebuts nothing. A genuine rebuttal would offer a contrasting perspective or alternative evidence about the emissions limits themselves.
cards.h: → fallacy + what a real rebuttal would do
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Not every personal remark is ad hominem; a real conflict of interest can bear on credibility.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'You say I text too much at dinner, but you're always checking email at the table too.'
cards.a: Tu quoque ('you too'): it deflects the criticism by accusing the critic of the same behavior, which says nothing about whether texting at dinner is a problem. It looks like a rebuttal but offers no contrasting perspective on the claim itself.
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Both people can be wrong at once, so hypocrisy in the critic never settles the criticism.

cards.q: Contrast how concession is used in Rogerian argument versus in classical refutation.
cards.a: In Rogerian argument, concession comes first and is genuine: the writer grants the opposing view's validity to build trust before proposing common ground. In classical arrangement, concession usually comes in the refutation, after the writer's case, granting a minor point so the rebuttal that follows seems fair.
cards.n: The same concession lands differently depending on where it sits; say what its placement does to the audience.

cards.q:
Identify which of the CED's three kinds of concession each sentence makes (accepting all or part of a competing claim; agreeing it is correct under different circumstances; acknowledging a limitation of one's own argument):
1. 'Opponents are right that the market would draw some shoppers away from the grocery store.'
2. 'In a larger city with an existing market district, the mill might well be better used as housing.'
3. 'My survey reached only residents who attend town meetings, so it may overstate enthusiasm.'
4. 'If the repairs truly cost $2 million, I would agree the plan should wait.'
5. 'The critics' figures on repair costs are accurate.'
6. 'No one knows yet whether vendors will stay past the first year, and my case depends on it.'
cards.a:
1 → accepts part of the competing claim
2 → agrees it would be correct under different circumstances
3 → acknowledges a limitation of the writer's own argument
4 → agrees the competing claim is correct under a different set of circumstances (a higher cost)
5 → accepts part of the competing claim (its figures)
6 → acknowledges a limitation of the writer's own argument
cards.h: → one kind of concession per line
cards.n: Item 4 is conditional, not a full surrender; a concession under different circumstances keeps the writer's position for the actual case.

cards.q: Explain where a concession is most effective when placed within a body paragraph.
cards.a: Early, before the writer's own point: granting the opposing point first shows fairness, and the rebuttal or refutation that follows gets the last and most memorable word. A concession placed after the writer's point reads as a retreat and leaves the opposing view echoing.
cards.h: → concede first → fairness shown → rebuttal gets the last word → reader ends on the writer's claim
cards.n: 'It is the rule to concede first' gives no reason; explain what the order does to the reader's final impression.
o: An early concession disarms a skeptical reader, who then hears the rebuttal as reasonable rather than defensive.
Readers weigh what comes last most heavily, so the writer's claim should close the paragraph.

w.a: Concessions should come last so the essay ends on a fair note.
w.why: ending on the opposition's point weakens the writer's claim

w.a: Where the concession goes does not matter as long as it is there.
w.why: placement changes what the reader carries away

cards.q: Explain the risk of placing a concession at the very end of an argument essay.
cards.a: Readers carry away the final paragraph; ending on a point granted to the opposition, with no rebuttal after it, leaves the counterargument as the last word and makes the writer's position seem to weaken at the close. Concede earlier, then rebut, and end on the writer's own claim.
cards.h: → ending weighs most → unanswered concession last → opposition gets the final word → thesis seems to fade
cards.n: 'It is confusing' is vague; say that the final impression favors whatever comes last.
o: A late concession can look like a writer losing confidence, which undermines everything argued before.
Sophistication comes from integrating the concession into the reasoning, not from tacking it onto the conclusion.

w.a: Ending with a concession always shows maturity and earns the sophistication point.
w.why: a concession tacked on at the end is not integrated complexity

w.a: Concessions belong only in the conclusion so they do not interrupt the argument.
w.why: they work best where they can be answered

cards.q: Explain why conceding part of an opposing argument can enhance a writer's credibility.
cards.a: A concession shows the writer has weighed the opposition honestly rather than caricaturing it, so readers trust the writer's judgment where the writer does disagree. It also narrows the dispute to the ground the writer can defend, which makes the rebuttal more convincing.
cards.h: → fair concession → writer seen as honest → trust transfers to the rebuttal → dispute narrowed to defensible ground
cards.n: 'It shows both sides' misses the effect; a concession earns trust for the writer's own position, it is not balance for its own sake.
o: Readers who hold the opposing view are more willing to listen once they see part of it accepted.
Conceding what the evidence clearly supports keeps the writer from defending indefensible ground.

w.a: Conceding a point means the writer's argument is weak.
w.why: a fair concession strengthens trust in what remains

w.a: Writers should concede as many points as possible to seem fair.
w.why: conceding everything leaves no position to defend

cards.q: Define a line of reasoning.
cards.a: A line of reasoning is the logical sequence of claims and supporting evidence that connects the thesis to the conclusion - the order in which ideas build so that each paragraph makes the next one possible.
cards.n: Row B rewards a line of reasoning: paragraphs in an arbitrary order cost points even when each is well written.

cards.q: Explain how to test whether an essay has a line of reasoning.
cards.a: Read only the topic sentences in order. If they form a coherent argument that arrives at the thesis, the line of reasoning holds; if they read as an unordered list of observations, it does not.
cards.n: This topic-sentence test is the fastest self-check in the final minutes of an FRQ.

cards.q: Explain the function of a topic sentence.
cards.a: A topic sentence states the paragraph's subclaim and links it to the thesis, telling the reader what this paragraph will prove and why it comes here. It should assert, not announce or summarize the source.
cards.n: 'In source B, the author discusses cost' is an announcement; a topic sentence must make an arguable point.

cards.q: Define unity in a paragraph.
cards.a: Unity means every sentence in the paragraph supports the single idea named in the topic sentence; nothing wanders into a different claim.
cards.n: The usual cause of lost unity is a good sentence the writer did not want to cut; if it proves a different point, it belongs elsewhere.

cards.q: Define coherence in writing.
cards.a: Coherence means the sentences and paragraphs connect so the reader can follow the movement of thought, achieved through transitions, repeated key terms, pronoun reference, and consistent order.
cards.n: Unity is about what belongs in a paragraph and coherence about whether the order can be followed, so an essay can have one without the other.

cards.q: Explain the standard structure of an argumentative body paragraph.
cards.a: Topic sentence stating the subclaim; specific evidence introduced with context; commentary explaining how the evidence proves the subclaim; and a link sentence tying the subclaim back to the thesis or forward to the next.
cards.n: Aim for at least two sentences of commentary for every one sentence of evidence.

cards.q: Decide when to start a new paragraph.
cards.a: Start a new paragraph when the subclaim changes, when a new source or piece of evidence requires its own analysis, when shifting from your case to the counterargument, or when a paragraph has grown so long the reader loses the claim.
cards.n: On a timed essay, breaks also buy readability: a reader working through hundreds of booklets finds a claim fastest at the top of one.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal addition and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Addition: furthermore, moreover, in addition, also, likewise. They signal to the reader that what follows adds another item of the same kind.
cards.n: These are the easiest transitions to overuse, since stacking furthermore and moreover makes a list look like reasoning without advancing it.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal contrast and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Contrast: however, yet, nevertheless, on the other hand, conversely. They signal to the reader that what follows opposes or turns against what came before.
cards.n: However needs a semicolon before it when it joins two independent clauses, and a comma alone in that spot creates a comma splice.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal causation and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Causation: therefore, consequently, thus, as a result, because. They signal to the reader that what follows is the cause or the effect of what came before.
cards.n: Because subordinates while therefore does not, so the punctuation differs: one joins clauses directly, the other needs a semicolon or period.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal concession and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Concession: admittedly, granted, of course, to be sure, while it is true that. They signal to the reader that what follows grants a point to the other side before it is answered.
cards.n: These words promise a turn, so a reader waits for the but or yet that follows; a concession left without one reads as surrender.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal exemplification and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Exemplification: for example, for instance, specifically, to illustrate, namely. They signal to the reader that what follows is a specific instance of the general claim.
cards.n: For example promises a case that fits the claim just made, which makes a mismatched example more damaging than no example at all.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal sequence and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Sequence: first, next, subsequently, meanwhile, finally. They signal to the reader that what follows comes next in an order of steps, stages, or priority.
cards.n: Sequence words describe order without proving connection, so first, second and third can hide the absence of a line of reasoning.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal emphasis and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Emphasis: indeed, above all, in fact, most significantly, especially. They signal to the reader that what follows is the most important point so far.
cards.n: These transitions make a claim about rank, so using one on every point flattens the very hierarchy they exist to create.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal conclusion and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Conclusion: in short, ultimately, on the whole, in conclusion, therefore. They signal to the reader that what follows closes the argument or sums it up.
cards.n: In conclusion is the weakest of these on a timed essay, because it announces the ending instead of doing anything with it.

cards.q: Explain the most common misuse of transitions.
cards.a: Using a transition whose relationship the sentences do not actually have - most often 'however' between two agreeing sentences or 'therefore' where no cause was established. The word then signals a logic the paragraph never performs.
cards.n: MC revision questions frequently test exactly this: the right answer replaces a mismatched connective.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called narration and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Narration: Tells a sequence of events as a story. It is best for making an abstract problem concrete and building emotional engagement.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: A narrative works as evidence only when the writer ties it back to the claim; left to stand alone it reads as a digression.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called description and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Description: Renders sensory and concrete detail about a subject. It is best for making a scene or condition vivid so the audience can judge it firsthand.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Description argues through what it selects: a scene rendered in sensory detail invites the verdict without ever stating it.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called definition and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Definition: Establishes what a key term means and does not mean. It is best when the argument turns on a contested term such as 'freedom' or 'fairness'.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Whoever wins the definition often wins the argument, which is why contested policy debates so often open by fighting over one word.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called exemplification and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Exemplification: Supports a generalization with a series of specific instances. It is best for showing that a pattern is real and widespread rather than isolated.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Three well-chosen instances can persuade more than one developed one here, since the point being proved is that the pattern is not isolated.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called comparison-contrast and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Comparison-contrast: Sets two subjects side by side to reveal similarity or difference. It is best for evaluating alternatives; organized point-by-point or subject-by-subject.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Point-by-point keeps the comparison visible but fragments each subject, while subject-by-subject flows better and risks two loose summaries.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called cause-effect and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Cause-effect: Traces why something happened or what it produced. It is best for arguments about responsibility or consequence; must guard against post hoc reasoning.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Strong cause-effect writing names the mechanism joining the two, because a sequence with no mechanism is correlation in disguise.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called process analysis and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Process analysis: Explains the steps by which something happens or is done. It is best for showing feasibility or exposing where a system breaks down.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Explaining how something works is itself a way to argue, since laying out each step makes a system's failure point hard to deny.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called classification and division and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Classification and division: Sorts items into categories, or breaks one subject into parts. It is best for imposing order on a sprawling issue so each part can be judged separately.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: The categories have to be mutually exclusive and cover the ground, or the argument built on them will leak at the overlaps.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called problem-solution and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Problem-solution: Establishes a problem, then proposes and defends a remedy. It is best for policy arguments; the solution must be shown to be both effective and feasible.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Weak versions skip feasibility and propose a remedy no one could fund or enforce, which is the first thing the opposition names.

cards.q: Explain why identifying a passage's method of development matters in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: The method is itself a rhetorical choice: choosing to define a term, narrate a case, or classify a field shapes what the audience sees as the issue. Naming the method lets you analyze the structure rather than only the sentence-level devices.
cards.n: Analyzing organization is a higher-level move than device-spotting and often supports the sophistication point.

cards.q: Explain what an effective introduction does on an AP Lang essay.
cards.a: It orients the reader to the issue in one or two sentences, narrows to the specific question at stake, and ends with a defensible thesis that previews the line of reasoning. Three to four sentences is plenty.
cards.n: The thesis must appear in the introduction or the conclusion; placing it last in paragraph one is the safest way to secure Row A.

cards.q: Identify introduction moves that waste time or hurt the score.
cards.a: 'Since the beginning of time' openings, dictionary definitions of common words, restating the prompt verbatim, announcing the essay's plan ('In this essay I will'), and long summary of the passage or sources before any claim.
cards.n: Every sentence spent on throat-clearing is a sentence not spent on commentary, which is where 4 of 6 points live.

cards.q: Explain what an effective conclusion does.
cards.a: It extends rather than repeats: it states what follows from the argument, names the stakes or implications, and may broaden to a related context. Two to four sentences is enough.
cards.n: A conclusion is a fine place to earn sophistication by naming limitations or broader implications.

cards.q: Identify conclusion habits to avoid.
cards.a: Mechanically restating the thesis and topic sentences, introducing brand-new evidence that cannot be analyzed, apologizing for the argument, or ending on a rhetorical question that undoes the position just taken.
cards.n: If you are out of time, one strong implication sentence beats a full formulaic restatement.

cards.q: Define the chronological organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Chronological: arranges material in time order. Typical use: narratives, historical causation, and process explanations.
cards.n: It is the easiest pattern to follow and the easiest to overuse, since narrating a sequence is not the same as arguing about it.

cards.q: Define the spatial organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Spatial: arranges material by physical position or location. Typical use: descriptions of place, scenes, and physical evidence.
cards.n: Spatial order shows up in analysis mostly inside descriptive passages, where the path the eye takes is itself a rhetorical choice.

cards.q: Define the order of importance organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Order of importance: arranges points from least to most (or most to least) significant. Typical use: persuasion, where ending on the strongest point leaves the final impression.
cards.n: Ending on the strongest point exploits recency while opening with it hedges against a reader who stops early, so audience decides.

cards.q: Define the general-to-specific organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: General-to-specific: moves from a broad principle down to particular cases (or the reverse). Typical use: deductive arguments and definitions applied to instances.
cards.n: The reverse direction, specific to general, is the inductive shape and tends to feel more like discovery to a reader.

cards.q: Explain how to signal an essay's organizational pattern to a reader.
cards.a: Use topic sentences that name the relationship to the previous paragraph, transitions matched to that relationship, and repeated key terms from the thesis, so the pattern is visible without announcing it ('my second point is').
cards.n: Announcing the structure aloud costs more than it gains, because my second point is reads as a checklist rather than an argument.

cards.q: Define synthesis as the term is used on the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Synthesis is combining material from multiple provided sources with your own reasoning to develop and support your own argument - the sources serve your position, rather than the essay reporting what each source says in turn.
cards.n: The Q1 essay is your argument using sources, not a survey of the sources.

cards.q: Explain how many sources the AP Lang synthesis essay requires and how to use them.
cards.a: You must incorporate and cite at least three of the provided sources in support of your argument; sources may be quoted or paraphrased, and one source can be used in more than one paragraph.
cards.n: Using more than three earns nothing by itself; poor commentary on six sources scores below strong commentary on three.

cards.q: Explain how to cite sources in-text on the synthesis essay.
cards.a: Refer to each source by its given label or the author's name in parentheses or in a signal phrase - '(Source C)' or 'Chen argues that...' Full bibliographic citations and a works cited page are not required.
cards.n: Uncited source material can cost the evidence point even if the ideas are accurate.

cards.q: Define an attributive tag (signal phrase) and give two examples.
cards.a: An attributive tag introduces borrowed material and names its origin, so the reader knows where the idea comes from and how to weigh it. Examples: 'As economist Dana Ruiz notes,...' / 'Source B counters that...'
cards.n: Verb choice inside the tag is an argumentative move: 'concedes,' 'claims,' and 'demonstrates' position the source differently.

cards.q: Explain what source-dropping is and how to avoid it.
cards.a: Source-dropping is inserting a quotation or citation with no framing before it and no commentary after it. Avoid it by introducing the source, quoting only the necessary words, and then explaining how it advances your claim.
cards.n: The fix is a sandwich: set up, quote, explain. A paragraph that ends on a quotation almost always needs one more sentence.

cards.q: Explain how to put two sources in conversation rather than listing them.
cards.a: Build the paragraph around your subclaim, then show the relationship between the sources - one extends, complicates, or answers the other - and explain what that relationship proves. The paragraph is organized by idea, not by source.
cards.n: 'While Source A treats cost as decisive, Source D shows the cost falls unevenly' is a conversation; two summaries are not.

cards.q: State the basic MLA in-text citation format for a print source.
cards.a: Author's last name and page number in parentheses with no comma, before the sentence's end punctuation: (Ruiz 42). If the author is named in a signal phrase, only the page number appears: (42).
cards.n: The parenthetical has to match the works cited entry, so whatever word opens that entry is the word that goes in the parentheses.

cards.q: Explain the MLA in-text citation when a source has no page numbers or no named author.
cards.a: With no page numbers (a website), cite the author's name alone. With no author, use a shortened form of the title in quotation marks or italics, matching the works cited entry.
cards.n: The AP synthesis essay accepts the simpler tag, so a parenthetical like (Source C) is enough to earn credit for attribution.

cards.q: Explain how to integrate a quotation grammatically into your own sentence.
cards.a: Make the quotation a syntactic part of your sentence: introduce it with a signal phrase and comma, blend it with 'that' and no comma, or weave short phrases into your own clause. The finished sentence must parse if the quotation marks were removed.
cards.n: Read the sentence aloud without the quotation marks - if it is ungrammatical, the integration failed.

cards.q: Explain when and how to use an ellipsis in a quotation.
cards.a: Use three spaced periods ( ... ) to mark words omitted from the middle of a quotation, and only when the omission does not change the author's meaning. No ellipsis is needed at the start of a quoted fragment.
cards.n: Cutting a qualifier out of a quotation with an ellipsis is a form of cherry picking, not a mechanical fix.

cards.q: Explain when to use square brackets inside a quotation.
cards.a: Use square brackets to insert your own words for clarity or grammatical fit - identifying a pronoun's referent, adjusting a verb tense, or changing capitalization - so the quotation reads correctly in your sentence.
cards.n: Brackets signal editing by you; anything inside them is your language, not the source's.

cards.q: Explain the 'so what' link that ends a body paragraph.
cards.a: The final sentence should state why the paragraph's subclaim matters to the thesis - the consequence, stake, or step it establishes - rather than restating the topic sentence in different words.
cards.n: This one sentence per paragraph is the cheapest reliable way to raise a Row B score.

cards.q: Explain where to place the counterargument paragraph and why.
cards.a: Place it after your strongest supporting paragraphs and before the conclusion, so the reader is already persuaded when the objection appears and you have the last word answering it. State the objection fairly, then refute or absorb it.
cards.n: Handling a genuine counterargument with nuance is one recognized route to the sophistication point.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal comparison and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Comparison: similarly, likewise, in the same way, by the same token. They signal to the reader that what follows is alike in kind to what came before.
cards.n: Comparison and addition get confused constantly: likewise asserts that two things are alike in kind, while also merely adds another item.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal condition and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Condition: if, unless, provided that, as long as, in the event that. They signal to the reader that what follows depends on a stated circumstance rather than holding unconditionally.
cards.n: Conditional transitions are qualifiers in disguise, narrowing a claim down to the circumstances where it can actually be defended.

cards.q: Define pronoun reference as a coherence device and its main risk.
cards.a: Using pronouns (it, this, they) to point back to a previously named idea, linking sentences without repeating the noun. Its main risk is an unclear antecedent, which leaves the reader guessing what it refers to.
cards.n: The riskiest case is a this with no noun after it, and adding one word, as in this omission, repairs most vague references.

cards.q: Define key-term repetition as a coherence device.
cards.a: Deliberately repeating a thesis's central word or phrase across topic sentences and transitions so the reader keeps tracking the same idea as it develops.
cards.n: Repeating the exact term from the prompt or thesis is a cheap, reliable way to keep an essay visibly unified.

cards.q: Contrast narration and description as methods of development.
cards.a: Narration tells a sequence of events as a story, organized in time; description renders sensory, concrete detail about a subject or scene, organized in space or impression. Narration moves; description dwells.
cards.n: Most passages mix the two, so the useful question is which one dominates a given paragraph and what that choice accomplishes.

cards.q: Contrast classification and division as methods of development.
cards.a: Classification sorts many separate items into shared categories; division breaks one single subject into its component parts. Classification groups outward from many things; division splits inward from one thing.
cards.n: Count the starting subjects to tell them apart: many things being sorted is classification, one thing being cut up is division.

cards.q: Define the categorical (topical) organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Categorical: arranges material by distinct types or categories rather than by time, space, or importance. Typical use: essays that survey several kinds of causes, groups, or examples side by side.
cards.n: This pattern carries no built-in progression, so the writer has to supply a reason for the order in which the categories arrive.

cards.q: Contrast point-by-point and block organization for a comparison-contrast essay.
cards.a: Point-by-point alternates between the two subjects within each paragraph, comparing one criterion at a time; block covers all of one subject first, then all of the other. Point-by-point keeps the comparison constant; block risks two disconnected halves.
cards.n: Point-by-point is usually safer under exam time pressure because the comparison stays visible throughout.

cards.q: Contrast paraphrase and direct quotation as ways to use a source.
cards.a: Paraphrase restates a source's idea in your own words, useful for background or dense material; direct quotation preserves exact wording, useful when the phrasing itself is evidence, such as loaded diction or a striking claim.
cards.n: Overusing direct quotation when paraphrase would serve better is a common way essays drift into summary.

cards.q: Define a block quotation and its MLA formatting trigger.
cards.a: A quotation of more than four lines of prose, set off from the paragraph as an indented block without quotation marks, with the parenthetical citation placed after the final punctuation.
cards.n: On a timed AP Lang essay, block quotations rarely earn their space; short, closely analyzed quotations score better.

cards.q: Explain the scoring consequence of citing fewer than three sources on the synthesis essay.
cards.a: The response cannot earn full Row B credit, since the task requires evidence drawn from and cited to at least three sources; reasoning built on personal opinion alone, however well developed, is scored as under-evidenced.
cards.n: Three is the floor rather than the target, and citing more than three does nothing on its own unless each one is actually analyzed.

cards.q: Contrast unity and coherence in a paragraph.
cards.a: Unity means every sentence supports the one idea in the topic sentence, with nothing off-topic; coherence means the sentences connect smoothly through transitions and reference, so the idea's development is easy to follow.
cards.n: A paragraph can be unified but still incoherent if its on-topic sentences jump around without links.

cards.q: Identify four effective ways to open an AP Lang essay besides stating the thesis outright.
cards.a: A brief relevant anecdote, a striking statistic, a short apt quotation, or a specific concrete scenario tied directly to the issue. Each should lead in one or two sentences to the thesis, not wander.
cards.n: Any of these fails the moment it runs past two sentences, because introduction length is time taken from the body paragraphs.

cards.q: Explain the call-to-action technique as a way to end an argument essay.
cards.a: The conclusion names a specific action the audience should take or a specific change that should follow from the argument, converting the essay's claim into a concrete next step rather than a restated summary.
cards.n: Vagueness kills the move: we must do better is a mood, while a named actor doing a named thing is an actual call.

cards.q: Explain the difference between macro transitions and micro transitions.
cards.a: Macro transitions connect one paragraph to the next, signaling how the whole subclaim relates to the last; micro transitions connect sentences within a single paragraph, guiding the reader through one line of thought.
cards.n: Essays usually fail at the macro level, where a paragraph opens with however and never says what it is contrasting with.

cards.q: Explain why a chart, photograph, or cartoon in a synthesis source set counts as a citable source.
cards.a: The prompt treats every numbered source as eligible evidence regardless of format; a graphic makes an argument through its data or imagery just as a prose source does, and citing it satisfies the three-source requirement.
cards.n: Visual sources are chronically underused, so a paragraph that analyzes the cartoon or the graph well stands out to a reader by contrast.

cards.q: Explain what it means for a thesis to preview (roadmap) the line of reasoning.
cards.a: The thesis briefly signals the order or categories of support to come, such as naming the grounds the essay will argue from, so the reader knows the shape of the argument before the body paragraphs begin.
cards.n: A roadmap thesis is not required for the Row A point, but it makes the reasoning easier for a reader to follow.

cards.q: Define plagiarism as it applies to the synthesis essay.
cards.a: Presenting a source's words or ideas as your own without attribution, whether by omitting a citation or by paraphrasing too closely to the original wording without crediting the source.
cards.n: Close paraphrase with a citation attached is still a problem, because the wording has to change as well as the credit being given.

cards.q: Contrast a coordinating conjunction and a conjunctive adverb as transitional tools.
cards.a: A coordinating conjunction (and, but, so) joins two independent clauses with just a comma before it; a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, moreover) needs a semicolon before it and a comma after, and can also open a new sentence.
cards.n: Using a comma alone before however creates a comma splice - a mechanical error MC revision questions test directly.

cards.q: Contrast cohesion and coherence in writing.
cards.a: Cohesion is the local, sentence-to-sentence stitching, such as pronouns, repeated terms, and transitions; coherence is the larger sense that the whole piece makes sense and moves toward a purpose.
cards.n: Writing can be cohesive at the sentence level while still failing to cohere as an argument.

cards.q: Identify what breaks a line of reasoning even when each paragraph is individually well written.
cards.a: Paragraphs that could be reordered without changing the essay's meaning, subclaims that repeat rather than build on each other, and body paragraphs that never connect back to the same governing thesis.
cards.n: The reorder test is the fastest diagnostic, and it can be run on an outline before a single paragraph has been written.

cards.q: State the MLA in-text citation format for a source with two authors.
cards.a: Both last names joined by and, followed by the page number, with no comma before the page: (Ruiz and Chen 42). If named in a signal phrase, only the page number appears in parentheses.
cards.n: For three or more authors MLA uses the first last name plus et al., as in (Ruiz et al. 42), again with no comma before the page.

cards.q: Contrast a subclaim and a topic sentence.
cards.a: A subclaim is the idea a paragraph exists to prove, an arguable point that supports the thesis; a topic sentence is the actual sentence that states that subclaim to the reader.
cards.n: The distinction matters while planning, since outlining subclaims first keeps you from wording ideas you have not actually chosen yet.

cards.q: Explain why quoting an entire long sentence from a source usually weakens Row B more than a short quotation would.
cards.a: A long quotation leaves less room for commentary and often includes material the writer never analyzes, so the paragraph reads as evidence with thin explanation; a short, precisely chosen quotation lets nearly every word be unpacked.
cards.n: A workable ratio is about two sentences of commentary for every quoted line, since Row B scores explanation and not quoted volume.

cards.q: Define what counts as a visual or quantitative source in an AP Lang synthesis set.
cards.a: Any source presented as a chart, graph, table, photograph, cartoon, map, or infographic rather than continuous prose, still counted as one of the required sources if cited.
cards.n: Students sometimes forget to cite these sources at all, treating them as decoration rather than as a required source.

cards.q: Explain the difference between describing a chart and analyzing one in a synthesis essay.
cards.a: Describing restates what the numbers or image show; analyzing explains why that trend or image matters to the writer's argument and what conclusion it supports.
cards.h: → what it shows vs. why it matters
cards.n: Row B rewards analysis; a sentence that only restates the chart's data reads closer to summary.

cards.q: Identify the mistake: an essay paragraph spends four sentences listing every number on a bar graph before stating any claim about them.
cards.a: Data-dumping; reciting the chart's figures without connecting them to an argument reads as summary rather than analysis.
cards.n: One figure chosen for what it proves beats every figure recited, and the reader can already see the chart without the guided tour.

cards.q: Explain how to cite a graph or chart source with no named author in an AP Lang synthesis essay.
cards.a: Cite it by its source label, such as (Source C), matching whatever label the exam packet assigns the visual source.
cards.n: The same labeling convention applies to a photograph, cartoon, or map with no named creator.

cards.q: Explain what a political cartoon contributes to a synthesis source set that a prose source usually cannot.
cards.a: A cartoon compresses an argument into a single symbolic image, letting a writer analyze visual choices like exaggeration or juxtaposition as evidence of the cartoonist's stance.
cards.h: → what it adds that prose cannot
cards.n: Cartoons reward the same analysis as prose: name the exaggeration or symbol, then say what position it pushes the viewer toward.

cards.q: Apply a qualifier while citing a graph: rewrite 'The chart proves teen screen time causes anxiety' to match what a correlational graph can actually support.
cards.a: 'The chart suggests a correlation between teen screen time and anxiety' - a graph showing two trends rising together supports correlation, not proof of causation.
cards.n: Two trends rising together is genuinely useful evidence; the error is only in overstating what that relationship proves.

cards.q: Explain how to put a statistic from a graph source into conversation with a claim from a prose source in the same paragraph.
cards.a: State the prose source's claim, then show the graph's numbers either confirming or complicating it, so the two sources visibly respond to each other rather than sitting in separate paragraphs.
cards.n: Complicating a source is usually richer material than confirming it, since the tension between sources is what synthesis is scored on.

cards.q: Decide which detail from a bar graph is more useful as synthesis evidence: the exact value of one bar, or the overall trend across all the bars.
cards.a: The overall trend; a single bar's exact value rarely supports an argument on its own, while the trend across the whole graph shows a pattern the writer can build a claim around.
cards.h: → pattern over a single data point
cards.n: An exact value still has a place in a sentence, but it should serve the trend the writer is arguing, not stand alone.

cards.q: Explain why a synthesis essay should still explain a chart's axis labels or units in a sentence before analyzing it.
