cards.a: A reader who has not seen the source needs enough orientation to follow the analysis; skipping this can make even a sharp observation about the data confusing.
cards.n: One clause is enough here, and spending three sentences on orientation slides back into summarizing the chart rather than using it.

cards.q: Identify what is missing: a paragraph analyzes a photograph's composition in detail but never states what claim the photograph is meant to support.
cards.a: A stated claim; strong analysis of a visual source still has to connect back to the writer's own argument, not float as observation alone.
cards.n: Detailed formal analysis of an image can look impressive while still earning little credit if it never connects to the thesis.

cards.q: Explain why over-relying on the one visual source in a synthesis set can weaken an essay's line of reasoning.
cards.a: A single image usually cannot carry a whole paragraph's argument, so leaning on it alone tends to produce description instead of the sustained reasoning readers reward.
cards.n: Treat the image as one voice among several and pair it with a prose source, so the paragraph has something to reason between.

cards.q: Contrast the kind of commentary a chart's numbers can support versus what a photograph's composition can support.
cards.a: A chart's numbers support claims about scale, trend, or comparison, while a photograph's composition supports claims about emphasis, framing, or emotional appeal.
cards.n: A single source can sometimes offer both kinds of evidence, so look for whichever the writer's specific claim actually needs.

cards.q: Explain how to handle a visual source that seems to contradict the claims in the prose sources.
cards.a: Use the contradiction directly: acknowledge the tension and explain what it reveals, since disagreement among sources is exactly the material a strong line of reasoning can analyze.
cards.h: → contradiction is material, not a problem
cards.n: Quietly dropping an inconvenient source is closer to cherry picking, and the omission is visible when the source set is this short.

cards.q: Define an infographic and explain why it can be treated as a single source even though it combines text and images.
cards.a: A design that blends text, icons, and data visuals into one unified piece; it counts as one source because it presents one coordinated argument, not several separate ones.
cards.n: Treat every element in the infographic, text and image alike, as part of one argument when analyzing it.

cards.q: Explain the risk of quoting a caption under a photograph as if it were the photograph's own analysis.
cards.a: The caption is the source's framing of the image, not the writer's own analysis, so leaning on it without adding independent commentary can read as summary rather than argument.
cards.n: The caption is evidence of how the source wants the image read, which is worth analyzing in its own right if you say so explicitly.

cards.q: Explain why quoting a graph's exact figure can strengthen a synthesis claim more than a rounded summary of it.
cards.a: An exact figure, like 'rose from 12 to 47 percent,' shows the scale of a change precisely, while a vague summary like 'increased a lot' gives a reader nothing concrete to weigh.
cards.n: Precision also signals to the reader that the writer engaged closely with the source rather than skimming it.

cards.q: Explain why opening an AP Lang essay with a broad, generic claim about 'society' or 'history' usually hurts more than it helps.
cards.a: A generic opening delays the actual argument, wastes limited time, and often produces an unfalsifiable statement no one could disagree with, working against a specific, defensible thesis.
cards.h: → wastes time, produces an unfalsifiable claim
cards.n: Since the dawn of time and throughout history are the stock versions, and a reader has seen them hundreds of times by May.

cards.q: Identify the introduction habit: an essay opens by defining a dictionary word from the prompt before making any claim.
cards.a: The dictionary-definition opening - a low-value move that consumes a sentence without advancing an argument, since dictionary definitions rarely illuminate the actual dispute.
cards.n: A prompt's own key term rarely needs 'the dictionary defines X as' - readers already know common words.

cards.q: Contrast a hook that earns its place in an AP Lang introduction and one that only delays the thesis.
cards.a: A hook that earns its place connects directly to the essay's claim, such as a striking detail from the passage or sources. A hook that only delays the thesis is a generic anecdote with no clear link to the argument that follows.
cards.n: If you could delete the opening sentence and lose nothing, delete it.

cards.q: Apply an effective opening move: write a one-sentence introduction opener for an essay arguing that social media has weakened, not strengthened, local news.
cards.a: A strong opener states the stakes directly: as local newspapers close by the hundreds, the platforms that promised to replace them have instead hollowed out the audience that once kept them alive.
cards.n: Notice what the model sentence avoids: no definition of social media, no sweep through history, and the claim is already visible.

cards.q: Explain how an effective AP Lang conclusion differs from a simple restatement of the thesis.
cards.a: An effective conclusion extends the argument's implications, such as its stakes or a broader consequence, rather than repeating the same sentence in different words, which adds nothing a reader has not already read.
cards.n: A quick test is whether the conclusion could be moved to the introduction unchanged; if it could, it has added nothing.

cards.q: Identify the conclusion habit: an essay's final paragraph introduces a brand-new piece of evidence not discussed anywhere in the body.
cards.a: A new-evidence conclusion - introducing unsupported material this late leaves no room to develop it and can read as an afterthought rather than a synthesis of the argument.
cards.h: → new evidence too late to develop
cards.n: Save new evidence for a body paragraph; the conclusion's job is to make the existing case land, not expand it.

cards.q: Contrast a conclusion that broadens the stakes of an argument and one that merely summarizes the body paragraphs.
cards.a: A conclusion that broadens the stakes connects the specific claim to a larger consequence, giving the argument weight beyond the essay itself. A summarizing conclusion just restates each point already made, adding no new value.
cards.n: Broadening the stakes is often where Row C sophistication is earned in a conclusion.

cards.q: Explain the risk of ending an AP Lang essay mid-argument because time ran out.
cards.a: An essay that stops without any concluding move loses the chance to reinforce the line of reasoning, though a reader typically will not penalize length alone if the thesis and evidence rows are already earned.
cards.n: A one-sentence wrap-up beats no conclusion at all, but never at the cost of an undeveloped body paragraph.

cards.q: Explain how topic sentences reveal whether an essay has a genuine line of reasoning.
cards.a: If the topic sentences of every body paragraph, read in sequence with nothing else, form a logical progression that builds toward the thesis, the essay has a line of reasoning; if they read as an unordered list, it does not.
cards.h: → read only the topic sentences in order
cards.n: This is worth doing in the last minute of a timed essay, since one weak topic sentence is far faster to fix than a whole paragraph.

cards.q: Contrast a line of reasoning built on addition and one built on escalation.
cards.a: An additive line of reasoning stacks separate, roughly equal reasons side by side. An escalating line of reasoning orders reasons so each builds on or intensifies the one before it, ending on the strongest point.
cards.n: An escalating structure often reads as more sophisticated, since the order itself becomes part of the argument.

cards.q: Identify the problem: an essay's three body paragraphs each restate the thesis in different words instead of advancing a distinct reason.
cards.a: The paragraphs are redundant rather than progressive - a line of reasoning needs each paragraph to contribute a new, distinct reason, not repeat the same idea with different examples.
cards.n: Padding an essay with lightly reworded restatements is a common trap of five-paragraph autopilot.

cards.q: Explain why a line of reasoning matters more to an AP Lang score than the number of body paragraphs.
cards.a: Row B rewards a coherent line of reasoning across the essay, not a paragraph count; three tightly connected paragraphs that build an argument outscore five that repeat the same point in different words.
cards.n: The five-paragraph habit is the trap here, since a fourth and fifth paragraph added for symmetry usually repeat rather than advance.

cards.q: Define a transitional echo as a coherence device.
cards.a: Restating a key word or idea from the end of one paragraph at the start of the next, so the connection between them is explicit rather than assumed.
cards.n: An echo does what a transition word cannot, showing which idea carries over rather than only signaling that something does.

cards.q: Explain how parallel sentence structure across paragraphs can build coherence in an essay.
cards.a: Repeating a grammatical pattern at each paragraph's opening or closing signals that the paragraphs are doing comparable work in the argument, helping a reader track the essay's structure without extra explanation.
cards.n: This is repetition working structurally rather than stylistically, reinforcing arrangement instead of emphasizing a single line.

cards.q: Identify the coherence problem: an essay uses 'this' five times in one paragraph, each time pointing to a different idea from the sentence before.
cards.a: Vague pronoun reference - 'this' with no clear single antecedent forces a reader to guess which idea it points to each time, breaking the paragraph's coherence.
cards.n: A quick fix is to add a noun right after 'this,' such as 'this pattern' or 'this omission,' so the reference is never ambiguous.

cards.q: Contrast global coherence and local coherence in an essay.
cards.a: Global coherence is whether the essay as a whole builds toward its thesis across paragraphs. Local coherence is whether sentences within a single paragraph connect smoothly to each other.
cards.n: A paragraph can read smoothly sentence to sentence and still fail to advance the essay's larger line of reasoning.

cards.q: Explain the risk of a body paragraph that opens with evidence instead of a topic sentence.
cards.a: Without a topic sentence framing the claim first, a reader must infer the paragraph's point from the evidence alone, which can obscure the argument even when the evidence itself is strong.
cards.n: A reader should never have to reverse-engineer a paragraph's claim from the quotation alone.

cards.q: Identify the problem: a body paragraph presents two unrelated pieces of evidence for two different subclaims without transitioning between them.
cards.a: The paragraph lacks unity - a single paragraph should develop one controlling idea; two subclaims crammed together without a transition should be split into two paragraphs or connected explicitly.
cards.n: Two subclaims in one paragraph usually signals an outline problem rather than a writing problem, so repair it at the planning stage.

cards.q: Explain the evidence-to-commentary ratio a strong AP Lang body paragraph should aim for.
cards.a: Commentary explaining and connecting the evidence should outweigh the evidence itself, often two or three sentences of analysis for every one sentence of quoted or cited material.
cards.n: A paragraph that is mostly quotation with a one-sentence wrap-up rarely earns full Row B credit.

cards.q: Explain the concession-turn-refutation pattern for handling a counterargument in one sentence.
cards.a: State the opposing point honestly, mark a pivot with a word like 'however' or 'yet,' then explain why the writer's position still holds. Skipping the turn leaves the concession unanswered.
cards.n: The turn word is the load-bearing part, and writers who drop it end up sounding as though they agree with the objection.

cards.q: Identify the turn word doing the work in: 'Critics are right that the program is costly. Yet the cost of inaction is far higher.'
cards.a: 'Yet' - it signals the pivot from conceding the critics' point to refuting it by reframing the comparison.
cards.n: Other common turn words include 'however,' 'but,' 'still,' and 'nonetheless.'

cards.q: Explain the risk of devoting too much space to a counterargument in a body paragraph.
cards.a: If the opposing view is developed in more detail and with more vivid evidence than the writer's own refutation, the paragraph can end up making the other side's case more persuasively than the writer's.
cards.n: A counterargument should be stated fairly, but never argued more fully than it is answered.

cards.q: Contrast dismissing a counterargument and substantively refuting one.
cards.a: Dismissing a counterargument rejects it without engaging its logic or evidence, often in a single flat sentence. Substantively refuting it engages the opposing reasoning directly and shows specifically where it falls short.
cards.n: A dismissed counterargument reads as evasive to a reader and rarely earns sophistication credit.

cards.q: Explain how engaging a strong counterargument, rather than a weak one, can earn the Row C sophistication point.
cards.a: Choosing the opposition's best point and still answering it shows the writer has tested the argument against real resistance, which is the kind of complexity readers reward. Refuting an easy, straw-man version does not.
cards.n: Row C is rarely earned by a phrase, so this only counts when the strong objection is answered fully rather than mentioned once.

cards.q: Explain why signaling an essay's organizational pattern early helps a reader follow the argument.
cards.a: Naming the pattern in the introduction or first topic sentence, such as moving from most to least urgent, lets a reader predict how the argument will unfold and notice each new paragraph's role in that plan.
cards.n: This is a small move but a real one for Row C, since it shows deliberate control over structure.

cards.q: Decide the better organizational pattern for an essay arguing a city's transit failures caused a specific 2019 accident: chronological, or order of importance.
cards.a: Chronological - readers need the sequence of failures in the order they occurred to see how one led to the next; order of importance would obscure the causal chain the essay is arguing for.
cards.n: Let the claim choose the pattern: an argument about causation needs sequence, while an argument about severity needs ranking.

cards.q: Explain how a synthesis essay thesis should engage with the range of provided sources without simply agreeing with all of them.
cards.a: A strong synthesis thesis stakes out the writer's own defensible position on the issue, using the sources as evidence for that position, even when the position aligns more with some sources than others.
cards.n: Agreeing with every source produces a summary with no position, and a thesis that no source could contest is not defensible.

cards.q: Identify the weakness: a synthesis essay cites three sources but never explains how any two of them relate to each other.
cards.a: The sources are listed, not synthesized - true synthesis puts sources in conversation with each other and with the writer's claim, not just alongside each other.
cards.n: A simple fix: end the paragraph with one sentence naming exactly how the two sources agree, disagree, or complicate each other.

cards.q: Define a parenthetical citation used for a source identified only by letter in the AP Lang synthesis source set.
cards.a: A citation using the source's assigned letter, such as (Source C), rather than an author's name, since synthesis sources are typically labeled A through F or G on the exam.
cards.n: This is the AP Lang exam's own shorthand, distinct from standard MLA author citation.

cards.q: Explain why citing a source by letter alone, with no attributive tag, is weaker than naming what the source is.
cards.a: '(Source B)' tells a reader nothing about the source's credibility or type, while a tag like 'a 2021 CDC report (Source B) found' lets the reader weigh the evidence while reading, not just after checking a citation.
cards.h: → what each version tells the reader
cards.n: This costs little extra time and directly strengthens the credibility of the evidence being cited.

cards.q: Define style in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: The characteristic way a writer uses language: the combined effect of diction, syntax, imagery, figurative language, and tone that distinguishes one writer's prose from another's.
cards.n: Style is never neutral; every stylistic pattern is evidence of an attitude toward the subject and audience.

cards.q: Define syntax.
cards.a: The arrangement of words, phrases, and clauses within sentences, including sentence length, type, and order of elements.
cards.n: Syntax commentary is the fastest way out of a diction-only essay; describe the pattern, then its effect.

cards.q: Identify what a shift (or pivot) in a passage is and how to spot one.
cards.a: A point where tone, diction, syntax, or perspective changes direction. Markers include but, yet, however, a paragraph break, a change in verb tense or person, or a sudden short sentence after long ones.
cards.n: Shifts are gold on Q2: analyze what changes and why the writer needed the audience moved at that moment.

cards.q: Define anaphora and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the same word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences. e.g. We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields.
cards.n: Effect: builds rhythm and cumulative momentum, drilling the repeated idea into memory and making the claim feel inevitable.

cards.q: Define epistrophe and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the same word or phrase at the end of successive clauses. e.g. government of the people, by the people, for the people.
cards.n: Effect: lands the emphasis on the repeated term, so the audience leaves holding that word rather than the ones around it.

cards.q: Define symploce and give an example.
cards.a: Anaphora and epistrophe combined: successive clauses begin with the same word and end with the same word. e.g. When there is talk of hatred, let us stand against it; when there is talk of violence, let us stand against it.
cards.n: Effect: the fixed frame spotlights the one element that changes, making the varied middle term feel like the true subject.

cards.q: Define anadiplosis and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the last word of one clause at the beginning of the next. e.g. Fear leads to anger; anger leads to hate; hate leads to suffering.
cards.n: Effect: chains the ideas into a causal sequence, so a contestable claim feels like logical dominoes falling.

cards.q: Define epanalepsis and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the same word or phrase at both the beginning and the end of a clause or sentence. e.g. Nothing is worse than doing nothing.
cards.n: Effect: closes the sentence in a circle, creating a sense of inescapability or of returning to an unavoidable fact.

cards.q: Define epizeuxis and give an example.
cards.a: Immediate repetition of a word with no words in between. e.g. Never, never, never give up.
cards.n: Effect: raw intensification that reads as emotion rather than argument, conveying urgency the sentence's content alone would not.

cards.q: Define repetition as a rhetorical strategy and give an example.
cards.a: Deliberate reuse of a word, phrase, or structure for emphasis rather than by accident. e.g. Free at last, free at last, thank God Almighty, we are free at last.
cards.n: Effect: marks what matters, creates rhythm the ear remembers, and unifies a passage around a single idea.

cards.q: Define antithesis and give an example.
cards.a: Contrasting ideas set against each other in parallel grammatical structure. e.g. That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
cards.n: Effect: sharpens a messy issue into two clean opposites and makes the speaker sound balanced and decisive.

cards.q: Define chiasmus and give an example.
cards.a: A reversal of grammatical structure in two successive phrases, in an ABBA pattern, without necessarily repeating the same words. e.g. By day the frolic, and the dance by night.
cards.n: Effect: the mirrored shape feels designed and inevitable, lending an ordinary observation the weight of a maxim.

cards.q: Define antimetabole and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the same words in reverse grammatical order. e.g. Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country.
cards.n: Effect: the reversal makes the idea feel discovered rather than asserted, and its symmetry makes it endlessly quotable.

cards.q: Contrast chiasmus and antimetabole.
cards.a: Both invert structure in an ABBA pattern, but antimetabole repeats the identical words in reverse order, while chiasmus reverses only the grammatical structure. Every antimetabole is a chiasmus; not every chiasmus is an antimetabole.
cards.n: If the same words come back flipped, name it antimetabole; if only the shape flips, chiasmus is safer.

cards.q: Define parallelism and give an example.
cards.a: Using the same grammatical form for elements of equal importance. e.g. reading widely, writing daily, and thinking carefully.
cards.n: Effect: signals that the items carry equal weight and makes complex material easy to follow, which reads as control and authority.

cards.q: Define isocolon and give an example.
cards.a: Parallel elements that are also equal in length and rhythm. e.g. Buy it, use it, break it, fix it.
cards.n: Effect: the metrical evenness makes a line sound engineered and sloganlike, easy to chant and hard to forget.

cards.q: Define tricolon and give an example.
cards.a: A series of three parallel words, phrases, or clauses. e.g. life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
cards.n: Effect: three feels complete to the ear; when the third element is longest (ascending tricolon), the series builds to a climax.

cards.q: Define zeugma and give an example.
cards.a: A construction in which one word, usually a verb, governs two or more others, often in different senses. e.g. She stole his wallet and his heart.
cards.n: Effect: compresses the literal and figurative into one stroke, producing wit or an ironic equation of unlike things.

cards.q: Define asyndeton and give an example.
cards.a: Deliberate omission of conjunctions between coordinated words, phrases, or clauses. e.g. I came, I saw, I conquered.
cards.n: Effect: accelerates the pace and makes a list feel breathless or open-ended, as if it could continue indefinitely.

cards.q: Define polysyndeton and give an example.
cards.a: Deliberate repetition of conjunctions between every item in a series. e.g. and the rain and the wind and the cold and the dark.
cards.n: Effect: slows the pace and piles items up so the accumulation feels overwhelming, exhausting, or relentless.

cards.q: Contrast the effects of asyndeton and polysyndeton.
cards.a: Asyndeton removes conjunctions to speed the sentence and suggest an incomplete, urgent list; polysyndeton adds conjunctions to slow the sentence and make the list feel heavy and unending. Both alter pace, in opposite directions.
cards.n: Both are about pacing; if you can say faster or slower and why that matters here, you have real commentary.

cards.q: Define ellipsis as a syntactic device and give an example.
cards.a: Omission of words the reader can supply from context. e.g. Some students go to the library; others, to the gym.
cards.n: Effect: tightens and quickens the prose and flatters readers by trusting them to fill the gap.

cards.q: Define metaphor and give an example.
cards.a: A direct comparison asserting that one thing is another, without like or as. e.g. Time is a thief.
cards.n: Effect: transfers the connotations of the comparison onto the subject, quietly framing how the audience should judge it.

cards.q: Define simile and give an example.
cards.a: A comparison of two unlike things using like or as. e.g. The room went as quiet as a chapel.
cards.n: Effect: makes the unfamiliar concrete while keeping the comparison explicit and limited, so the writer controls how far it extends.

cards.q: Define analogy and give an example.
cards.a: An extended comparison that maps the relationship in a familiar case onto an unfamiliar one in order to explain or argue. e.g. Running a national budget is like running a household budget.
cards.n: Effect: makes complex reasoning accessible, but it is only as strong as the mapping; a broken mapping is a false analogy.

cards.q: Define extended metaphor and give an example.
cards.a: A single metaphor sustained across several sentences or an entire passage, with its details developed. e.g. describing a political campaign as a voyage, then continuing with charts, storms, mutiny, and landfall.
cards.n: Effect: supplies a controlling frame the reader keeps interpreting through, so the comparison shapes an entire argument, not one line.

cards.q: Define conceit and give an example.
cards.a: An elaborate, surprising extended metaphor linking two strikingly unlike things. e.g. Donne comparing two lovers to the twin legs of a drawing compass.
cards.n: Effect: displays ingenuity and forces the reader to grant an unexpected likeness, making the writer's cleverness part of the appeal.

cards.q: Define metonymy and give an example.
cards.a: Substituting the name of something closely associated with a thing for the thing itself. e.g. The White House announced new sanctions; the crown demanded taxes.
cards.n: Effect: compresses an institution into a single image and can deflect responsibility from the actual people acting.

cards.q: Define synecdoche and give an example.
cards.a: A figure in which a part stands for the whole or a whole stands for a part. e.g. All hands on deck; boots on the ground.
cards.n: Effect: focuses attention on the relevant part, which can heroize (hands as labor) or dehumanize (boots as soldiers).

cards.q: Contrast metonymy and synecdoche.
cards.a: Synecdoche substitutes a part of the thing for the whole (hands for sailors); metonymy substitutes something associated with but not part of the thing (the crown for the monarchy). Synecdoche is a subset of substitution by part.
cards.n: If the substituted word names a physical piece of the thing, call it synecdoche; if it is merely linked to it, metonymy.

cards.q: Define hyperbole and give an example.
cards.a: Deliberate exaggeration for effect, not intended to be taken literally. e.g. I have explained this a million times.
cards.n: Effect: signals the intensity of the speaker's feeling and can generate humor or expose an opponent's position as absurd.

cards.q: Define understatement and give an example.
cards.a: Presenting something as smaller or less significant than it actually is. e.g. calling a category five hurricane a bit of weather.
cards.n: Effect: the gap between event and description does the work, conveying composure, dark humor, or contempt.

cards.q: Define litotes and give an example.
cards.a: A form of understatement that affirms something by negating its opposite. e.g. She is no fool; the results were not bad.
cards.n: Effect: makes praise or criticism sound measured and restrained, which reads as confidence rather than enthusiasm.

cards.q: Define verbal irony and give an example.
cards.a: Saying the opposite of what is meant, with the gap available to the audience. e.g. remarking What lovely weather during a downpour.
cards.n: Effect: creates complicity with the audience who catch the gap, forming an in-group that shares the speaker's judgment.

cards.q: Define situational irony and give an example.
cards.a: A discrepancy between what is expected to happen and what actually happens. e.g. a fire station burning down.
cards.n: Effect: exposes the distance between human plans and outcomes, which writers use to critique confidence or systems.

cards.q: Define dramatic irony and give an example.
cards.a: A situation in which the audience knows something a character does not. e.g. Oedipus vowing to punish the murderer the audience knows is himself.
cards.n: Effect: builds tension and places the audience in a superior position, inviting judgment of the unknowing figure.

cards.q: Define sarcasm and give an example.
cards.a: Sharp, mocking verbal irony aimed at a target, usually marked by tone of voice. e.g. saying Nice work after someone drops the tray.
cards.n: Effect: wounds or belittles the target and can alienate audiences who identify with it, unlike gentler verbal irony.

cards.q: Define satire and give an example.
cards.a: A mode that uses irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose vice, folly, or abuse, implying that reform is needed. e.g. Swift's A Modest Proposal.
cards.n: Effect: turns laughter into leverage, shaming an audience toward change while letting the writer avoid direct accusation.

cards.q: Define Horatian satire and give an example.
cards.a: Gentle, playful, amused satire that laughs with human folly rather than condemning it. e.g. a light send-up of parents obsessed with youth sports.
cards.n: Effect: keeps the audience comfortable enough to recognize themselves in the target instead of getting defensive.

cards.q: Define Juvenalian satire and give an example.
cards.a: Bitter, indignant, moralizing satire that treats its target with contempt. e.g. Swift's proposal that the poor sell their children as food.
cards.n: Effect: provokes outrage rather than laughter, positioning the target as a moral offense demanding response.

cards.q: Contrast Horatian and Juvenalian satire.
cards.a: Horatian satire is light, witty, and tolerant, treating folly as laughable and human; Juvenalian satire is harsh, bitter, and moralizing, treating vice as intolerable. The difference is tone and the severity of the implied indictment.
cards.n: Naming which kind of satire, and why the writer needed that severity for that audience, is a strong sophistication move.

cards.q: Define paradox and give an example.
cards.a: A statement that appears self-contradictory yet reveals a truth on reflection. e.g. The more you learn, the more you realize how little you know.
cards.n: Effect: stalls the reader into rethinking, so the insight feels earned rather than handed over.

cards.q: Define oxymoron and give an example.
cards.a: Two contradictory terms placed side by side in a single phrase. e.g. deafening silence, bittersweet, cruel kindness.
cards.n: Effect: compresses tension into two words, signaling that the subject resists a simple label.

cards.q: Contrast paradox and oxymoron.
cards.a: An oxymoron is a compressed contradiction within a phrase (jumbo shrimp); a paradox is a full statement or situation that seems contradictory but proves meaningful. Scale is the difference: phrase versus proposition.
cards.n: Students label every paradox an oxymoron. If it is a whole idea rather than a two-word pair, call it paradox.

cards.q: Define allusion and give an example.
cards.a: A brief, indirect reference to a well-known person, text, event, or work, left unexplained. e.g. calling a costly victory his Waterloo.
cards.n: Effect: borrows the authority and emotion of a shared reference and quietly tests whether the audience belongs to that shared culture.

cards.q: Define apostrophe as a rhetorical device and give an example.
cards.a: Direct address to an absent person, an abstraction, or an inanimate thing. e.g. O Death, where is thy sting?
cards.n: Effect: raises the emotional pitch and dramatizes the speaker's relationship to the idea, making the audience witnesses to it.

cards.q: Define personification and give an example.
cards.a: Attributing human qualities or actions to an animal, object, or abstraction. e.g. The wind whispered through the pines; justice demands an answer.
cards.n: Effect: makes abstractions feel like agents with intentions, so the audience responds to an idea as it would to a person.

cards.q: Define imagery and give an example.
cards.a: Language that appeals to the senses (sight, sound, touch, taste, smell) to create a vivid experience. e.g. the sharp tang of diesel over wet asphalt.
cards.n: Effect: makes the audience experience a claim rather than merely accept it, which produces pathos without explicit emotional appeal.

cards.q: Define symbolism and give an example.
cards.a: The use of a concrete object, action, or image to represent an abstract idea. e.g. a flag standing for national identity and sacrifice.
cards.n: Effect: lets a writer argue about an abstraction through something the audience can see, feel, and already values.

cards.q: Define juxtaposition and give an example.
cards.a: Placing two contrasting elements side by side so the comparison is unavoidable. e.g. describing a gleaming new stadium and then the shuttered school across the street.
cards.n: Effect: the reader draws the comparison unaided, so the judgment feels self-generated rather than imposed by the writer.

cards.q: Define rhetorical question and give an example.
cards.a: A question asked for effect rather than to obtain an answer, because the answer is assumed. e.g. Are we to stand by and do nothing?
cards.n: Effect: recruits the audience into supplying the answer, so agreement feels like their own conclusion.

cards.q: Define hypophora and give an example.
cards.a: A device in which the writer raises a question and then immediately answers it. e.g. What must we do now? We must vote, and we must not stop there.
cards.n: Effect: seizes control of the agenda by anticipating the audience's question and casting the speaker as the one with answers.

cards.q: Define aporia and give an example.
cards.a: An expression of real or feigned doubt or uncertainty about how to proceed. e.g. I scarcely know where to begin, or what words could possibly be adequate.
cards.n: Effect: signals humility and sincerity, disarming a skeptical audience before the speaker makes a confident claim.

cards.q: Define alliteration and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of initial consonant sounds in nearby words. e.g. a wild and windy winter west.
cards.n: Effect: binds words into a unit the ear treats as one idea, making the phrase memorable and quotable.

cards.q: Define assonance and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words. e.g. the light of the fire is a sight.
cards.n: Effect: creates internal music that slows the line and knits its words together without the emphasis of rhyme.

cards.q: Define consonance and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of consonant sounds within or at the end of nearby words. e.g. the lumpy, bumpy road; pitter patter.
cards.n: Effect: adds subtle cohesion and can make a passage feel harsh or soft depending on which consonants recur.

cards.q: Define onomatopoeia and give an example.
cards.a: A word that imitates the sound it names. e.g. buzz, clang, hiss, thud.
cards.n: Effect: collapses distance by putting the reader inside the scene, hearing rather than being told.

cards.q: Define cacophony and give an example.
cards.a: A deliberately harsh, discordant arrangement of sounds. e.g. the cracked jackhammer clattered and scraped.
cards.n: Effect: makes the subject feel unpleasant or violent, so the sound of the prose delivers a verdict the words never state.

cards.q: Define euphony and give an example.
cards.a: A pleasing, harmonious arrangement of sounds, typically using soft consonants and long vowels. e.g. the low lull of the summer meadow.
cards.n: Effect: makes the subject feel calm or beautiful, aligning the reader's ear with the writer's approval.

cards.q: Define periodic sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence in which the main clause is withheld until the end, after introductory modifiers. e.g. Despite the rain, the delays, and the cold that cut through every coat, we marched.
cards.n: Effect: creates suspense by making the reader hold the modifiers until the payoff, which lands the main idea with force.

cards.q: Define loose (cumulative) sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence that states its main clause first and then adds modifying phrases. e.g. We marched, soaked to the skin, exhausted, still singing.
cards.n: Effect: feels natural and conversational, giving immediate clarity and then enriching it detail by detail.

cards.q: Contrast periodic and loose sentences by effect.
cards.a: The periodic sentence delays the main clause to build suspense and emphasize the ending; the loose or cumulative sentence delivers the main clause first and accumulates detail after, sounding relaxed and immediate.
cards.n: Naming which one a writer chose, and what the delay or the immediacy does to a reader, is textbook Row B commentary.

cards.q: Define balanced sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence whose two halves are equal in grammatical structure and length, usually joined by a semicolon or conjunction. e.g. To err is human; to forgive, divine.
cards.n: Effect: equality of form implies equality of the ideas, giving the statement an authoritative, proverbial ring.

cards.q: Define simple sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence containing one independent clause and no dependent clause. e.g. The bill failed.
cards.n: Effect: after a run of long sentences, a short simple sentence lands like a verdict, which is why writers save them for the turn.

cards.q: Define compound sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence with two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or a semicolon. e.g. The bill failed, but the movement grew.
cards.n: Effect: grants the two ideas equal grammatical weight, presenting them as parallel realities rather than ranking them.

cards.q: Define complex sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence with one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. e.g. Although the bill failed, the movement grew.
cards.n: Effect: subordination ranks the ideas; whatever sits in the independent clause is what the writer wants the reader to carry away.

cards.q: Define compound-complex sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence with two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. e.g. Although the bill failed, the movement grew, and new donors appeared.
cards.n: Effect: holds layered causation in a single breath, useful when a writer wants complexity to feel manageable.

cards.q: Define independent clause and give an example.
cards.a: A group of words with a subject and a verb that expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence. e.g. the jury returned a verdict.
cards.n: Effect: what a writer places in independent clauses is what the sentence asserts; everything else is framing.

cards.q: Define dependent (subordinate) clause and give an example.
cards.a: A clause with a subject and verb that cannot stand alone because it begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. e.g. although the jury deliberated for six days.
cards.n: Effect: material placed in dependent clauses is demoted to background, a quiet way to concede a point without conceding emphasis.

cards.q: Define appositive and give an example.
cards.a: A noun or noun phrase placed beside another noun to rename or identify it. e.g. Marie Curie, a two-time Nobel laureate, refused to patent her method.
cards.n: Effect: smuggles credentials or evidence into a sentence without a new claim, which is quiet, efficient ethos building.

cards.q: Define absolute phrase and give an example.
cards.a: A phrase consisting of a noun plus a participle (with modifiers) that modifies an entire sentence rather than one word. e.g. Her hands trembling, she signed the paper.
cards.n: Effect: layers a cinematic detail onto the main action without subordinating it, so image and event arrive together.

cards.q: Define participial phrase and give an example.
cards.a: A phrase beginning with a present or past participle that functions as an adjective. e.g. Shouting over the crowd, she finished her sentence.
cards.n: Effect: packs action into modifiers so sentences stay dense and forward-moving instead of stopping for a second clause.

cards.q: Define subordination and give an example.
cards.a: Placing one idea in a dependent clause so that it supports rather than competes with the main clause. e.g. Because the data were incomplete, the panel withheld judgment.
cards.n: Effect: creates a hierarchy of importance, telling the reader which idea is the point and which is merely a condition.

cards.q: Define coordination and give an example.
cards.a: Joining grammatically equal elements with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). e.g. The panel withheld judgment, and the report was delayed.
cards.n: Effect: presents ideas as equals, which can suggest accumulation or refuse to rank causes the writer does not want ranked.

cards.q: Contrast subordination and coordination as rhetorical choices.
cards.a: Coordination gives ideas equal weight and lets them accumulate; subordination ranks them, pushing one into the background as cause, condition, or concession. The choice reveals what the writer treats as the main point.
cards.n: Look for although and while clauses: a writer often buries the opposing view there and keeps the main clause for the claim.

cards.q: Explain the rhetorical effect of sentence variety.
cards.a: Varying sentence length and structure prevents monotony and creates emphasis by contrast: a short sentence among long ones stops the reader, and a long accumulating sentence after short ones can feel like mounting evidence or exhaustion.
cards.n: Never say the writer uses varied syntax and stop. Point to the specific contrast and what it makes the reader feel at that moment.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the colon and give an example.
cards.a: A colon follows an independent clause to introduce a list, explanation, appositive, or quotation. e.g. The problem was simple: nobody had read the bill.
cards.n: Effect: it makes a promise and then delivers, so whatever follows the colon receives the spotlight.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the semicolon and give an example.
cards.a: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction, or separates items in a complex list. e.g. The vote failed; the coalition held anyway.
cards.n: Effect: asserts a tight logical relationship without naming it, forcing the reader to infer the connection.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the dash and give an example.
cards.a: A dash sets off an interruption, an appositive, or an emphatic addition. e.g. The committee agreed on one thing — and only one — that time had run out.
cards.n: Effect: creates the feel of speech breaking in, giving the set-off material sudden emphasis or the intimacy of an aside.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of parentheses and give an example.
cards.a: Parentheses enclose supplementary material that is not part of the main structure. e.g. The measure passed (barely) on the third vote.
cards.n: Effect: lowers the volume, marking the material as an aside, a qualification, or a wry comment the writer will not elevate.

cards.q: Define anastrophe (syntactic inversion) and give an example.
cards.a: Reversal of normal word order for emphasis or effect. e.g. Powerful you have become; into the valley of death rode the six hundred.
cards.n: Effect: throws stress onto the fronted element and lends the voice an elevated, formal, or archaic quality.

cards.q: Define active voice and give an example.
cards.a: A construction in which the grammatical subject performs the action. e.g. The board rejected the proposal.
cards.n: Effect: assigns responsibility plainly and keeps prose direct, which reads as confidence and accountability.

cards.q: Define passive voice and give an example.
cards.a: A construction in which the subject receives the action; the actor appears in a by phrase or is omitted entirely. e.g. The proposal was rejected (by the board).
cards.n: Effect: shifts emphasis to the thing acted upon and can erase the actor, which is why bureaucratic prose favors it.

cards.q: Explain when passive voice is a deliberate rhetorical choice rather than a flaw.
cards.a: When the actor is unknown, obvious, or irrelevant; when the receiver of the action deserves emphasis; when the writer wants to maintain a neutral, institutional tone; or when the writer intends to obscure responsibility, as in mistakes were made.
cards.n: Do not call passive voice weak writing on the exam. Ask who disappears from the sentence and who benefits from that disappearance.

cards.q: Define polysemy and give an example.
cards.a: The capacity of a single word to carry multiple related meanings. e.g. right, meaning correct, a direction, and an entitlement.
cards.n: Effect: lets a writer play meanings against one another so a single word does double argumentative duty.

cards.q: Define pun and give an example.
cards.a: A play on words exploiting multiple meanings or similar sounds. e.g. A bicycle cannot stand on its own because it is two tired.
cards.n: Effect: humor lowers the audience's guard, and the display of wit builds the speaker's ethos as clever and quick.

cards.q: Define invective and give an example.
cards.a: Harsh, abusive denunciation of a person or thing, often in an extended verbal attack. e.g. Shakespeare's strings of insults such as you whoreson, beetle-headed knave.
cards.n: Effect: vents and incites indignation, rallying those who already agree while risking the appearance of unfairness to everyone else.

cards.q: Define colloquialism and give an example.
cards.a: An informal word or expression drawn from everyday speech, used in writing. e.g. gonna, no big deal, y'all.
cards.n: Effect: closes distance with the audience and signals authenticity or membership in a shared community.

cards.q: Define aphorism and give an example.
cards.a: A concise statement of a general truth or principle. e.g. A penny saved is a penny earned.
cards.n: Effect: sounds like inherited wisdom, so a contestable claim can slip past scrutiny as common sense.

cards.q: Define epigram and give an example.
cards.a: A brief, witty, often paradoxical saying. e.g. Wilde's I can resist everything except temptation.
cards.n: Effect: wit purchases credibility, and the memorable phrasing carries the argument further than the evidence alone would.

cards.q: Contrast aphorism and epigram.
cards.a: An aphorism states a general truth and aims at wisdom; an epigram aims at wit, usually with a paradoxical or surprising turn. Aphorisms instruct; epigrams delight, and often instruct by surprising.
cards.n: Wilde is the reference point for epigrams and Franklin for aphorisms, which is a quick way to keep the two terms apart.

cards.q: Define anecdote and give an example.
cards.a: A short account of a single incident, often personal, used to illustrate a point. e.g. opening an essay on health care with one patient's night in a waiting room.
cards.n: Effect: converts an abstract claim into a human case, producing pathos and the feel of evidence from a single instance.

cards.q: Define exemplum and give an example.
cards.a: A brief illustrative story or case cited to support a general claim or moral. e.g. citing Cincinnatus returning to his farm as proof that power can be surrendered.
cards.n: Effect: makes a general principle concrete and demonstrable, the classical form of arguing from example.

cards.q: Define apophasis and give an example.
cards.a: Bringing up a subject by claiming to pass over it, so the audience registers the point while the speaker denies making it. e.g. I won't mention his three arrests, since that has nothing to do with tonight's vote.
cards.n: Effect: delivers the accusation while preserving deniability, so the speaker seems fair while still landing the blow.

cards.q: Define procatalepsis and give an example.
cards.a: Anticipating an opponent's objection and answering it before the opponent can raise it. e.g. Some will say this plan costs too much - but doing nothing will cost far more within a decade.
cards.n: Effect: seizes control of the argument's agenda and makes the speaker look prepared rather than defensive.

cards.q: Contrast procatalepsis and hypophora.
cards.a: Procatalepsis raises and answers an opponent's objection to defuse it in advance; hypophora raises the writer's own question and answers it to structure an argument. One preempts a challenge, the other organizes an explanation.
cards.n: Both arrive as a question, so decide by whose question it is: an opponent's objection raised early, or the writer's own setup.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The senator lost her temper and, moments later, the vote.'
cards.a: Zeugma. The single verb lost governs two different objects, temper and the vote, in two different senses at once.
cards.n: The pleasure comes from the sudden slide between literal and figurative senses, which is also what makes zeugma read as wry.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'We will rebuild after the flood. We will rebuild after the fire. We will rebuild after every disaster.'
cards.a: Anaphora. The phrase We will rebuild repeats at the start of each successive clause, building momentum toward the final claim.
cards.n: Anaphora is the easiest device to spot and the easiest to under-analyze, so commentary has to name what the repetition builds toward.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'This is a plan built by workers, tested by workers, and paid for by workers.'
cards.a: Epistrophe. The phrase by workers repeats at the end of each successive clause, so the audience leaves the sentence holding that phrase.
cards.n: Epistrophe emphasizes what the clauses have in common, while anaphora emphasizes what changes after the repeated opening.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The company promised safety for its workers and profit for its owners; it delivered profit for its owners and injury for its workers.'
cards.a: Chiasmus. The grammatical structure of the first clause reverses in the second (ABBA), though the words are not all repeated.
cards.n: Chiasmus reverses the structure while antimetabole reverses the actual words, so check whether the same words came back.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The company did not choose its workers; the workers chose the company.'
cards.a: Antimetabole. The same words (company, workers, choose) repeat in reversed grammatical order, making the reversal itself the point.
cards.n: Antimetabole is a subtype of chiasmus, so calling this chiasmus is never wrong, only less precise than it could be.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The council voted, the funding passed, the project began.'
cards.a: Asyndeton. The conjunctions between the three clauses are omitted, giving the sequence a rapid, almost breathless pace.
cards.n: Asyndeton also implies the list could keep going, since nothing marks a final item the way a closing and would.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'And the delays and the excuses and the broken promises finally caught up with the campaign.'
cards.a: Polysyndeton. The conjunction and repeats before every item, slowing the sentence and making the accumulation feel heavy and relentless.
cards.n: Asyndeton and polysyndeton are opposites in form but share an effect of accumulation: one speeds it up, the other makes it weigh.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The proposal is not without its problems.'
cards.a: Litotes. The claim is affirmed by negating its opposite (not without problems), which softens the criticism into understatement.
cards.n: Litotes is a specific kind of understatement built from a double negative, so use the narrower term whenever the negation is there.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The plan requires patience. Patience is what the board has never had.'
cards.a: Anadiplosis. The last word of the first sentence, patience, becomes the first substantive word of the next, chaining the two ideas together.
cards.n: Chained through several clauses this becomes gradatio, a build that can walk a reader step by step into the writer's conclusion.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'I hardly know how to answer such an accusation - where would a person even begin?'
cards.a: Aporia. The speaker expresses genuine or feigned uncertainty about how to respond, which can disarm the audience before a confident reply follows.
cards.n: Feigned aporia is the usual version, and it buys ethos by making a fully prepared answer look reluctant and hard won.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'What do we owe the next generation? We owe them a planet no worse than the one we inherited.'
cards.a: Hypophora. The writer poses a question and then immediately supplies the answer, controlling the direction of the argument.
cards.n: Hypophora also structures a paragraph, since the question can act as a topic sentence that the rest of the paragraph answers.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The old factory brought jobs to this town; the new one brought only debt.'
cards.a: Antithesis. Two contrasting ideas, jobs and debt, are set against each other in parallel grammatical structure to sharpen the comparison.
cards.n: Antithesis needs both the opposition and the parallel frame; contrasting ideas in mismatched structures is only contrast.

cards.q: Identify the device: a report describes the CEO's newly renovated yacht in one paragraph and the factory's broken safety gear in the next.
cards.a: Juxtaposition. Placing the two contrasting images side by side, without commentary, lets the reader draw the unflattering comparison unaided.
cards.n: This is an arrangement choice rather than a word choice, so the commentary has to point at the order of the paragraphs, not the diction.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'Every reform since has been measured against that summer, the district's own Waterloo.'
cards.a: Allusion. The brief, unexplained reference to Waterloo borrows the shared cultural meaning of a final, crushing defeat without spelling it out.
cards.n: An allusion is a bet on shared knowledge, so it also reveals what the writer assumes the audience has read or remembers.

cards.q: Identify the device: after a factory explosion injures dozens, an executive calls it 'a bit of an inconvenience for the schedule.'
cards.a: Understatement. Describing a serious, injury-causing event as a minor inconvenience deliberately minimizes it; the gap reads as callous or evasive.
cards.n: Understatement works only when the audience already knows the real scale, and the gap between the two does all the rhetorical work.

cards.q: Identify the sentence type: 'After the vote failed, after the funding dried up, after the last volunteer quit, the clinic finally closed.'
cards.a: Periodic sentence. The main clause, the clinic finally closed, is withheld until the end, after introductory clauses build suspense toward it.
cards.n: Periodic sentences are rare, so finding one in a passage is nearly always a signal that the withheld clause carries the weight.

cards.q: Identify the sentence type: 'The clinic closed, its doors locked, its equipment sold, its patients scattered to clinics an hour away.'
cards.a: Loose (cumulative) sentence. The main clause, the clinic closed, comes first, and modifying details pile on afterward to enrich it.
cards.n: Most English sentences are loose by default, which is why a periodic one stands out whenever a writer finally builds to a delay.

cards.q: Identify the voice and its likely rhetorical purpose: 'Mistakes were made in the handling of the funds.'
cards.a: Passive voice. The sentence omits who made the mistakes, letting the writer avoid naming or blaming a specific actor - a common evasive use of passive construction.
cards.n: Contrast with active: The treasurer misused the funds names the actor directly.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'How much longer can this city pretend the water is safe to drink?'
cards.a: Rhetorical question. It is posed not to gather an answer but to imply one, drawing the audience into agreeing without stating the claim outright.
cards.n: A rhetorical question is answered by silence while hypophora answers itself aloud, and that difference is what MC items test.

cards.q: Contrast metaphor and simile.
cards.a: A simile compares two unlike things explicitly using like or as; a metaphor asserts that one thing is the other with no comparing word. Metaphor states the equation outright, while simile keeps it at arm's length.
cards.n: Simile is easier to defend as illustrative; metaphor commits harder and so carries more persuasive risk and force.

cards.q: Contrast euphony and cacophony.
cards.a: Euphony arranges sounds to be pleasing and harmonious, typically soft consonants and long vowels; cacophony arranges sounds to be harsh and discordant, typically hard consonants in clusters. The sound signals the writer's judgment.
cards.n: Read the line aloud to test it, and remember the effect only counts as analysis once it is tied to what the passage argues.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'The senator, a decorated veteran, refused to discuss the vote.'
cards.a: An appositive: 'a decorated veteran' renames senator, adding a credential in a compact aside rather than a full clause.
cards.n: Appositives let a writer smuggle in characterization or credibility without slowing the sentence with a new clause.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'The crowd fell silent, its collective breath held, as the verdict was read.'
cards.a: An absolute phrase: 'its collective breath held' modifies the whole main clause rather than a single noun, adding a vivid simultaneous detail.
cards.h: → noun + participle modifying the whole clause
cards.n: Absolute phrases modify the whole clause, not a single word, which is why they resist being folded into a simple adjective.

cards.q: Explain why a writer would set an appositive off with dashes instead of commas.
cards.a: Dashes make the appositive feel like an interruption or emphasis, drawing the reader's eye, while commas fold it in more quietly as background information.
cards.n: The grammar is identical either way; the punctuation choice is entirely about how much attention the aside should get.

cards.q: Explain the rhetorical effect of stacking two absolute phrases in one sentence.
cards.a: Stacked absolute phrases let a writer layer several simultaneous images or conditions onto one main action, creating a cinematic, slow-motion effect.
cards.n: Overusing this move across many sentences can feel overwritten, so save it for a single high-impact moment.

cards.q: Apply subordination to this pair to emphasize the job loss: 'The town lost its factory. Three hundred jobs disappeared overnight.'
cards.a: Subordinate the first idea: 'When the town lost its factory, three hundred jobs disappeared overnight,' putting the emphasis in the independent clause on the jobs.
cards.n: Whatever sits in the independent clause reads as the sentence's main point; the subordinate clause supplies background.

cards.q: Apply coordination to this pair to give both ideas equal weight: 'The mayor cut the ribbon. Protesters lined the sidewalk.'
cards.a: Coordinate them with a conjunction: 'The mayor cut the ribbon, and protesters lined the sidewalk,' which keeps both images equally prominent instead of subordinating either.
cards.n: Coordination claims the two events belong together, so the conjunction does argumentative work: and joins them, but sets them against each other.

cards.q: Contrast the rhetorical effect of a semicolon, a colon, and a dash used at the same junction in a sentence.
cards.a: A semicolon balances two equal, related ideas; a colon announces that an explanation or list is about to deliver on a promise; a dash breaks in for emphasis or an abrupt aside.
cards.n: Three punctuation marks can often connect the same two ideas, but each frames the reader's expectation differently.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The board had one option left: resign.'
cards.a: The colon sets up the single word 'resign' as a blunt, delayed payoff, giving it more weight than a comma would.
cards.n: A colon promises that what follows will deliver on what came before; here the promise is a one-word gut punch.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The vote was close; the consequences were not.'
cards.a: The semicolon signals that the two clauses are tightly related and worth weighing against each other, without subordinating either one.
cards.n: The compression is the point: a period would let the reader lose hold of the first clause before the second lands on it.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The plan was approved - barely - after three hours of debate.'
cards.a: The dashes interrupt the sentence to insert 'barely' as a pointed aside, forcing the reader to notice how narrow the approval was.
cards.n: Dashes read as more informal and abrupt than parentheses, which cushion an aside more gently.

cards.q: Contrast anaphora and epistrophe by where the repeated words fall.
cards.a: Anaphora repeats words at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences, while epistrophe repeats them at the end; anaphora drives forward and epistrophe hammers a close.
cards.n: Some passages use both at once, repeating a word at a clause's start and again at its end, so trace the repetition physically through the sentence.
x: repetition at the start vs. the end

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: 'we can not dedicate, we can not consecrate, we can not hallow this ground.'
cards.a: Anaphora; repeating 'we can not' at the start of each clause builds toward the admission that words cannot match the soldiers' sacrifice.
cards.n: Lincoln uses the anaphora to deflate the ceremony itself before redirecting attention to the unfinished work of the living.

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Kennedy's inaugural: 'we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship.'
cards.a: Parallelism — a tricolon of three matched verb-plus-object phrases with 'any' in the same slot each time. It is NOT anaphora: the clauses begin with pay, bear and meet, and anaphora needs the repeated word at the start of each clause.
cards.h: → name the scheme, and say why it is not anaphora
cards.n: A standing trap: repetition in the same position inside each clause is still not anaphora unless that position is the beginning.

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: 'government of the people, by the people, for the people.'
cards.a: A tricolon on parallel prepositional phrases, with 'the people' repeated at the end of each - closer to epistrophe than anaphora since the repetition lands at the close.
cards.n: This line is often mislabeled as anaphora; the repeated words fall at the end of each phrase, not the start.

cards.q: Identify the device in Kennedy's inaugural: 'Ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.'
cards.a: Antithesis and antimetabole - antimetabole being the chiasmus in which the identical words come back reversed: country/you, then you/country, sharpening the contrast between receiving and giving.
cards.n: Naming antimetabole rather than the broader chiasmus shows a reader you can see the exact structure, not just the contrast.

cards.q: Contrast the two devices at work in Kennedy's line 'ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.'
cards.a: It is antithesis because it opposes two contrasting ideas, and chiasmus because the second clause reverses the grammatical order of the first.
cards.n: A single line can carry more than one device at once; identify both the contrast and the mirrored structure.

cards.q: Identify the technique Swift leans on in A Modest Proposal by having an economist calmly recommend eating Irish infants.
cards.a: A sustained ironic persona whose deadpan logic exposes the real cruelty of English policy toward the Irish poor, rather than stating the criticism directly.
cards.n: The persona is the whole device, so quoting the narrator's cold arithmetic proves the irony better than quoting the shocking proposal.

cards.q: Identify the satire type in A Modest Proposal.
cards.a: Juvenalian satire; Swift's proposal is bitter and biting, using shocking irony to condemn real suffering rather than to gently amuse.
cards.n: Because the target is real, ongoing suffering rather than a mild social habit, calling this Horatian would badly undersell the essay's anger.

cards.q: Explain why A Modest Proposal's title is itself ironic.
cards.a: Calling a proposal to eat infants 'modest' signals from the first word that the speaker's calm reasonableness cannot be trusted, priming readers to look past the surface argument.
cards.n: Verbal irony operates here at the level of one adjective, which makes the title the cheapest quotable evidence in the whole essay.

cards.q: Define parody and give an example.
cards.a: A work that imitates another text's style or conventions closely enough to be recognized, exaggerating it for comic or critical effect.
cards.n: Parody depends on the audience recognizing the original; without that recognition the joke does not land.

cards.q: Define lampoon and give an example.
cards.a: A short, sharply mocking piece aimed at a specific person or institution, using ridicule rather than balanced argument to attack its target.
cards.n: Lampoon names the attack while satire names the mode, so a lampoon is satire aimed at one target with the gloves off.
x: a piece that ridicules a specific target

cards.q: Define caricature and give an example.
cards.a: A description or portrayal that exaggerates a subject's distinctive features or traits to make them ridiculous, often reducing a person to one exaggerated trait.
cards.n: Caricature works because the exaggerated trait is still recognizably drawn from something real about the subject.
x: exaggerated portrayal of a real subject

cards.q: Contrast parody and lampoon by what each one imitates.
cards.a: Parody imitates a text's style or form to mock it, while lampoon attacks a specific person or institution directly without needing to imitate anything.
cards.h: → imitates a form vs. attacks a target
cards.n: A single piece can do both at once: parody a genre while also lampooning a specific person writing within it.

cards.q: Contrast caricature and stereotype as satirical tools.
cards.a: Caricature exaggerates a specific, real subject's own traits for comic effect, while a stereotype flattens an entire group into a generic, assumed set of traits.
cards.n: Caricature is a deliberate technique writers can be praised for; calling writing stereotyped is usually a criticism, not a technique.

cards.q: Decide which satirical tool fits: a cartoon exaggerates a senator's already-large ears and nose to mock his vote.
cards.a: Caricature; the humor comes from exaggerating the senator's own physical features rather than imitating a text or attacking an institution generally.
cards.n: Caricature has to start from something real, so the analytic move is naming the trait exaggerated and the judgment it invites.

cards.q: Explain why a writer often subordinates the less important of two ideas rather than presenting them as separate sentences.
cards.a: Subordinating one idea signals to the reader which point is secondary, so the sentence argues for a hierarchy of importance instead of listing facts as equals.
cards.n: A string of equal simple sentences gives a reader no hierarchy, which is how choppy prose can be grammatically flawless and unpersuasive.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'Determined to finish before dark, the crew worked through the storm.'
cards.a: A participial phrase, 'Determined to finish before dark,' opening the sentence and front-loading the crew's motivation before naming their action.
cards.n: Don't confuse this with an absolute phrase; a participial phrase modifies the subject specifically, not the whole clause.

cards.q: Explain the effect of opening a sentence with a participial phrase rather than the subject.
cards.a: It delays the main subject and verb, forcing the reader to hold a condition or motive in mind before learning who acted, which can heighten suspense or foreground cause.
cards.n: The risk is a dangling modifier, since the phrase attaches to whatever subject follows and will attach to the wrong one if you let it.

cards.q: Contrast the rhetorical effect of a single absolute phrase versus a full subordinate clause conveying the same idea.
cards.a: An absolute phrase feels compressed and image-like, almost cinematic, while a subordinate clause with 'because' or 'as' makes the same relationship feel more logically explicit.
cards.n: Both can convey simultaneity or cause, but the absolute phrase reads as more literary and less argumentative.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields.'
cards.a: Anaphora; repeating 'we shall fight' at the start of each clause builds mounting resolve through accumulation.
cards.n: The repeated clause holds still while the place changes, so the sentence enacts the idea that ground may shift and resolve will not.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here.' (Gettysburg Address)
cards.a: Antithesis; contrasting 'say' and 'did' sets empty words against enduring action, undercutting the speech's own occasion to redirect focus to the soldiers.
cards.n: Lincoln's prediction turned out to be wrong, and that irony is standard material for the sophistication point on this speech.

cards.q: Apply an appositive to add a credential to this sentence: 'The engineer warned that the bridge was unsafe.'
cards.a: 'The engineer, a thirty-year veteran of municipal inspections, warned that the bridge was unsafe' - the appositive adds authority without a separate clause.
cards.h: → noun phrase, not a new clause
cards.n: An appositive works here because 'a thirty-year veteran' is a noun phrase, not a full clause with its own verb.

cards.q: Contrast 'which' and 'that' in formal written English.
cards.a: 'That' introduces a restrictive clause essential to identifying the noun and takes no comma; 'which' introduces a nonrestrictive clause adding extra, removable information and is set off by a comma.
cards.h: → essential, no comma vs extra, comma
cards.n: Misusing 'which' for a restrictive clause is one of the most common style errors AP readers notice, even though it rarely triggers a Row B penalty alone.

cards.q: Define a comma splice and give an example.
cards.a: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma with no coordinating conjunction, such as 'The evidence was strong, the jury still hesitated.' It should be a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a conjunction.
cards.h: → two sentences glued by just a comma
cards.n: Comma splices turn up constantly in revision-in-context items, where the credited fix is usually a semicolon or an added conjunction.
x: two sentences joined by only a comma

cards.q: Define a dangling modifier and give an example.
cards.a: A descriptive phrase placed so it appears to modify the wrong word, often because the word it should modify is missing, as in 'Having finished the report, the printer jammed,' where the printer did not finish the report.
cards.h: → modifier with no clear noun to attach to
cards.n: Dangling modifiers are common in rushed timed writing when a sentence gets restructured mid-thought.

cards.q: Contrast 'who' and 'whom' in formal usage.
cards.a: 'Who' is a subject pronoun, used when the pronoun performs the action, as in 'who wrote the letter.' 'Whom' is an object pronoun, used when the pronoun receives the action, as in 'to whom it may concern.'
cards.n: A quick test: if 'he' fits, use 'who'; if 'him' fits, use 'whom.'

cards.q: Define a misplaced modifier and give an example.
cards.a: A descriptive word or phrase positioned too far from the word it modifies, creating an unintended meaning, as in 'She almost drove her kids to school every day,' which suggests she rarely finished the drive rather than that she nearly did it daily.
cards.h: → modifier too far from its target word
cards.n: Reading the sentence and asking what word sits right next to the modifier usually catches the error fast.

cards.q: Explain the parallel structure error in 'The policy will reduce costs, improving morale, and it protects jobs.'
cards.a: The three items in a series should share the same grammatical form; mixing a base verb, a gerund, and a full clause breaks the parallelism. A corrected version reads 'reduce costs, improve morale, and protect jobs.'
cards.h: → match the grammatical form across a series
cards.n: Broken parallelism is easy to miss in a timed essay because each clause sounds fine read alone.

cards.q: Contrast a restrictive and a nonrestrictive clause.
cards.a: A restrictive clause narrows down which specific thing is meant and cannot be removed without changing the sentence's meaning. A nonrestrictive clause adds extra detail that could be deleted without changing which thing is meant.
cards.n: This same essential-vs-extra distinction underlies the which/that rule tested elsewhere in this unit.

cards.q: Explain why subject-verb agreement errors increase when a long prepositional phrase sits between the subject and the verb.
cards.a: A writer's ear tracks the noun closest to the verb rather than the true subject, producing errors like 'The list of items are long,' where 'list,' not 'items,' is the actual subject requiring a singular verb.
cards.h: → nearest noun, not the true subject, misleads the ear
cards.n: Cross out the prepositional phrase and reread what is left, since the sentence usually corrects itself once the noise is gone.

cards.q: Define malapropism and give an example.
cards.a: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one, producing an unintentionally absurd meaning, as in saying someone is 'the pineapple of politeness' instead of 'pinnacle.'
cards.h: → wrong word, similar sound, absurd result
cards.n: A malapropism is an error within the world of the text; authors often put one in a character's mouth on purpose to reveal something about them.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'That lawyer is a real wolf in cheap clothing.'
cards.a: Malapropism - 'cheap' is mistakenly substituted for the similar-sounding 'sheep's,' replacing the intended idiom with an absurd, unintended meaning.
cards.n: Malapropisms are a favorite device for characterizing a pompous or careless speaker in satire.

cards.q: Define bombast and give an example.
cards.a: Pompous, overblown language that is far more elevated or dramatic than its subject deserves, such as calling a minor scheduling conflict 'an unprecedented catastrophe.'
cards.h: → inflated language for a small subject
cards.n: Bombast is a judgment rather than a neutral label, so calling a passage bombastic is already a criticism of the writer.

cards.q: Define vitriol and give an example.
cards.a: Harsh, bitterly critical language meant to wound or condemn, sharper and more personal in its hostility than ordinary criticism, such as branding an opponent's plan 'a con dressed up as compassion.'
cards.n: Vitriol and invective overlap; vitriol emphasizes bitterness, invective emphasizes direct verbal abuse.

cards.q: Define a vignette as a form of evidence in a passage.
cards.a: A brief, vivid scene or descriptive sketch used to illustrate a point through a single concentrated image rather than a fully developed narrative.
cards.h: → short vivid scene, not a full story
cards.n: A vignette differs from an anecdote in scale: an anecdote usually has a beginning, middle, and end; a vignette is closer to one frozen image.

cards.q: Contrast an anecdote and a vignette as forms of evidence.
cards.a: An anecdote is a brief story with a sequence of events leading to a point. A vignette is a single vivid scene or image with little to no narrative sequence, favoring atmosphere over plot.
cards.n: The test is whether anything changes: an anecdote turns on an event, while a vignette holds still and asks to be looked at.

cards.q: Define idiolect in style analysis.
cards.a: The distinctive, individual pattern of word choice, syntax, and speech habits unique to one speaker or writer, as opposed to the shared conventions of a whole dialect or era.
cards.h: → one writer's own signature pattern of language
cards.n: Analyzing a passage's idiolect matters most when a writer's individual voice, not any single device, is what drives the passage's effect.

cards.q: Explain how a sudden shift in register can function as a rhetorical choice within a passage.
cards.a: Dropping from formal, elevated diction into a blunt colloquial phrase, or the reverse, can jolt a reader's attention, signal sincerity breaking through formality, or mark a pivot in the writer's argument.
cards.n: Register shifts are easy to quote and easy to misdate, since a phrase that felt blunt in 1960 can read as neutral to a reader now.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'The White House issued a statement denying the allegations.'
cards.a: Metonymy - 'the White House' substitutes for the president or presidential administration, a closely associated entity standing in for what it represents.
cards.n: Metonymy hides a choice here: naming the building instead of a person spreads responsibility across a whole institution.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'All hands were needed on deck before the storm hit.'
cards.a: Synecdoche - 'hands' stands in for the sailors as whole people, a part representing the whole.
cards.n: Synecdoche also runs the other way, whole for part: 'Germany beat Brazil' puts a nation in place of eleven players. Do not use 'Washington' for the government as the example — that is metonymy, an associated place standing in for an institution, like 'the White House'.

cards.q: Define a maxim and contrast it with an aphorism.
cards.a: A maxim is a short statement of practical wisdom meant as a guide to conduct, such as 'measure twice, cut once.' It differs from an aphorism mainly in emphasis: a maxim gives advice for action, while an aphorism states a general truth.
cards.n: Maxims usually arrive in the imperative, and that grammatical mood is the fastest tell that advice rather than observation is on offer.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'Fortune favors the bold.'
cards.a: An aphorism - a short, memorable statement expressing a general truth in a self-contained sentence.
cards.n: Proverb would also be defensible, since the line is traditional, but aphorism is the safer label for a printed AP passage.

cards.q: State the overall format of the AP English Language and Composition exam.
cards.a: Section I: 45 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes, worth 45% of the score. Section II: three free-response essays in 2 hours 15 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period), worth 55%.
cards.h: → two sections with times and weights
cards.n: Total testing time is 3 hours 15 minutes; the FRQs are worth more than the entire MC section.

cards.q: State what Section I of the AP Lang exam contains.
